units.la: IBELLOS de CRVCE quos scripsi, meritissimo advos defero, patriae nostrae primores viri. Primum, quia in solo vestro concepti natique sunt, in hac Louanienfi vrbe: tum quia aura fauoris vestri elicuit, qui me benigne huc arcessendum putastis, bono rei litterariae & juuentutis. Laudo hunc animum, atque etiam miror. qui in tot circumstantibus turbis, & cum undique insonuit bello-
units.tr: I dedicate these little books on the Cross, which I have written, to you, most deserving men, the leading citizens of our homeland. I do so first because they were conceived and born in your land, in this city of Leuven, and second because the breath of your favour, which judged that I should be summoned here kindly for the good of letters and of the young, has blown them into being. I praise this spirit of yours and indeed I marvel at it, that amid so many surrounding disturbances, and while the trumpet of war sounds on every side, you have not neglected the pipes and flutes of the Muses, so to speak, and the arts of peace, in the midst of arms. That you do this rightly and usefully, prudent men perceive more clearly than the common crowd. For truly, illustrious Orders, these arts are not merely the ornaments of the commonwealth but its aids and props.

units.la: Note: the first word "LIBELLOS" is set with a large historiated woodcut initial "L"; it is read here as IBELLOS with the initial letter as printed. bellorum tuba; tibias tamẽ & fistulas,vt sic dicam, Musarum cogitatis, & pacis artes neglectum non itis inter media arma. Quod recte & vtiliter à vobis fieri, prudentes magis sentiunt quàm vulgus. Nam reuerâ, inclyti Ordines, hæc non ornamenta solùm reip. sunt, sed auxilia & fulcra. Tollite; quid nisi squalor & tenebræ occupant, & ferox quædam, aut vt verius dicam, ferina vita? Ab omni æuo (Annales sacros & profanos cõsulite) Deus exstare artes istas voluit, velut pharos & lucentes quosdam ignes in tempestuoso mari. Istæ pacem dirigunt, bellum dirimunt: istæ vitia virtutésque premunt aut excitant, testes temporum, arbitræ meritorum. Reges, & magna illa nomina, obliuionem æternam iamnunc cogitent, nisi pennatus iste currus euehat, & ostendat per æuum & per gentes. Quid argumenta colligo? vno verbo rem dixi, Deus exstare artes istas voluit: & hoc quoque ab eo, quod vos juuatis. Eat in sæcula, suisse in vnâ prouinciâ per quinque amplius lustra bellum, ídque ciuile, imò intestinum; collapsa tractu, aut dejecta impetu omnia; publicam priuatámque inopiam: vos animo stetisse dites & vberes, & de rebus salutaribus judicásse magis quàm computásse. Enimuerò facite itá Ordines, manum labenti patriæ supponite, nec præsentia solùm in oculis habete, sed sutura. Potens ille Deus viuit, & magnus noster Rex: vterque auxiliabitur, ille & iste in suâ caussâ. Interea CRVCEM accipite, atque etiam ferte. Vt columna, quæ recta stat, impositò magis pondere firmatur: sic altas rectásque mentes oportet, non cedere oneri, sed obniti. Vos per vos facietis, ita vterque ille faueat & auxilietur, quem dixi. Louanij, pridie Nonas Nouemb.
units.tr: Take them away: what else would possess us but squalor and darkness, and a savage, or, to put it more truly, a brutish kind of life? From the beginning of time (consult the sacred and the profane annals) God willed these arts to exist, like lighthouses and bright fires in a stormy sea. They direct peace and dissolve war; they check or rouse vices and virtues, witnesses of the times and judges of merit. Kings and those great names should already be thinking of eternal oblivion, unless this winged chariot carries them aloft and shows them through all ages and nations. Why do I gather arguments? I have said the matter in one word: God willed these arts to exist, and this also from the fact that you support them. Let it go down to posterity that for more than five lustra there was war in one province, and that a civil war, indeed an internal one; everything had collapsed in its course or been cast down by its violence, public and private poverty ensued; yet you stood firm in spirit, rich and fruitful, and judged of salutary matters rather than merely counting costs. Indeed, do this, Orders: support the hand to a falling fatherland, and keep before your eyes not only the present but the future. The mighty God lives, and our great King; both will help, that one and this one, in their own cause. Meanwhile, take up the Cross and bear it too. As a column that stands upright is made firmer by the weight laid upon it, so high and upright minds ought not to yield to a burden but to strive against it. You will do it through yourselves, and may each of those I have named favour and aid you.

units.la: AD LECTOREM.
units.tr: TO THE READER.

units.la: HAbes Lector quæ de Cruce scri-psimus, sed germana. Antea atque alibi quæ edita ( credes hoc nobis) non sunt nostra. Quid ergò? non illa dictauimus? Fortasse. Sed ô imperitiam! quasi edendi illo sine. Reuerentior posteritatis sum: & aliud scio esse Schedia, aliud Opera; nec subitaria hæc nostra dedicanda in Memoriæ templo. Quid, quod alij grauius etiam peccant? qui excipiunt aut intercipiunt dicta aut oratiunculas nostras, & in contumeliam mei divulgant. Aliter non accipio. Aeuum hoc ut multis delictis fibulam, itâ petulantia & licentia laxat: & quod auet procacissimus quisque, id etiam audet. Ego semel & seriò testor, audite qui in Europâ. NIHIL MEVM EST, AVT ERIT, QVOD NON DE AVTOGRAPHO MEO, ET ME VOLENTE, SIT EXPRESSVM. Quicunque aliter, mihi injuriam facit, vobis fucum. Deus bone, hæc monenda publice esse? Ecce in bona opésque externas jus est non vino mihi solùm sed mortuo, & solatium fati est voluntas ultrà fatum: in istis animi & ingenij vere bonis non idem erit? Reprimite Principes qui potestis, & vos lectores quâ potestis: illi punienpuniendo, vos spernendo. Ego praeter testari nihil habeo. & hoc etiam addo, Siquid vsquam praeter religionem morésque veterum, non agnosco: & tibi adhaereo Statu felix Ecclesia, cui totam doctrinam Apostoli Petrus & Paulus cum sanguine suo profuderunt. Haec ex animo scripta, ut in animum demittas, te, per spes tuas & per quidquid carum est, Lector rogo.
units.tr: You have what we have written, but only the genuine part. Earlier and elsewhere, what has been published (you may believe this of us) is not ours. What then? Did I not dictate those things? Perhaps I did. But oh, the inexperience! As if I had allowed them to be published. I have more respect for posterity, and I know that a draft is one thing and a finished work another. These hasty pieces of mine should not be dedicated in the temple of memory. What of the fact that others sin even more seriously, who catch up or intercept my sayings or little speeches and spread them abroad to my disgrace? I cannot accept this otherwise. This age loosens the clasp on many offences in the same way that it loosens wantonness and licence, and whoever is most shameless also dares what he desires. I testify once and for all, and in earnest, to those who are in Europe: NOTHING IS OR WILL BE MINE THAT HAS NOT BEEN PRINTED FROM MY OWN AUTOGRAPH AND WITH MY CONSENT. Whoever does otherwise does me an injury and deceives you. Good God, must these things be warned about in public? Look: over goods and external property the right remains not only to a living man but to a dead one, and the will beyond fate is the solace of fate; will it not be the same in those truly good things of the mind and talent? Princes, restrain this, as you can, and you readers, as you can: they by punishing, you by scorning. Beyond bearing witness I have nothing. I add this too: if I acknowledge anything anywhere beyond the religion and customs of the ancients, I do not. And I cling to you, happy the Church, for whose sake Peter and Paul poured out their whole teaching together with their blood. I have written these things from the heart, so that you may take them to heart; I ask you, reader, by your hopes and by whatever is dear to you.

units.la: IN IVSTI LIPSI V. CL. DE CRVCE LIBRVM, ad Principes Christianos Elegia Ioannis Bochii S. P. Q. Antuerpiensi à Secretis.
units.tr: On the Books of Justus Lipsius, Most Distinguished Man, On the Cross, to the Christian Princes: An Elegy by Johannes Bochius, Secretary to the Senate and People of Antwerp.

units.la: [?]IQVA salutiferi tangit vos gloria signi, Si qua fides, si quis religionis amor; Si meritum Crucis, & studiū vos excitat vllum, Et memores vestri nominis esse iuuat; Christiadum o proceres, positis aduertite mentes Rebus, & hoc vno figite corda libro.
units.tr: Whether the glory of the saving sign touches you, if there is any faith in you, any love of religion; if the worth of the Cross and any zeal for it stir you, and it pleases you to be mindful of your name, O nobles of the Christians, turn your minds to other matters and fix your hearts on this one book.

units.la: Hic decus, & factis seges hic vberrima vestris, Laurus & hic vero Principe digna viret.
units.tr: Here is your glory, here a most abundant harvest of your deeds, and here the laurel flourishes, worthy of a true prince.

units.la: Quâ genus humanum deuicta morte triumphat Arbore, cui nostrae stemma salutis inest.
units.tr: By this tree the human race triumphs over conquered death, the tree in which the emblem of our salvation resides.

units.la: Ipsa Dei pietas ramorum amplexibus haeret, Et riguus Christi sanguine vernat apex.
units.tr: The very piety of God clings to the embrace of its branches, and the crown, watered by the blood of Christ, flourishes.

units.la: De trunco fidei pendent mysteria nostrae, Majestate Deus, corpore verus homo.
units.tr: From the trunk of our faith hang the mysteries: God in majesty, true man in body.

units.la: Radicem cruor innocui purissimus agni, Qui lauat humanae vulnera sortis, alit.
units.tr: The root is nourished by the blood of the innocent Lamb, most pure, who washes away the wounds of human fate.

units.la: O crux, o columen, spes vnica, planta salutis, O lignum aetherij fertile depositi.
units.tr: O cross, O pillar, sole hope, plant of salvation, O wood fertile with the heavenly deposit!

units.la: Noxia prima fuit miseris mortalibus arbor, Damna sed haec medicâ nostra resarcit ope.
units.tr: The first tree was a harmful one for wretched mortals, but this one makes good our losses with its healing power.

units.la: Protulit illa necem, vitam hac, erat illa doloris Mater, at haec plausus, laetitiaeque fuit.
units.tr: That one brought forth death, this one life; that was the mother of sorrow, but this one of applause and joy.

units.la: Perque nefas, vitiumque suo de semine, caelum Clauserat illa, fores hac reserante patent.
units.tr: Through wickedness and sin springing from its seed, that tree had closed heaven; by this one, the gates lie open, unbarred.

units.la: Illam Tænario fallax è gurgite serpens Occupat, impietas, & furor, ira, dolus.
units.tr: The deceitful serpent from the Taenarian abyss seized that tree: impiety, fury, anger, and guile.

units.la: Hanc natus genitore Deo, qui fœderis obses, Lethæo veteres carcere traxit auos.
units.tr: This tree was taken by the Son, God from God, who as hostage of the covenant drew our ancient forefathers out of the Lethean prison.

units.la: Nec voluit seros Erebo parere nepotes, Colla sed excusso libera ferre iugo.
units.tr: Nor did he wish his late descendants to be born to Erebus, but to bear their necks free, the yoke shaken off.

units.la: Victricis vexilla Crucis, credentibus omenExtulit, imperij signa futura sui.
units.tr: He raised the banners of the victorious Cross as an omen for believers, the signs of his future rule.

units.la: Vmbrarum hæc oculis haud aspicit arbiter æquis,Sævit, & auxilijs expedit arma nouis.
units.tr: The judge does not look on the shades with an even eye; he rages and prepares his arms with new aids.

units.la: In Crucis excidium Latias aptare securesApparat, & dominæ concitat urbis opem.
units.tr: For the destruction of the Cross he prepares to fit Latin axes, and he rouses the aid of the mistress city.

units.la: Primáque Cæsareus tentauit verbera lictorIncassum, & rabie proficiente nihil.
units.tr: And first the Caesarean lictor tried his blows in vain, and with his rage growing, achieved nothing.

units.la: Nam lignum Crucis ad quosvis obduruit ictus, Statúque magis, quanto cædituc illa magis.
units.tr: For the wood of the Cross hardened against every blow, and stood the firmer the more it was struck.

units.la: Christiadûmque fides numerum cruciatibus auget,Et Crucis imperium crescere pœna facit.
units.tr: And the faith of the Christians grows in number through torments, and punishment makes the empire of the Cross increase.

units.la: Crux vicit crucis artifices, tormenta propago,Vnus & innumeros Christus in orbe Deos.
units.tr: The Cross conquered the makers of crosses, the tortures were their offspring, and the one Christ conquered the countless gods in the world.

units.la: Non tamen antiquus furiarum in sede quiescitHostis, at indicto prælia Marte ciet.
units.tr: Yet the ancient enemy does not rest in the seat of the Furies, but stirs up battle with war declared.

units.la: Omnia conquirit pœnarum inuenta, tyrannos,Monstra, faces, laqueos, slagra, metalla, feras.
units.tr: He searches out every invention of punishment: tyrants, monsters, torches, nooses, whips, metals, and wild beasts.

units.la: Donec Romuleos Christi victoria fascesSubdidit, & victo Cæsare iura dedit.
units.tr: Until Christ's victory subdued the Roman fasces, and Caesar, conquered, surrendered his rights.

units.la: Hinc aquilæ cessêre Cruci, vastumque per orbemCrux fuit augustis gloria prima viris.
units.tr: Hence the eagles yielded to the Cross, and across the vast world the Cross was the first glory of the august men.

units.la: Vt quoties fera barbaries, aut nominis hostisChristiadûm, sacræ mouerit arma Cruci,
units.tr: Whenever savage barbarism, or the enemy of the Christian name, has stirred arms against the sacred Cross,

units.la: Arsacides, vel mollis Arabs, Macedûmque phalanges,Pontus, & Ismarij Luna superba dacis;
units.tr: whether the Arsacids, or the soft Arab, or the phalanxes of Macedon, or Pontus, or the proud moon of the Dacians,

units.la: Aut Scytha, vel Garamas, mediis vel Syrtibus Ammen, Errorum aut furiis gens agitata nouis,
units.tr: or the Scythian, or the Garamantes, or Ammon amid the Syrtes, or a people driven mad by new furies of error,

units.la: Protinus intrepidis animis, armisque paratis,Sancta salutifera pro Cruce turba stetit.
units.tr: at once, with fearless spirits and arms ready, the holy and saving throng has stood for the Cross.

units.la: Nunc idem, & rabie nunc imminet hostis eadem,
units.tr: Now the same enemy threatens again with the same rage,

units.la: O proceres, eadem caussa tuenda Crucis.
units.tr: O nobles, the same cause of the Cross must be defended.

units.la: Iungite communes fata in communia dextras,
units.tr: Join your right hands, turning your separate fates into common fates,

units.la: Ne pereant omnes, dum sibi quisque cauet.
units.tr: Lest all perish while each takes care only for himself.

units.la: Crux acies volet in medias, hoc vincite signo,
units.tr: The Cross will fly into the midst of the battle; conquer under this sign,

units.la: Cui didicit famulas mors dare victa manus.
units.tr: To which death, conquered, has learned to give its servile hands.

units.la: Quod stygij tremuere lacus, quod mundus, & hostis
units.tr: At which the Stygian lakes trembled, at which the world and the enemy

units.la: Quo viso, trepida perdidit arma fuga.
units.tr: at its sight, lost their arms in trembling flight.

units.la: Haec monet antiqui scrutator Lipsius aevi,
units.tr: This is what Lipsius, searcher of the ancient age, admonishes,

units.la: Et stimulos scriptis subdit ad arma suis.
units.tr: and adds spurs to his writings for taking up arms.

units.la: Vile crucis quondam leti genus eruit umbris,
units.tr: He has rescued from the shades the vile kind of death of the cross,

units.la: Poenaque supplicij quanta, quibusque fuit.
units.tr: and how great the punishment of execution was, and for whom.

units.la: Exemploque docet, tantum si dedecus insons
units.tr: And by example he teaches that if an innocent man bore such shame of death,

units.la: Mortis, ob humani criminis acta tulit;
units.tr: for deeds of human crime;

units.la: Si Deus esse reus voluit, culpamque piauit,
units.tr: if God willed to be the accused and atoned for the guilt,

units.la: Deleuitque necem morte, cruore nefas;
units.tr: and wiped out death by death, and sin by blood;

units.la: Hortari benefacta Crucis vos stringere ferrum
units.tr: then he urges you to draw the sword for the good deeds of the Cross,

units.la: Pro Cruce, coniunctas sumere tela manus.
units.tr: and to take up weapons with joined hands for the Cross.

units.la: Hoc vos sancta fides (nam defensoribus istis
units.tr: This holy faith asks you this (for such defenders

units.la: Tempus eget) pietas, officiumque rogant.
units.tr: the time requires), and piety and duty ask it too.

units.la: Arma dabunt superi victricia, tessera Christus,
units.tr: The gods above will give victorious arms, Christ the watchword,

units.la: Crux signum, noster buccina Iustus erit.
units.tr: the Cross the sign, and our trumpet will be Justus.

units.la: DE IVSTI LIPSI LIBRIS DE CRVCE, MICHAELIS VANDER-HAGEN ANTVERPIENSIS Ad Lectorem Epigramma.
units.tr: On the Books on the Cross by Justus Lipsius: An Epigram by Michael Vander-Hagen of Antwerp, to the Reader

units.la: SI te prisca iuuant: hoc, docti, DE CRVCE, LIPSI, Ingentis plenum, volue, laboris opus. Supplicium Crucis ille vetus describit ad vnguem, Quale fuit, nostram SALVIFICAMQVE CRVCEM: In qua hominum lapsus, scelerumque Piator, atrocem Mortem, insons, multo sanguine passus erat. Vnde noua extinctis lux extitit, vnde sepultis Vita oriens, rutilam sustulit alta facem. Vnde redemptio & alma reconciliatio manant: Vnde perennantis flumina pacis eunt. Ista vetustatis referat penetralia, Lector, Vtere eo, & quantus, disce, vir ille fiet.
units.tr: If ancient things delight you, learned reader, take up this work of great labour, Lipsius's On the Cross. He describes with precision that ancient punishment of the cross, what it was like, and our cross, the saving cross, on which the Expiator of human falls and crimes, though innocent, suffered a dreadful death with much blood. From it a new light arose for the dead, and from it life, rising for the buried, lifted its bright torch on high. From it flow redemption and gracious reconciliation; from it the rivers of lasting peace run. Reader, let him unfold the inner secrets of that ancient world. Make use of it, and learn what a great man he will become.

units.la: IN CLAR. V- IRI IVSTI LIPSI DE CRVCE LIBROS.
units.tr: TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS MAN JUSTUS LIPSIUS, ON HIS THREE BOOKS ON THE CROSS.

units.la: LIpsi, Palladis decus corona,
units.tr: Lipsius, crown and glory of Pallas,

units.la: Lipsi, delicium nouem Sororum,
units.tr: Lipsius, darling of the nine Sisters,

units.la: Quo nec est melior benigniórque:
units.tr: than whom none is better or kinder:

units.la: Iam loquax nimium, nec æqua lingua,
units.tr: Let no tongue, too garrulous and unfair,

units.la: Quæ, vah, artibus abrogare sanctam
units.tr: that is wont, alas, to rob holy

units.la: Virtutem solet ac politiori
units.tr: virtue of its arts and of refined

units.la: Doctrina, reprimetur illa, nam tu,
units.tr: learning, be silenced, for you,

units.la: Qui doctissimus unus es virorum,
units.tr: who alone are the most learned of men,

units.la: Unus es simul optimus virorum. Est cura pietas, & ipsa virtus,
units.tr: are also alone the best of men. Piety is a care, and virtue itself,

units.la: Hac doctrina velut politur auro.
units.tr: is polished by this learning as if with gold.

units.la: Testes DE CRVCE sunto tres Libelli
units.tr: Witnesses ON THE CROSS let be three books

units.la: Docti, Jupiter! & pij libelli.
units.tr: learned, by Jupiter, and pious books.

units.la: Conjunctam, bone lector, hic videre
units.tr: Here, kind reader, you may see

units.la: Virtutem licet eruditioni.
units.tr: virtue joined with learning.

units.la: Commissa Crux quid nobis sit? exemplis testibusque allerta, tum etiam vestigio nostræ linguæ. Cap. VIII. sol. 15.
units.tr: What is the cross, committed to us? Be warned by examples and witnesses, and also by the trace of our own language. Chap. VIII, p. 15.

units.la: Affirmata Crux Immissa è scriptis maximè Patrum: ipsi alij per alios, & imaginibus per nos etiam, explicati. Cap. IX. sol. 17.
units.tr: The cross affirmed as fixed upright (Crux Immissa), explained mainly from the writings of the Fathers, both by others and, through the pictures, by us as well. Chap. IX, p. 17.

units.la: In quâ Crucium formâ Christus mortem tulerit? videri in ultimâ, argumento è Patribus & picturis. Ruffini non bona fides notata in verbis Pauli citandis sive explicandis. Cap. X. fo. 22.
units.tr: In what shape did Christ bear his death? To be seen in the last chapter, by argument from the Fathers and from pictures. The bad faith of Ruffinus noted in citing and explaining the words of Paul. Chap. X, fol. 22.

units.la: Apud plerasque gentium Cruces ferè visitatas. Apud Syros, Iudæos, Ægyptios, Persas, Afros, Græcos, maximè Romanos. Quando apud eos cœperit? An & apud Germanos? Cap. XI. folio 24.
units.tr: The crosses in use among most peoples: among the Syrians, Jews, Egyptians, Persians, Africans, Greeks, and especially the Romans. When did they begin among them? And among the Germans as well? Chap. XI, fol. 24.

units.la: Apud Romanos vile fuisse hoc supplicium, & plurimùm seruorum. Quas ob causas ij affecti. Cap. XII. sol. 26.
units.tr: Among the Romans this punishment was cheap, and was applied mostly to slaves. For what causes were these people so punished? Chap. XII, p. 26.

units.la: Etiam liberi quidam in crucem dati, sed viliores aut nocentiores: ut Latrones, Sicarij, Falsarij, atque alibi & Fures. Cap. XIII. folio 29.
units.tr: Some free men too were given to the cross, but those of lower rank or greater guilt: such as robbers, assassins, forgers, and elsewhere also thieves. Chap. XIII, fol. 29.

units.la: Quæ causa falsò assignata in Cruce Christi? videri Innouationem & Seditionem esse. Cap. XIIII. sol. 30.
units.tr: What cause was falsely assigned for the cross of Christ? To be seen as innovation and sedition. Chap. XIV, p. 30.

units.la: Crux interdum liberè & laxè vagata: in hostes, in seditiosos, In Christianos, in fæminas denique. Cap. XV. sol. 31.
units.tr: The cross sometimes wandered freely and loosely: against enemies, against seditious persons, against Christians, and finally against women. Chap. XV, p. 31.

units.la: LIBRI SECVNDI,
units.tr: BOOK TWO

units.la: Transitio ad Modum figendi præmissum de atrocitate hujus
units.tr: A transition to the mode of fastening mentioned before, concerning the atrocity of this punishment, which is called the Highest and Extreme. Chapter 1, page 33.

units.la: supplicij, quod Summum & Extremum dictum. Cap. i. sol.33.
units.tr: There are two modes of fastening, the common and the rare. In the former, flogging always went before. Chapter 2, page 34.

units.la: Duplex figendi Modus, Vulgaris & Rarus. In illo Flagellatio ex
units.tr: Two ways of fixing to the cross: the common and the rare. In the former, flogging always came first.

units.la: more semper anteiuit. Cap. ii. sol. 34.
units.tr: As was the custom. Chap. ii, p. 34.

units.la: Flagellorum & Virgarum discrimen. Illa magis vilia, & magis
units.tr: The difference between scourges and rods: the former were baser, and the latter more cruel.

units.la: acerba esse. solere & talis asperari. Cap. iii. sol. 35.
units.tr: They were usually made harsher in this way. Chap. iii, p. 35.
