units.la: IVSTI
units.tr: JUSTUS LIPSIUS

units.la: IVSTI LIPSI DE CRVCE LIBRI I. CAP. I.
units.tr: Justus Lipsius, On the Cross, Book I, Chapter I.

units.la: Precatiuncula. Materies & ordo operis.
units.tr: A short prayer. The subject matter and plan of the work.

units.la: AGGREDIOR de CRVCE scribere, sed tuam prius opem auxiliumque inuocans qui eam consecrasti, & infame illud lignum instrumentum fecisti publicæ salutis. Tu Deus à Deo genite, homo ex homine genite, hominibus genite, da mihi vera, da recta scribere, tibi in honorem, Cruci in splendorem, nobis in fructum. Materies & ordo mei operis iste. Quid Crux, & Cuiusmodi fuerit: Vbi, Quare, Quomodo, & Quatenus vsurpata. Hæc omnia non distincte solùm, sed diffusè dicam: nec displicebit accuratio illi, cui salutare hoc signum placebit.
units.tr: I am about to write about the CROSS, but first I call upon your help and aid, you who consecrated it and made that infamous wood the instrument of public salvation. You, God begotten of God, man begotten of man, begotten for men, grant me to write what is true and right: to you for honour, to the Cross for splendour, to us for profit. This is the subject matter and plan of my work: what the Cross is and what kind of thing it was; where, why, how, and how far it has been used. I shall say all of this not only distinctly but at length, and the careful detail will not displease anyone to whom this saving sign is dear.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Crucis nomen polysemon. Hæc nostra Gabalus etiam dicta, item Infelix lignum, & Infame. Sed & Crux non in ligno.
units.tr: The name Crux has several meanings. This thing is also called Gabalus, and Unlucky Wood, and Infamous. But a cross is not always made of wood.

units.la: CRVX significatione duplici, Laxâ & Adstrictâ. Illa est, cùm pro omni angore, tormento, atque etiam interitu sumunt. vt Comici passim, qui Abire jubent in malam Crucem: vt Gracchus, qui dixit (alio etiam genere) Malo Cruce perire: vt Plautus de homine merso aquis, Abstractum in maximam malam Crucem. Sed & Terentius à cruciando, Meretrices dixit Cruces: nec dissimiliter Plautus, Aliqua mala Crux semper est, quæ aliquid petat. Paullo diuersius illud ejusdem: Quæ te mala Crux agitat? quod adfine istis, Quæ laruæ, aut quæ intemperiæ? At Adstricta significatio est hæc mea, & vulgo receptissima, cùm peculiariter cruciatum & interitum notamus in ligno. Quid ita? credo, quia eximius ille, mors tarda & plane cum sensu. Dixerunt & alio nomine Gabalum. Nonius ex Varrone citat: Nos barbari quòd nocentes in gabalum suffigimus homines, vos non barbari noxios absoluitis. Quæ vox etiam in prisci s Glossis, sed vocali media mutante: Gabulum, Βάσανος. explicatúque laxè, vt vides, & pro quocunque tormento. Dixerunt aliter, Infelicem arborem, lignum, stipitem. In carmine horrendo apud Liuium: Caput obnubito, arbori infelici suspensuspendito. De Cruce accipi res docet, & Cicero, qui in eâ pro Rabirio palàm sic interpretatur. & Seneca: Inuenitur qui velit adactus ad infelix illud lignum trahere animam tot tormenta tracturam.
units.tr: The word Crux has two senses, a loose one and a strict one. In the loose sense it means any anguish, torment, or even destruction, as the comic writers everywhere bid someone go "to the bad cross" (in malam Crucem). So Gracchus said "to perish by a bad cross" (in another construction), and Plautus of a man dunked in water says "dragged off to the greatest bad cross." Terence also called prostitutes "crosses," from the torment they cause, and Plautus, not very differently, says "there is always some bad cross that seeks something." That same writer's "What bad cross is driving you?" is a little different, but close to "What ghosts, or what fits of madness?" The strict sense, which is mine here and the most widely accepted, is used when we specifically mean torture and death on a wooden post. Why so? I think because that is the distinctive kind of death: slow, and fully felt. They also called it by another name, Gabalus. Nonius cites Varro: "We barbarians fix guilty men on a gabalus, but you non-barbarians let the guilty go free." The word also appears in old glossaries, with the middle vowel changed: "Gabulum, torture." It is explained loosely, as you see, as any kind of torment. They also said "unlucky tree," "wood," or "stake." In a dreadful song in Livy: "Cover his head, hang him from the unlucky tree." The context shows this refers to the cross, and Cicero, who in his speech for Rabirius plainly interprets it so, agrees. So does Seneca: "There is someone who would be willing, once driven to that unlucky wood, to draw out a breath that must endure so many torments."

units.la: Minutius Felix: Deus ligneus, rogi fortasse vel infelicis stipitis portio: id est, crucis. Dixit & Infamem Poëta incertus
units.tr: Minucius Felix: "A wooden god, perhaps a part of a funeral pyre or of an unlucky post," that is, of the cross. An unknown poet also called it "Infamous":

units.la: Noxius infami districtus stipite membra, Sperat & à fixâ posse redire Cruce.
units.tr: "The guilty man, bound with limbs on an infamous post, hopes he may return from the fixed cross."

units.la: Natæ appellationes à judicio & sensu vulgi, quibus hoc supplicium in horrore pariter & vilitate. Itaque Apuleius (in meo quidem & prisco libro) Damnatam Crucem dixit. *Damnata, inquit, jam Crucis candidatus: bene, & pro hoc sensu. Etsi autem Crux proprie in ligno: tamen adnoto, similitudine etiam itâ dictam suspensionem aut fixionem in aliâ paratura, puta in monte aut petrâ. Sic Tertulliano sunt Cruces Caucasorum, alludenti ad Promethea illic affixum: quem ipsum Lucianus describit & appellat σαυρωθέντα. Sic & Manilius de Andromedâ, quæ in scopulo vincta & ceto exposita: Et cruce virgine à moritura puella pependit.
units.tr: These names arise from the judgment and feeling of the common people, by which this punishment is marked both with horror and with contempt. So Apuleius (in my own copy, and in an older one) called it "the damned cross": "Already a candidate for the damned cross," which fits this sense well. Yet although a cross is properly of wood, I note that by similarity the suspension or fixing on some other frame, say on a mountain or a rock, is also called so. Thus Tertullian has "the crosses of the Caucasus," alluding to Prometheus fixed there, whom Lucian himself describes and calls "crucified." Likewise Manilius of Andromeda, who was bound to a rock and exposed to a sea monster: "She hung on a virgin cross, a girl about to die."

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Nomina phrasesque ad hoc supplicium: Figere, Configere, Cruciare. item Cruciarius, pro appendendo.
units.tr: Names and phrases for this punishment: figere, configere, cruciare. Also cruciarius, in the sense of one to be hanged.

units.la: CRVCIS hæc nomina: supplicij quod per eam, ista. Cruci suffigere. vt Velleius de piratis, quos Cæsar, inquit, Cruci suffixit. In cruce suf-figere.
units.tr: These are the names for the cross and for the punishment carried out upon it: Cruci suffigere, as Velleius says of pirates, whom Caesar, he says, fixed to a cross. In cruce suffigere.

units.la: *Vulgo destinata.
units.tr: *Commonly so designated.

units.la: Cruces in petra. figere. vt Hirtius. Juba Numidas eos, qui loco amisso fugâ se receperant, in cruce omnes suffixit. Item Cruci affigere, & Cruci figere, crebra in libris. Illud minùs, Figere απλώς & sine additione. Tertullianus sic vtitur: Taceo quod figitur (Christus:) in hoc enim venerat. Quod idem Configere Paulinus Nolanus Episcopus dixit:
units.tr: Crosses on a rock: figere, as Hirtius says: Juba fixed all the Numidians who had fled to safety after losing their position, on a cross. Likewise cruci affigere and cruci figere are common in the books. Less common is figere [ἀπλῶς] used absolutely and without addition. Tertullian uses it thus: I say nothing of how he was fixed (Christ), for he had come for this. The Bishop Paulinus of Nola used configere in the same way:

units.la: Agnoscant trepidi, quem confixêre rebelles. de Christo ad iudicium venturo. Etsi Tertullianus paullo aliter, veterem hominem confixum esse Christo dicit: quod vulgò, vna crucifixum. Suo etiam & proprio verbo appellarunt Cruciare. Ausonius: Cruciauerat illic Spreta olim, memore Veneris, Proserpina Adonim.
units.tr: Let the trembling recognize him whom the rebels fixed to the cross, speaking of Christ who will come to judgment. Tertullian, though, says in a slightly different way that the old man was fixed with Christ, which is commonly rendered crucified together with him. They also used a word of their own, cruciare. Ausonius: There Proserpina, once scorned and mindful of Venus, had tortured Adonis.

units.la: Hegesippus: Capiebantur innumeri (Iudæi,) quingenti ferme ad diem cruciabantur. quod est in crucem agebantur: atque Iosephus in istâ ipsâ re dixerat, ἀνεσαυροδυντος. Paulinus:
units.tr: Hegesippus: Countless Jews were taken, about five hundred, and were tortured daily, that is, were led to the cross. Josephus, in this very matter, had said anesaurodyntos [ἀνεσαυροδυντος]. Paulinus:

units.la: Cruciatâ in carne coruscum Agnoscant trepidi.
units.tr: The trembling recognize the glittering one in his tortured flesh.

units.la: Glossæ veteres: Cruciat, crucificat, σταυροῖ. Ita & Cruciarius dictus, is qui in cruce, vel qui eâ dignus. In ipsâ, vt Petronius: Cruciarij vnius parentes vt viderunt, noctu laxatam custodiam, detraxêre pendentem. Et in Declamationibus Calpurnij Flacci inscriptio: Pædagogus cruciarius, & Peregrinus cruciarius. de his qui appensi iam in cruce. At qui eâ digni, per conuicium aut minas quoque sic nominati. Isidorus: Cruciarius, eo quòd sit cruce dignus.
units.tr: The old glosses: cruciat, crucificat [σταυροῖ]. So too cruciarius is used of one who is on the cross, or who deserves it. Of one actually on it, as in Petronius: When the parents of one crucified man saw that the guard had been loosened at night, they took him down while he was hanging. And in the declamations of Calpurnius Flaccus there are the titles Pedagogue cruciarius and Foreigner cruciarius, referring to those already hanging on the cross. But those who merely deserve it are so named by way of insult or threat too. Isidore: Cruciarius, because he is worthy of the cross.

units.la: Ita eadem: Crucifixi, catus. Crucia-rius, ό σαυρώτης. gnus. Apuleius: Nec tantillum cruciarius ille deterritus. Ammianus: Longum est, quæ cruciarius ille conflauit.
units.tr: So the same glosses: crucifixus, ...; cruciarius [ὁ σταυρώτης], the crucifier. Apuleius: That cruciarius was not in the least daunted. Ammianus: It would be long to tell what that cruciarius contrived.

units.la: CAP. IIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 4.

units.la: Græcorum verba ad Crucem & crucifixionem. Hesychius & Ouidius emendati, iste etiam explicatus.
units.tr: Greek words for the Cross and crucifixion. Hesychius and Ovid corrected, and this passage also explained.

units.la: ISTA Latinis: Græcis duo ferè Crucis nomina, Σταυρὸς & Σκόλοψ. Illud frequentius: quod tamen proprie non nisi stipitem signat singularem & erectum. Latinè dixeris Palum siue Vallum. Eustathius: Σταυροὶ, ὀρθὰ καὶ ἀπωξυμμένα ξύλα· τὰ ὲς σκιάεσα ὥσπερ τοῖς μὴ λαλοῦσιν ἀγχωμὸς· γλῶσσ̈ ὴ ὥσπερ ... τῶν εἰς ἀέρα σαίνουσι ... εἰς βύρος ἵσαται. ἡ αὐτὴ Σκόλοπες λέγουσι: Stauri sunt ligna recta & pracuta: quæ & Stauara dicuntur ab ijs qui minùs ingenuè loquuntur. facta vox, vel quod ad aërem stent, vel quod in latum. Hi ipsi & Scolopes dicuntur. Quod ait, εἰς βύρος vel in latum, de pluribus iunctis verum est, vt solet in castrorum vallo. Neque immuto; etsi ex Hesychio paullo aliter deriuante, posim. Ille sic: Σταυροὶ, ὡ καταπεπηγότες σκολοπες, χαλκηκες, καὶ πωῦλα τὰ ἑσθία ξύλα. Ἀπὸ ἐσαναι σαυροὶ, ἡ ἐν ἐ εἰς τὸ ἀέρα ἵσαται: Stauri, defixi stipites sunt, valli, & omnia ligna recta stantia: ab eo quòd stent Stauri, vel quod ad auram consistant. Allusisse ad postremum hoc etymon Prudentius videatur. —Crux istum tollat in auras
units.tr: THESE are the Latin points. The Greeks have two main words for the Cross, Σταυρὸς and Σκόλοψ. The first is more common, though properly it denotes only a single upright stake. In Latin you may say palus or vallum. Eustathius: "Stauroi are upright and pointed pieces of wood, which some call ... as those who speak less elegantly do; the word was made either because they stand up against the air, or because they stand in a row [εἰς βύρος]." The same are called Skolopes. Stauri are straight and sharp pieces of wood, which are also called stauara by those who speak less elegantly. The word is formed either because they stand toward the air, or because they stand in a row. These same are also called scolopes. What he says, that they stand in a row or in latum, is true of several stakes joined together, as is usual in the rampart of a camp. I do not alter the text, although I could derive it a little differently from Hesychius. He writes: "Stauroi are fixed stakes, palisades, bronze-tipped, and all upright standing wood. They are named from standing [ἀπὸ ἐσαναι], as stauroi, or because they stand upright in the air." Stauri are fixed stakes, ramparts, and all straight standing wood: named from their standing, stauri, or because they stand firm in the air. Prudentius seems to have alluded to this last etymology: —Let the cross raise him into the breezes,

units.la: Viuentesq; oculos offerat alitibus.
units.tr: And offer his living eyes to the birds.

units.la: Hæc Grammatici. sed Lucianus ingeniosè & pro argumento, in Iudicio vocalium, deriuat à Tau litterâ, quæ figurâ crucem refert. Ait Ἀπὸ τοῦ (ξ̄ Ταῦ) καὶ τὰ τεχνήματα τῶ ποιηρῶ τῶν πονηρῶν ἐπωνυμίᾳ ζωνελθεῖν: ab ista etiam, instrumento pessimo (cruci) pessimum nomen venisse. Atque hoc in fine etiam dialogi iterat. Iam Σκόλοψ proprie, vallum, sudemque significat acutam. Hesychius: Σκόλοπες, ὀξέα ξύλα ὀρθά: Scolopes, acuta ligna, recta. Homerus: ——Σκόλοπες γὰρ ἐν αὐτῇ [τάφρῳ] Ὀξέες ἑστᾶσιν.
units.tr: These are the grammarians' views. But Lucian, cleverly and to suit his purpose in the Judgment of the Vowels, derives the word from the letter Tau, which in shape represents a cross. He says: "From the Tau [ταῦ] and the contrivances of the wicked man, the worst name came to the worst instrument." From this also, the worst instrument (the cross) received the worst name. He repeats this at the end of the dialogue as well. Now Σκόλοψ properly means a stake, a palisade, and a sharp pointed post. Hesychius: Skolopes, sharp upright pieces of wood: scolopes, sharp, straight wood. Homer: "For sharp stakes stand in it [the trench]."

units.la: Ibi Eustathius: Σκόλοπες, ὀρθὰ ξύλα καὶ ὀξέα, ἃ καὶ σαυρὸς ἐκάλουν· ἐφ᾽ ὣς ἀνεσταυρώθη καὶ ἀνεσκολοπίσθη ἐλέγοντο: Scolopes recta ligna et acuta, quae et Stauros vocabant: in quibus appensi, cruci aut vallo figi dicebantur. Et bene, quod duo illa verba suggerit, quibus ipsam crucifixionem signabant, Ἀνασταυρoῦν & Ἀνασκολοπίζειν. Ita enim plerumque composite, ad elationem scilicet fixionemque in alto notandam: etsi alias etiam simpliciter, Σταυροῦν & Σκολοπίζειν. Sunt & alia duo verba, quibus vulgò valdè vsi, Προσπηλοῦν & Κρεμάννυμι siue Ἀνακρεμάννυμι. quorum illud clauarionem ipsam in ligno proprie notat, hoc suspensionem. In illo, scriptoris aliquis error videtur apud Hesychium: Προσπήλω, ἀνέσρω. atque ego rescribam, ἀνεσταύρω. In isto, saepe interpretum, qui ad suspensionem vulgarem & in laqueo aptant. Ita quod
units.tr: There Eustathius says: Skolopes are straight and sharp pieces of wood, which were also called stauroi. Those on which people were hung were said to be crucified and impaled: scolopes are straight and sharp pieces of wood, which were called stauroi; those on which men were hung were said to be fixed to a cross or a rampart. He rightly points out the two verbs by which they designated crucifixion itself, anastaurousthai [ἀνασταυρoῦν] and anaskolopizein [ἀνασκολοπίζειν]. These are usually compounds, to mark the raising and fixing on high; though elsewhere they are also used simply, staurousthai [Σταυροῦν] and skolopizein [Σκολοπίζειν]. There are also two other verbs, which the common people used a great deal: prospēloun [Προσπηλοῦν] and kremannymi or anakremannymi [Κρεμάννυμι, Ἀνακρεμάννυμι]. The first properly denotes the driving of the nail into the wood, the second the hanging up. In the first, there seems to be a copyist's error in Hesychius: "Prospēlō, anestrō." I would rewrite it as anestaurō [ἀνεσταύρω]. In the second, interpreters often apply it to the ordinary hanging by a noose.

units.la: Hesychius correctus.
units.tr: Hesychius corrected.

units.la: quod Arrianus narrat de Muficano: τὸν τρεμαίσαυ Αλέξανδρος κελεύει ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ γῇ: aliter versum legi, cùm sic debuerit: Hunc Alexander crucifigi in suapte regione iubet. Curtius satis praeit, qui scribit in crucem sublatum. Ità quod Diodorus Siculus in ejusdem Alexandri rebus, de Tyro captâ: ὧν ὃ νέους πάντας, οὓς ὡς ἐλάττους τῶν διςχιλίων, ἐκρέμασεν: idem Curtius rectè: Duo millia crucibus affixa, per ingens litoris spatium pependerunt. Et exempla pluscula. Tale apud Latinos ipsum Suspendere, quod ad Crucem referendum moneo iuuentutem. Vt in Silio:
units.tr: As for what Arrian tells of Mausicanus: Alexander orders him to be hanged [τὸν ... Αλέξανδρος κελεύει ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ γῇ]. I read the verse otherwise, though it ought to have been: Alexander orders him crucified in his own land. Curtius, who writes lifted up onto the cross, is sufficiently clear. Likewise Diodorus Siculus, in his account of the same Alexander, on the capture of Tyre: he hanged all the young men, as they were fewer than two thousand. Curtius rightly: Two thousand, fixed to crosses, hung over a vast stretch of the shore. There are many more examples. So among the Latins the very word suspendere, which I advise young readers to refer to the Cross. As in Silius:

units.la: Hunc postquam diro suspensum robore vidit.
units.tr: When he saw him hung on the cruel oak.

units.la: In Senecâ: Latrocinium fecit aliquis. quid ergo meruit? ut suspendatur. in Ouidio:
units.tr: In Seneca: "Someone committed robbery. What then has he deserved? That he be hanged."

units.la: More vel intereas capti suspensus Achai,
units.tr: In Ovid:

units.la: Qui miser aurifera teste pependit aquâ.
units.tr: "Or like the Achaean, held captive and hanged, who wretchedly hung by the gold-bearing water."

units.la: Quibus versibus vera historia & sensus è Polybio reddatur iste. Antiochus rex per fraudē Achæum ex arce Sardium deduxit, & per insidias cepit. Καὶ ἔδωξε, addit, πρῶτον μὲν ἀνεωπεμάσαυ τὸν Ταλαίπωρον, μὴ ὃ ταῦτα τῷ κεφαλῇ ἀποτεμόντας αὐτὸς, καταρρίψαντας ἐς ὄνειον ἅπαν, ἀνασαυρῶσαι τὸ σῶμα: Et visum est, primo admutilare illum miserum & extremas partes succidere, deinde capite ejus resecto & in asininum culleum conjecto, reliquum corpus crucifigere. Hæc res: sperne aliorum inanes logos. Sed & mecum lege, teste pependit aqua: non triste aut reste, quod vulgatur. Vult enim, eum non in ipsâ aurifera aquâ, id est Pactolo, suspensum: quî potuit? sed juxta eam, atque illâ quasi arbitrâ & inspectante. Pactolus autem haud longè Sardes, vbi hæc gesta.
units.tr: These verses express the true story and meaning from Polybius. King Antiochus, by trickery, led Achaeus down from the citadel of Sardis and seized him by ambush. "And it seemed best," he adds, "first to mutilate that wretch, cutting off his extremities, then, after cutting off his head and throwing it into a donkey's skin, to crucify the rest of the body" [ἀνασταυρῶσαι τὸ σῶμα]. And it seemed best, first to mutilate that wretch and cut off his extremities, then, with the head removed and cast into an ass's hide, to crucify the rest of the body. That is the account; disregard the empty tales of others. Read also with me teste pependit aqua, not triste or reste, as is commonly printed. For he means that he was hung not in the golden water itself, that is the Pactolus, but near it, with the river as it were a witness and onlooker. The Pactolus is not far from Sardis, where these things were done.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Diuisio prima Crucium: & de specie vetustissimâ dictum, Affixione. Tertullianus per occasionem correctus, atq; Ipsis eadem cum Cerere existimata.
units.tr: The first division of crosses; and of the most ancient form, the affixion. Tertullian, corrected in passing, and his Ceres thought to be the same as Isis.

units.la: VERBA non vltrà me tenent: rem ordiamur. cui illustrandæ duplex genus Crucium statuo, Simplex & Compactum. Illud voco, cùm in uno simplicique, ligno fit affixio, aut infixio. Quæ crux, meo judicio, prima fuit, & in aliam speciem à rudi hac ventum. Sed ea quoque duplex, vt tetigi: altera ad Affixionem, altera ad Infixionem. Nam alias ad arborem siue stipitem alligabant figebantue hominem. vt in Cupidine crucifixo Ausonij, quem sic describit: Eligitur macto myrtus notissima luco, Inuidiosa Deum poenis. Cruciauerat illic Spreta olim, memorem Veneris, Proserpina Adonim. Hujus in excelso suspensum stipite Amorem, Deuinctum post terga manus, substrictaq; plantis Vincula moerentem, nullo moderamine poenae Adfigunt.
units.tr: Words no longer hold me; let us get to the matter. To illustrate it I lay down a twofold kind of cross: Simple and Compound. I call the first that in which the affixion or infixion is made on one simple piece of wood. In my judgement this was the first cross, and from this rough form we came to another. But this too is twofold, as I have touched on: one is by affixion, the other by infixion. For they sometimes tied a man to a tree or a stake, or fastened him to it, as in Ausonius's Cupid Crucified, which he describes thus: "The myrtle, best known of all, is chosen from the sacred grove, hateful to the gods for its punishments. There Proserpina, once scorned, mindful of Venus, had tormented Adonis. On the high trunk of this myrtle they fix Love, bound with his hands behind his back and his feet bound with cords, grieving, with no measure of punishment."

units.la: Verba omnia nota: videbis & in arboris stipite appensum, nec manibus expansis, sed a tergo deuinctis, denique nec clauis sed funibus substri-ctum. Simile in Tertulliano, de Tiberio: qui Saturni sacerdotes, vt inquit, in eisdem arboribus templi sui, obumbratricibus scelerum, votiuis Crucibus exposuit. In Martyrologio, de Paphnutio: Ipse palmæ arbori affigitur, ceteri autem ferro necantur. Nec ambigimus arbores plerumque huic rei seruisse, præsertim in grandi numero cruciandorum, siue recisas leuiter & ad Crucem aptatas, siue etiam comantes. Sed & in stipite simplici idem fuit.
units.tr: Every word here is clear. You will see that he is hung on the trunk of a tree, his hands not stretched out but bound behind his back, and finally fastened not with nails but with ropes. Something similar is in Tertullian, on Tiberius, who, as he says, set out the priests of Saturn on the very trees of his temple, which shaded his crimes, on votive crosses. In the Martyrology, about Paphnutius: He himself is fixed to a palm tree, while the others are put to death by the sword. Nor do we doubt that trees were often used for this purpose, especially where there were large numbers to be tortured, whether trees lightly trimmed and fitted to make a cross, or even with their leaves still on. But the same was also done with a single upright stake.

units.la: Ex Tertulliano: Quanto distinguitur à Crucis stipite Pallas Attica, vel Ceres Farrea, quæ sine effigie, rudi palo & informi ligno prostant? Nam rudem ecce palum componit & assimilat cum Cruce. Sed in eius verbis menda de Cerere Farreâ. Cur enim sic appellet? an quia far inuenerit? esto. atqui non omnis Ceres sic effigiata, sed certa aliqua, & in loco quem voluit expressum: sicut de Pallade, quæ Athenis. Legendum arbitror, Faria siue PhaPharia: quasi dixerit Cererē, quæ in Ægypto. Et intellegi credam Isidem: quę nomine diuertit à Cerere, numine communicat. Ità Herodotus: Δημήτρ δἐ, Ισις. In Apuleio, ipsa de se Isis: Me primigenij Phryges Pessinuntiam matrem nominant, me Eleusinij vetustam deam Cererem. Eusebius de Præparatione: Φασὶ τὸν Αἰγυ-πτιοι τὸν μὲν Ὀσιριν εἶναι τὸν Διόνυσον, τὸν δὲ Ισιν τὸν δἠμητρα: Aiunt Ægyptij Osirim esse Bacchum, Isidem vero Cererem.
units.tr: From Tertullian: How far is Attic Pallas, or Farrean Ceres, who stand without an image, on a rough post and a shapeless piece of wood, distinguished from the stake of the Cross? For see, he compares the rough post with the Cross. But there is a fault in his words, in "Farrean Ceres". Why would he call her that? Because she discovered grain (far)? Granted. Yet not every Ceres was represented in this way, but some particular one, and in the place he meant, just as Pallas was at Athens. I think we should read Pharia, as if he had said the Ceres who is in Egypt. And I believe Isis is meant, who differs from Ceres in name but shares her divine power. So Herodotus: "But Demeter is Isis" [Δημήτηρ δὲ Ἶσις]. In Apuleius, Isis herself says of herself: The first-born Phrygians call me the Mother of Pessinus, the Eleusinians call me the ancient goddess Ceres. Eusebius, in the Preparation for the Gospel: "The Egyptians say that Osiris is Bacchus, and Isis is Demeter" [Φασὶ τοὺς Αἰγυπτίους τὸν μὲν Ὄσιριν εἶναι τὸν Διόνυσον, τὴν δὲ Ἶσιν τὴν Δήμητρα]: The Egyptians say that Osiris is Bacchus, and Isis Ceres.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Altera Simplicis Crucis species, Infixio. Seneca, Hesychius, Plato, Plinius, illustrati.
units.tr: Another species of the simple cross: impalement (infixio). Illustrated from Seneca, Hesychius, Plato and Pliny.

units.la: ATQVE hæc fuit in Simplici Cruce Affixio: Est & in eâdem Infixio, qualis? cum nudum hominem erecto acuto stipiti infigebant, eâ formâ & facie quam exempla hæc docebunt. Seneca: Video istic Cruces nec unius generis, sed aliter ab aliis fabricatas. Alij capite conuerso in terram suspendere,
units.tr: This was the affixing in the simple cross. There is also, in the same kind, impalement (infixio). What was it like? They drove a naked man onto an upright sharpened stake, in the form and shape that the following examples will show. Seneca: I see here crosses that are not of one kind, but built in different ways by different people. Some hang the man with his head turned down toward the ground,

units.la: Lib. xr. de Asin. — Lib. xi. cap. i. pendêre, aliį per obscœna stipitem egerunt. Duo in ijs verbis obserues, & Cruces varias fuisse, quod nunc diducimus: & inter eas, Infixionem. Quam magis etiam aperit idem Seneca: Cogita hoc loco carcerem & Cruces, & adactum per medium hominem, qui per os emergat, stipitem. Viden' clarè medium hominem scissum & transfossum? Atque id imagine etiam illustrat Hesychius: Σκόλοψιν, ὡς ὀπίσσων· τὰ γὰρ παλαιὰν τῶν κακεργουμένων ἀνεσκολόπι-ζον, ὀξυώντες ξύλου διὰ ραχέως καὶ ξυότς, καθάπες τῶν ὀπισθομένων ἰχθὺς ἐπὶ ὀβελίσκων: Sudifixionem dixeris, quasi Assationem. Nam antiquitùs maleficos sudi infigebant, acuto ligno penetrantes spinam & dorsum, sicuti assos in verubus pisces. Vbi amplius disco, proprie hoc esse Σκόλοψιν; & Σκολοπίζειν vbi legitur, plerumque referendum ad hanc formam. Ista Crux nescio an Mæcenati etiam descripta: cuius versus apud Senecam iam olim sic legimus: Hanc mihi, vel acutâ Si sedeam Cruce, sustine. Vita dum superest, bene est.
units.tr: Lib. xr. de Asin. — Lib. xi. cap. i. hang him, while others drove the stake up through the private parts. In these words you should notice two things: that there were various kinds of cross, which we are now setting out, and that among them there was impalement. Seneca makes this even clearer: Think here of the prison and the crosses, and the stake driven through the middle of the man, coming out through his mouth. Do you see clearly the man split and pierced through the middle? Hesychius also illustrates this with an image: Skolopsin, as of those roasted on a spit [Σκόλοψιν, ὡς ὀπίσσων· τὰ γὰρ παλαιὰν τῶν κακεργουμένων ἀνεσκολόπι-ζον, ὀξυώντες ξύλου διὰ ραχέως καὶ ξυότς, καθάπες τῶν ὀπισθομένων ἰχθὺς ἐπὶ ὀβελίσκων]. You might call it sudifixion, as if it were roasting. For in ancient times they fixed wrongdoers on stakes, driving a sharpened piece of wood through the spine and back, just as fish are skewered on spits and roasted. From this I learn more clearly that this is properly the skolops [Σκόλοψιν]; and where we read of impaling [Σκολοπίζειν], it is mostly to be understood as referring to this form.

units.la: Vult miser & adsuspirat viuere, etiam inter tormenta, & in istâ maximè cruciante Cruce, quam signanter dixit Acutam. Sed aijt etiam Sedere: bene. Nam ille profectò habitus hominis ab infero in superum sic transfixi. Hoc ipsum genus Ἀνασκινδυλεύεσ dictum Græcis, quasi diffindere & dissecare. Hesychius: Ἀνασκινδυλεύεσ, ἀνασκολοπιζῆσαι. Plato eo verbo visus: Μασιγώσε), σερεβλώσε), τε
units.tr: I do not know whether Maecenas also described this cross, whose verse we have long read in Seneca: If I must sit on this sharp cross, bear it for me. While life remains, all is well. The wretched man wishes and sighs to live, even amid torments, and above all on this most agonising cross, which he deliberately called sharp. But he also says sit: well put. For that is certainly the posture of a man transfixed from below upward. The Greeks called this very kind of death anaskindyleusis [Ἀνασκινδυλεύεσ], as if to say to split and to cut apart. Hesychius: anaskindyleuesthai [Ἀνασκινδυλεύεσ], that is, to impale upward [ἀνασκολοπιζῆσαι]. Plato uses the word in this sense: [Μασιγώσε), σερεβλώσε), τε]

units.la: Epist. XXIII.
units.tr: Epist. XXIII.

units.la: Ex. De Repub. [λωτῶν ὁ πόλις καὶ παθῶν δικασιν δυλαδυ[?]ς]: Fla-gellabitur, distorquebitur, denique omnia mala passus Cruce diffindetur. Plinij etiam verba huc reserā narrantis, Polybium cum Scipione in Africā leones homicidas crucifixos vidisse, quia ceteri metu poenæ similis absterrerentur eâdem noxâ. Quis enim credat operosam & compositam crucifixionem illam fuisse? non ego: & accipiam de hac promptâ & fortuitâ in stipite infixione, siue etiam affixione.
units.tr: From the Republic [λωτῶν ὁ πόλις καὶ παθῶν δικασιν δυλαδυ[?]ς]: He shall be flogged, racked, and at last, having suffered every evil, be split on the cross. Pliny also, when he tells of this, relates that Polybius, with Scipio in Africa, saw man-killing lions crucified, so that the others, frightened by the fear of a punishment like theirs, might be deterred from the same crime. For who would believe that this crucifixion was an elaborate and carefully arranged affair? Not I. I take it to mean that quick and improvised impalement on a stake, or indeed fixing to it.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: Chapter VII.

units.la: In genere de Cruce Compactâ: tum de primâ ejus specie, Decussatâ. & an hæc sit Andreana?
units.tr: In general on the compound cross; then on its first kind, the decussate; and whether this is St Andrew's cross?

units.la: AT Compacta Crux est, quæ manu facta, idque è duplici ligno. Ita septuaginta Interpretes Ptolomæani, libro Iosuæ quà vulgò est, lignum, & Chaldæo paraphraste, Crux, ipsi verterunt * ξύλον δίδυμον: bene sanè, ad hanc formam. Hæc est plena & vera Crux, in quâ brachia etiam explicantur, atque ideo Patibulum non semel dicta. Huius species triplex, vt distinctè imò curiosè edisseram, & semel tollam dubitationes aut lites. Est Decussata, est Commissa, est Immissa. Illa prima mihi dicitur, in quâ duo ligna directa & aequabilia, inter se obliquantur. Decussare hoc enim Romani dixerunt. Hieronymus: Decussare, est per medium secare, veluti si dua regula concurrant ad speciem litteræ X quæ figura est Crucis. Nec minùs clarè Isidorus: X littera, & in figurâ Crucem, & in numero decem demonstrat. Obscurius paullo alij Patres & Doctores nostri, vt Iustinus Martyr: qui illud Platonis in Timæo, Ἐχίασεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ: Decussavit eum in universo: adsueueranter ad Christum & Crucem nostram retulit, quo nisi hoc aspectu? Iam cùm transuersis obliquatisque manibus benedictionem Iacobi eâdem aptant: quid nisi hæc forma in oculis? Damascenus: Ἰακὼβ προσκυνήσας τὸ ἄκρον τῆς ῥάβδου, συνπλαγμένας ταῖς χερσὶ τῶν υἱῶν Ἰωσὴφ εὐλογήσας, καὶ τὸ σημεῖον διαγράφει Σταυροῦ: Iacob adorans extremum virga, alternantibus manibus liberos Ioseph benedicens, etiam signum hoc Crucis describit manifestissimo. Quid χεῖρες ἱστᾶς συνπλαγμένας etsi non ambiguum, tamen audiamus Cedrenum commodè explicantem. Ἰσραὴλ (idem cum Iacobo) τὰς χεῖρας ἀμείβων, τὴν μὲν δεξιὰν ἐπὶ νεωτέρου, τὴν ἀριστερὰν ἐπὶ πρεσβυτέρου τῶν κεφαλῶν πιθεὶς: Israël manus perpermutans, dextram quidem in iuniori, sinistram vero in senioris caput imponens. Et Tertullianum in ista ipsa re: Impositis & intermutatis manibus benedixit, & quidem ita transversim obliquatis inter se, ut Christum deformantes, jam tunc portenderent benedictionem in Christum futuram. Quomodo Christum deformârunt illæ manus? imò Crucem: & sic mihi libido aliquando legere: sed refræno, & accipio Christum crucifixum. Hæc illa est quâ Andræanam hodie dicimus, validâ & satis veteri famâ diuum istum in eâ cruciatum. Anne verâ? facit me ut ambigam Martyrologium Romanum: in quo hoc saltem *legas, in Cruce suspensum. & magis Hippolytus, qui scribit Crucifixum Patris in arborem olivæ rectum. Quid magis contrà famam? Atque hæc fixio ad Simplicem nostram potiùs abeat, longè à Decussatâ.
units.tr: But the compound cross is one that is made by hand, and from two pieces of wood. So the Seventy interpreters of Ptolemy's time rendered it in the book of Joshua, where the common text has wood, and the Chaldee paraphrast, where it has cross: [xylon didymon] (a double wood). And rightly so, for this shape. This is the full and true cross, in which the arms also are extended, and for that reason it has been called the patibulum more than once. It has three kinds, which I will set out distinctly, indeed carefully, so as to settle doubts and disputes once and for all. There is the decussate, the joined, and the set-in. The first I call the one in which two straight and equal pieces of wood cross each other obliquely. For the Romans named this decussating. Jerome: To decussate is to cut through the middle, as when two rulers meet in the shape of the letter X, which is the figure of the cross. Isidore is no less clear: The letter X shows a cross in its figure, and ten in its number. Some of our other Fathers and teachers speak a little more obscurely, as Justin Martyr does, who, when he applied Plato's words in the Timaeus, [Echiasen auten en to kosmo], he decussated it in the universe, related them to Christ and our cross; and from what viewpoint but this? Again, when they apply the same to Jacob's blessing, with hands crossed and set obliquely, what else but this form is before their eyes? Damascene: [Iakob proskynesas to akron tes rabdou, synplagmenas tais chersi ton huion Iosep eulogesas, kai to semeion diagraphei Staurou]: Jacob, adoring the top of the staff, blessing the sons of Joseph with hands alternately crossed, also describes this sign of the Cross most plainly. What [cheires histas synplagmenas] means, though not doubtful, let us hear Cedrenus explaining it aptly: [Israel tas cheiras ameibon, tēn men dexian epi neroterou, tēn aristeran epi presbuterou tōn kephalōn theis]: Israel, exchanging his hands, placing the right on the younger and the left on the head of the elder. And Tertullian on this very matter: Laying on and interchanging his hands, he blessed; and indeed he crossed them obliquely in such a way that, by forming the figure of Christ, they already then foreshadowed the blessing to come upon Christ. How did those hands form Christ? Rather, the Cross. And so I am sometimes tempted to read it that way; but I restrain myself and accept Christ crucified. This is the cross which we today call St Andrew's, from a strong and fairly old tradition that that saint was tortured on it. Is the tradition true? The Roman Martyrology makes me doubt, in which at least you read legas, in Cruce suspensum. (Suspended on a cross.) Hippolytus does so even more, for he writes Crucifixum Patris in arborem olivae rectum. (The Father crucified on a straight olive tree.) What could be more contrary to the tradition? And this fixing should rather pass to our Simple one, far removed from the decussate.

units.la: Crux Andreana. — Vti & in Abdia lib. xxx.
units.tr: As also in Abdia, book 30.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Commissa Crux quid nobis sit? exemplis testibusq; asserta, tum etiam vestigio nostra lingua.
units.tr: What the joined cross is to us, asserted by examples and witnesses, and also by the trace it leaves in our own language.

units.la: IAM Commissam Crucem appello, cum ligno erecto breuius alterum superne, & in ipso capite committitur, sic vt nihil exstet. ea forma examussim est in T litterâ, quam vno ore omnes cum Cruce componunt. Lucianus vbi Tau accusatur: Τὸ γὰρ τοῦτο σῶμα τί φασι; ... ἀνθρώπους ἀποσολπίζειν ἐπ' αὐτά: Huius enim corporis filum tyrannos aiunt secutos, ejusq; speciem imitatos, simili deinde figura ligna fabricasse, & homines in ijs fixisse. Palàm est Crucem intelligi. Tertullianus: Ipsa enim littera Graecorum Tau, nostra autem T, species Crucis. Isidorus: Tau littera speciem crucis demonstrat. Hieronymus: Antiquis Hebraeorum litteris, quibus vsque hodie Samaritae vtuntur, extrema Tau Crucis habet similitudinem. Paulinus Nolanus: Christus non multitudine nec virtute legionum, sed iam tunc in sacramento Crucis, cuius figura per litteram Graecam Tau numero trecentorum exprimitur, aduersarios Principes debellauit. Adstruunt etiam pictura, & nostra lingua. In illis quidem, passim hodie videas D. Antonij vetustissimi monachi penulae & manui assui aut imponi hanc crucem. An quia Ægyptius ille vir, quibus iam olim notum tum, & inter sacra hoc signum? Certè in obeliscis, qui inde Romam vecti, sculptum sic vidimus ☥: cum anulo tamen vel ansulâ supernè, nec satis solidè scio ad quam rem aut vsum. Sed de præcipuâ ipsâ notâ, dignum aliquid notâ Ecclesiasticę nostræ historiæ prodiderunt. Ruffinus: Signum hoc dominicæ Crucis, inter illas quas dicunt ἱερογλυφικὰς id est Sacerdotales litteras habere Ægyptij dicuntur, velut vnum ex ijs quæ apud illos sunt litterarum elementis. Cuius litteræ seu vocabuli hanc asserunt esse interpretationem, VITA VENTVRA.
units.tr: NOW I call it the joined cross when a shorter beam is joined on top, at the head of an upright beam, so that nothing projects beyond. This shape exactly matches the letter T, which everyone compares with the cross. Lucian, where he accuses the Tau: "For what do they say of this body? ... that men were hung upon it. For they say that tyrants followed the thread of this body and imitated its shape, and then fashioned wooden frames of similar form and fixed men on them." It is plain that the cross is meant. Tertullian: "The Greek letter Tau is itself a cross, and our T is the form of the cross." Isidore: "The letter Tau shows the shape of a cross." Jerome: "In the ancient letters of the Hebrews, which the Samaritans still use today, the final Tau has the likeness of a cross." Paulinus of Nola: "Christ overcame the adversary princes not by a multitude or the strength of legions, but already then by the sacrament of the cross, whose figure is expressed by the Greek letter Tau, which has the value of three hundred." Pictures and our own language also support this. In pictures you may see everywhere today the cross of St Anthony, the most ancient monk, sewn on the cloak and sleeve or set upon them. Was it because that Egyptian man knew this sign long ago, and held it among their sacred things? Certainly on the obelisks, which were brought from there to Rome, we have seen it carved thus: ☥, though with a ring or loop above it; I do not know for certain for what purpose or use. But concerning this chief mark itself, our ecclesiastical history has handed down something worth noting. Rufinus: "This sign of the Lord's cross is said to be among those letters which they call hieroglyphic, that is, sacred letters, which the Egyptians have, as one of the elements of their writing. They assert that the interpretation of this letter or word is LIFE TO COME.

units.la: Sozomenus: Φασὶ δὲ ξ ναοῦ καθαιρεθέντος τούτῳ (ξ Σαραπίδος) λίθας τὰς καλλιμένων ἱερογλυφικῶν χαρακτήρων σαφεῖς ὁμοίως σημείῳ ἐμφερεῖς ἐγκεχαραγμένους τοῖς λίθοις διαφθῶναι. παρ' Ἱπηνιόνων ὁ τὰ διαδὲ ἐμνημονεῦσαν σημαῖναι ταύτην τῷ γραφῷ, ζωὴν ἐπεχομένῳ. Aiunt templo isto (Sarapidis) diruto & dissecto, quasdam ex ijs, quas vocant Hieroglyphicas notas, similes signo crucis inscriptas lapidibus apparuisse. Ab ijs autem, qui docti hæc talia, explicatam eam notam, significare Vitam venturam. In Suidâ etiam historiola hæc breuiter. Ἐπὶ Θεοδοσίου μεγάλου βασιλέως καθαιρεμένων τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν ἱερῶν, ἀνεδήσαν ἐν τῷ Σαραπίδος νεῷ ἱερογλυφικὰ γράμματα σαυροῦ ἔχοντα τύπους. ἀπὸ θεασάμενοι οἱ ἐξ Ἑλλήνων χειστιανίσαντες, ἔφασαν σημαίνειν τὸν σαυρὸν παρὰ τῆς ἱερογλυφικὰ γινώσκοντι γεγράμματα ζωῇ ἐπεχομένῳ. Theodosio magno regnante, cùm fana gentilium diruerentur, inuenta sunt in Sarapidis templo HieroHieroglyphica littera habentes Crucis formas. quas videntes ij qui gentilium Christo iam addicti erant, aiebant significare Crucem apud peritos Hieroglyphicarum notarum Vitam venturam. Atqui & a lingua argumentum petij, sed nostra. Nos inquam Belgae hodie, bacillos in hanc formam, quos aegrorum brachijs sustentaculum subijcimus, vocamus ipsa Latina voce Cruckas.
units.tr: Sozomen: They say that when the temple of Serapis was torn down and dismantled, certain of the so-called hieroglyphic characters, carved on the stones and resembling the sign of the cross, came to light. Those learned in such matters explained that this mark signifies the life to come [ζωήν]. In Suidas too this little story is told briefly: "In the reign of the great emperor Theodosius, when the pagan temples were being pulled down, hieroglyphic letters bearing forms of the cross were found in the temple of Serapis. Those of the Greeks who had become Christians, seeing them, said that the cross, according to those skilled in hieroglyphic letters, signifies the life to come." But I have also drawn an argument from language, our own. We Belgians today call the sticks which we put under the arms of the sick as a support, bent into this shape, by the Latin word itself, cruckas.

units.la: CAP. IX. Affirmata Crux Immissa e scriptis maxime Patrum: ipsi alij per alios, & imaginibus per nos etiam, explicati.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX. The inserted cross affirmed chiefly from the writings of the Fathers; the others explained by others, and by images, and also by us.

units.la: DENIQVE Immissa crux est, cùm ligno erecto transuersum alterum injungitur atque immittitur, sed sic ut ipsum secet. Ira eminentia hîc semper aliqua & capitellum, aliter quàm in Commissâ. Etiâ anguli hîc siue fines quaterni, illic terni. Quis de istâ ambiget? Ingerunt eam oculis Picturae pariter & Scripturae priscę. Sed illas omitto aut differo: hæ variæ & obuiæ sunt, atque ex iis eligam, non colligâ, nostro more.
units.tr: Finally, the inserted cross is when another beam is laid across the upright beam and inserted into it, but so that it cuts through it. Thus there is always some projection here, and a little head, unlike the joined cross. Here the ends or limits are also four, there three. Who would doubt this one? Both pictures and ancient writings present it to the eyes. But I set those aside or defer them: they are varied and at hand, and from among them I will choose rather than collect, as is my custom.

units.la: C. Justi-
units.tr: C. Justi-

units.la: Iustinus signanter in primis deformat aduersus Tryphonem. Explicat vetus illud vaticinium de Vnicorni, & ad Crucem sic aptat. Μονοκέρωτος γὰρ κέρατα ὑδενὸς ἄλλυ πεάγματος, ἢ χήματος ἔχοι ἀντιις ἁπεῖν & ἀποδεῖξαι εἰ μὴ ἐν τύπυ ὡς τὸν Σλωμὼν δεικνυσιν. ὅρᾶτον γὰρ ἐν ἐσι τὸ ξύλον, ἀφ' ὧν ἐσι τὸ ἀνώτατον μέρος εἰς κέρας ἐπηρμένον, ὅταν τὸ ἄλλο ξύλον τῷ ἁρμοσθῇ, & ἐκαλέωσεν ὡς κέρας τῷ ἑνὶ κέρατι παρεσθυγμένα τὰ ἄκρα φαίνεται). καὶ τὸ ἐν τῷ μέσῳ πηγνύμενον ὡς κέρας & αὐτὸ ἐξέχον ἐσιν, ἐφ' ᾧ ἐπέχονται) σταυρούμενοι: Unicornis enim cornua alteri rei aut figurae haud quispiam similia dixerit aut ostenderit, quàm illi quae Crucem refert. Rectum enim vnum est lignum à quo est suprema pars in cornu sublata, cum alterum lignum aptatum est: & vtrimque tanquam cornua illi vni cornu coniuncta, extrema apparent: & illud in medio defixum, & ipsum tanquam cornu eminet, in quo requiescunt & innituntur crucifixi. Obscuriuscula alibi verba, sed hac parte liquidissima, quòd eminens vnum cornu facit à vertice crucis. Iam alij Patrum, varia imagine, non sine lasciuia quadam ingeniorum & stili eam describunt & notificant. Vt Hieronymus: Ipsa species Crucis, quid est nisi forma quadrata mundi? Aues quando volant ad athera, formam Crucis assumunt. Homo natans per aquas, vel orans, forma Crucis visitur. Vt Tertullianus: Victorias adoratis, cum in Tropeis Cruces intestina sint tropaeorum. Omnes illi imaginum suggestus in signis, monilia crucium sunt. Sypara illa vexillorum & cantabrorum stola crucium sunt. Laudo diligetiam, noluistis incultas Cruces consecrare. Vt Minutius Felix: Cruces nec colimus, nec optamus. Vos plane, qui ligneos deos consecratis, cruces ligneas, ut deorum vestrorum partes, forsitan adoratis. nam & signa ipsa, & cantabra, & vexilla castrorum quid aliud quam inaurata Cruces sunt & ornata? Trophaea vestra victricia non tantum simplicis Crucis faciem, verum & affixi hominis imitantur. Signum sane Crucis naturaliter visimus in navi, cum velis tumentibus vehitur, cum expansis palmulis labitur; & cum erigitur iugum, Crucis signum est: & cum homo porrectis manibus Deum pura mente veneratur. Ita signo Crucis aut ratio naturalis innititur, aut vestra religio formatur.
units.tr: Justin, above all, describes it strikingly against Trypho. He explains that old prophecy about the unicorn and fits it to the cross: "For no one could say or show that the horns of the unicorn are like any other thing or figure, except the one which represents the cross. For the cross is one straight beam, from which the uppermost part rises like a horn when the other beam is fitted to it, and at each side the ends appear joined to that one horn; and the beam fixed in the middle stands out like a horn too, on which those who are crucified rest and lean." The words are rather obscure elsewhere, but in this part they are very clear, namely that the one projecting horn is made from the top of the cross. Next, others of the Fathers, with varied imagery and not without a certain playfulness of wit and style, describe and point out the cross. Thus Jerome: "What is the very shape of the cross but the square form of the world? When birds fly up to the heavens they take the form of a cross. A man swimming through the waters, or praying, is seen in the form of a cross." Thus Tertullian: "You worship victories, when the crosses are the very entrails of your trophies. All those raised platforms of your images on your standards are crosses. Those sypara, the stoles of your banners and standards, are crosses. I praise your diligence, in that you would not consecrate uncrafted crosses." Thus Minucius Felix: "We neither worship nor desire crosses. You indeed, who consecrate wooden gods, perhaps worship wooden crosses as parts of your gods. For what are your standards, your banners, and your military ensigns but crosses gilded and adorned? Your victorious trophies imitate not merely the appearance of a simple cross but also of a man fixed to it. Indeed we see the sign of the cross naturally in a ship, when it is carried with swelling sails, when it glides with its little sails spread; and when the yard is raised, it is the sign of the cross; and when a man with outstretched hands reverently worships God with a pure mind. Thus the natural reason rests upon the sign of the cross, or your religion is formed by it."

units.la: Vt Maximus Taurinensis: Grande est Crucis sacramentum, & si intellegamus, per hoc signum mundus ipse saluatur. Nam cum a nautis scinditur mare, prius arbor erigitur, velum distenditur, ut Cruce Domini facta aquarum fluenta rumpantur. Sed & bonus agricola, cum parat terra solum vertere, non nisi per signum Crucis id facere conatur. Dum enim aratro dentale subjicit, affixit (lege, affigit) aures, stiuam inserit, figuram Crucis imitatur. Calum quoque ipsum huius signi figura dispositum est. Nam cum quatuor partibus distinguitur, Oriente, Occidente, Meridiano, ac Septemtrione, quatuor quasi Crucis angulis continetur. Ipsius etiam incessus hominis, cum manus leuauerit, Crucem pingit. atque ideo elevatis manibus orare. orare praecipimur, ut ipso quoque membrorum gestu passionem Domini fateamur. Et diffusissimè omnium Iustinus: Καταναοήσατε πάντα τὰ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ, εἰ ἄνευ ξ χήματος τοῦτο (Σίλωρος) διοικεῖται, ἢ κοινωνίαν ἔχειν δυνατά. Θάλασσα μὲν γὰρ ὑ τέμνει, ἵνα μὴ τοῦτο τὸ τεφπαυον ὁ καλεῖται ἰσίον ἐν τῇ νηὶ σῳων μείνῃ. γῆ δὲ ἐκ ἀροῦται ἄνευ αὐτῆς. σκαπανεὺς δ' ἐργαςίαν ὑ ποιεῖ, ὑδὲ βαναυσουργοὶ ὁμοίως, εἰ μὴ διὰ τῶν τοῦ χήματος ἐχόντων ἐργαλείων. τὸ δὲ ἀνθρώπῳ χῆμα ὑδενὶ ἄλλῳ τῶν ἀλόγων ζῴων διαφέρει, ἢ τῷ ὀρθόν τε εἶναι, καὶ ἐκτάσιν χάρων ἔχειν, καὶ ἐν τῷ πεσσώπῳ ἀπὸ ξ μελωπίου τεταμένον τὸ λεόμενον μυξωτῆρα φέρειν, διὰ ἡ τε ἀναπνοὴ ἔστι τῷ ζῴῳ, καὶ ἴδεν ἄλλο δεικνύειν ἢ τὸ χῆμα τοῦ Σίλωρος· καὶ τὰ παρ' ὑμῖν δλεσύμβολα τῷ ξ χήματος τοῦτο δυνάμιν δηλοῖ. ** Μωμον καὶ τῶν τεοπαίων δ' ὧν αὐτε πεόδοι ὑμῖν πανταχοῦ γίνον), τ ἀρχῆς καὶ δυνάμεως τὰ σημεῖα ἐν τύποις δεικνύοντες, εἰ ἐ μὴ νοοῦντες ξ- ὁ περίτιετε. καὶ τῶν παρ' ὑμῖν ἀποθνησκόντων αὐτοκειμένων τὰς εἰκόνας ἐπὶ τούτῳ τῷ χήματι ἀνατίθετε, καὶ δεῖς διὰ γραμμάτων ἐπονομάζεις. Considerate omnia quae in mundo sunt, an sine signo hoc Crucis gubernentur, aut possint praebere sui usum. Mare enim non scinditur, nisi tropaeum istud, quod malus appellatur, salvum in navi maneat. Terra non aratur sine eo. Fossores vero opus non absolvunt, neque alij item operarij Mechanici, nisi per instrumenta quae formam hanc referant. At humana figura non aliâre belluis differt, quam quòd, & recta sit, & manuum extensionem habeat & in facie à fronte proteнtensum nasum per quem & respiratio animalibus est, neq; aliud demonstrat quàm signum hoc Crucis. Sed & apud vos notæ huius signi potentiam declarant: * cùm alia quaedam, tum tropæa, ob quæ progressus & expeditiones vbique vobis fiunt imperiĭ & potentiæ signa in istis præferentes, etsi ignorantes hoc facitis. Et Imperatorum qui apud vos mortui sunt, imagines in hac figurâ ponitis, & Deos per litteras appellatis.
units.tr: Thus Maximus of Turin: "Great is the sacrament of the cross, and if we understand it, the world itself is saved by this sign. For when the sea is cut by sailors, first a mast is raised and the sail is spread, so that by the cross of the Lord the flow of the waters is broken. Also a good farmer, when he prepares to turn the soil with the plough, tries to do it only by the sign of the cross. For when he fixes the share to the plough, he fastens the handles, and inserts the beam, and imitates the figure of the cross. The heaven itself too is arranged in the figure of this sign. For when it is divided into four parts, East, West, South and North, it is contained as by the four corners of a cross. Also the very gait of man, when he lifts his arms, paints a cross; and therefore we are taught to pray with raised hands, so that by that very gesture of the limbs we may confess the passion of the Lord." And most widely of all, Justin: "Consider all the things in the world: whether without this figure of the cross they could be governed or could offer their use. The sea is not cut unless that trophy which is called the mast remains safe in the ship. The earth is not ploughed without it. Diggers do not complete their work, nor do other mechanical workers, unless through the tools which bear this form. The human figure differs from the irrational animals in nothing but that it is upright, has its arms extended, and carries its nose projecting from the face, through which there is breathing for the living creature; and it shows nothing else but the sign of this cross. Also the marks of this sign among you declare its power: while certain other things do so, so too do the trophies, by which your advances and campaigns are made everywhere, bearing the signs of your rule and power in these forms, though you do this without understanding. And the images of your emperors who have died you set up in this figure, and you name the gods by letters."

units.la: Quæ pluscula posui, quia me quoq; inter exscribēdum delectarunt inuentiunculæ istæ Patrum. Spero & te, si plenè intelleges: atque adminiculum, figuras istas, habe.
units.tr: I have added these somewhat fuller passages because these little inventions of the Fathers delighted me too as I copied them out. I hope you too will be delighted, if you understand them fully; and take these figures as an aid.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: In quâ Crucium formâ Christus mortem tulerit? videri in vltimâ, argumento è Patribus & pictoris. Ruffini non bona fides notata in verbis Pauli citandis siue explicandis.
units.tr: In what form of cross Christ suffered death? That it is seen to be the last, by an argument from the Fathers and from a painter. The lack of good faith of Rufinus, noted in quoting or explaining the words of Paul.

units.la: HABES omnes Crucium species. In quâ earum ille mortuus, qui morte suâ nobis vita? Ne quærendum quidè censeam, nisi dubitasse & disputasse viderem viros graues & sacrorum peritos. ego arbitror & pronuncio, in hac postremâ. in illâ inquam, quæ quatuor finibus vniuersum orbem complexa est, non sine mysterio, quod toti orbi mortuus, Saluator noster pendit. Tangit hoc & docet Sedulius: Neue quis ignoret speciem Crucis esse colendam, Qua Dominum portauit ouans, ratione *potenti, Quatuor inde plagas quadrati colligit orbis. Splendidus auctoris de vertice fulget Eous, Occiduo sacra labuntur sidere planta, Arcton dextra tenet, medium laeua erigit axem.
units.tr: You have all the kinds of cross. Which of these was the one on which he died who gave us life by his death? I would not think it even necessary to ask, were I not seeing learned men, grave and skilled in sacred things, doubting and disputing. I hold and declare for the last form: that one, I say, which with its four arms embraces the whole world, and not without a mystery, since our Saviour hangs on it as one who died for the whole world. Sedulius touches on this and teaches: Lest anyone fail to know that the figure of the Cross is to be honoured, on which the Lord was carried in triumph, by a powerful reason it gathers from it the four quarters of the squared world. The bright East shines from the top of the Author, the sacred feet slide down toward the western star, the right hand holds the Arctic, the left raises the middle axis.

units.la: Et auctoritas etiam firma à D. Paulo. ejus hæc verba, Vt possitis comprehendere cum omnibus sanctis, quæ sit latitudo & longitudo, & sublimitas & profundum, plerique Doctorum veterum referunt ad Crucem. Augustinus: Erat latitudo, in quâ porrecta sunt manus; longitudo à terrâ surgens, in quâ erat corpus infixum; altitudo, ab illo innexo ligno sursum quod eminet; profundum, vbi fixa erat
units.tr: And the testimony of the blessed Paul is also strong. Most of the ancient teachers refer his words, That you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, to the Cross. Augustine: The breadth was where the hands were stretched out; the length, rising from the earth, was where the body was fixed; the height, from that wood joined to it, which rises upward; the depth, where it was fixed

units.la: Crux, & ibi omnis spes vitae nostrae. Damascenus: Ὥσπερ τὰ τέσσαρα ἄκρα ἐκ Σταυροῦ διὰ τοῦ μέσου κέντρου συνδεῖ καὶ συσφίγγον, οὕτω διὰ τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ δυνάμεως τό, τε ὕψος καὶ τὸ βάθος, μῆκος καὶ πλάτος, ἤτοι πᾶσα ὁρατὴ τε καὶ ἀόρατος κτίσις συνέχεται. Sicut quatuor extrema Crucis per medium centrum vinciuntur & junguntur: sic per divinam potentiam Sublimitas & Profunditas, Longitudo & Latitudo, sive omnis conspicua & inconspicua creatura continetur. Palàm & ipse quatuor fines nominat, & verba Pauli huc adaptat. Ruffinus cur dissentit? qui tres modò agnoscit, & ipsa Apostoli verba (nefas!) admutilat & detruncat. Docet, inquit, Apostolus Paulus illuminatos esse debere oculos cordis ad intelligendum quae sit altitudo, latitudo & profundum. Descriptio Crucis est, cuius eam partem quae in terram defixa est, profundum appellavit: altitudinem vero illam, quae in aerem porrecta sublimis erigitur: latitudinem quoque illam quae distenta in dextram laevamque protenditur. Mirum, & in verbis Pauli, & in eorum sensu longitudinem vbique improuidè omisit. An de industria ejecit? Culpa, si illud: crimen, si istud. Sed ad rem: Poëtae quoque & Pictores sunt à formâ istâ. Nonnus diserte scribit, Christum sublatum. Εἰς ξύλον τεσσαρακτυπον: in lignum quadrilaterum. Et in priscis sculpturis (illis merito fides) quadrata conspicitur haec forma. Constantinus Imp. in Labaro suo expressit: & Deus ipse in aëre ei deformarat. In columnis eiusdem Principis, quae nunc in cognomine vrbe (heu, quò ea recidit?) Crux eiusmodi ☥ insculpta visitur, & vtrimque ab alatis Genijs sustentatur. Quid, quod in Numis plurifariàm sic appâret? quorum alibi damus typos. Nec meo sensu, ambigi profecto potest, in tam veteri Christianorum sensu. Tamen sunt qui de Commissa siue de Tau formâ contendunt. nec damno, etsi dissideo: quia & illi si Titulum supernè addis, efficere atq; imaginari possis quaternos istos fines.
units.tr: Cross, and there all hope of our life. Damascene: [Ὥσπερ τὰ τέσσαρα ἄκρα ἐκ Σταυροῦ διὰ τοῦ μέσου κέντρου συνδεῖ καὶ συσφίγγον, οὕτω διὰ τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ δυνάμεως τό, τε ὕψος καὶ τὸ βάθος, μῆκος καὶ πλάτος, ἤτοι πᾶσα ὁρατὴ τε καὶ ἀόρατος κτίσις συνέχεται.] As the four ends of the Cross are bound and joined through the middle centre, so by the power of God height and depth, length and breadth, that is, every visible and invisible creature, is held together. Clearly he too names four ends and applies Paul's words to this. Why does Rufinus disagree? He acknowledges only three, and cuts and mutilates the Apostle's own words (shameful!). The Apostle Paul teaches, he says, that the eyes of the heart must be enlightened to understand what is the height, breadth and depth. It is a description of the Cross: the part of it fixed in the earth he called the depth, that part which rises high into the air the height, and the breadth is that which is stretched out to right and left. It is a wonder that he has everywhere carelessly omitted length, both in Paul's words and in their sense. Did he drop it on purpose? If by oversight, it is a fault; if on purpose, a crime. But to the matter: poets and painters too have this shape. Nonnus clearly writes that Christ was raised on [εἰς ξύλον τεσσαρακτυπον] a four-sided wood. And in early carvings (which deserve trust) this square form is seen. The Emperor Constantine expressed it on his standard, and God himself had shaped it for him in the air. On the columns of the same prince, which now stand in the city that bears his name (alas, to what has it fallen?), a cross of this kind, ☥, is seen carved, and it is upheld on either side by winged Genii. What of the fact that it appears in many ways on coins? I give pictures of these elsewhere. And in my judgement there can certainly be no doubt about it, given so ancient a sense among Christians. Yet there are those who argue for the crux commissa, or Tau form. I do not condemn them, though I disagree, because if you add the title above, you can also form and picture those four ends.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CAP. XI.

units.la: Apud plerasque gentium Cruces fere vsitatas. Apud Syros, Iudaeos, Aegyptios, Persas, Afros, Graecos, maximè Romanos. Quando apud eos coeperit? An & apud Germanos?
units.tr: Crosses were fairly common among most nations. Among the Syrians, Jews, Egyptians, Persians, Africans, Greeks, and especially the Romans. When did they begin among them? And among the Germans as well?

units.la: CRVCES satis vidimus: vbi gentium eae in vsu fuerint, addam. Etsi vno verbo pænè dixerim, vbique gentium receptas. Oriens quidem plerusque vsurpauit, idque jam olim. De Syris in Esthere scriptum: Suspensus est Aman in patibulo, quod paraverat Mardochaeo. De Iudaeis, in Iosuâ: qui regem eius (Hai) suspendit in patibulo vsque ad vesperam. Item in Numeris: Tolle cunctos Principes populi, & suspende eos contrà Solem in patibulis. Atque in sacris libris saepius. Aegyptios etiam vsos reperio vt Thucydides de rege Inaro: προδοσία ληφθεὶς ἀνεσταυρώθη: proditione captus, ptus, in crucem est actus. Et Iustinus, in eâdem Ægypto: Agathocles occiditur, & mulieres in vltionem Eurydices patibulis suffiguntur. Et Persas crebrò. Herodotus de Polycrate: Ἀποκλείνας δὲ μὲν οὐκ ἀξίως ἀπηγγέλη καὶ Οροίτης ἀνεσαύρωσε: Interficiens eum (quod indignum relatu sit) Orœtes in Cruce suffixit. Ammianus de suo ævo: Ælianus Comes & Tribuni patibulis scelestè suffixi: capti nempe à Persis. Sed Afros vel omnium creberrime: qui non in viles modò, sed illustrissimas personas adhibebant. Atq; à Senatu Carthaginensium etiam Duces, bella prauo consilio gerentes, etsi prospera fortuna subsecuta esset, Cruci suffigebantur: Video & Græcos visitasse. Certè Alexander Macedo Glaucum medicum, & Tyrios, & plures crucifixit. Etiam Xanthippus Atheniensis Artayctam Persam, de quo apud Herodotum in Calliope extremâ leges. Iam Romanis vetus veterrimumq; (verba Victoris vsurpabo) supplicium patibulorum. Si Liuio fides, statim sub primis regibus vsurparunt: & exemplum in Horatio, cui id sub Tullo parabatur. Etsi Cicero dissentire videtur,& horridum illud Carmen ad Tarquinium Superbum auctorem referre. Ʃ lictor, inquit, colliga manus. quæ non modò huius libertatis mansuetudinisq; non sunt, sed ne Romuli quidem, aut Numæ, sed Tarquinij, superbissimi ac crudelissimi regis ista sunt cruciatus carmina, Caput obnubito, arbori infelici suspendito. Quæ tamen aut populariter & ad caufsam
units.tr: We have seen enough crosses; I will add where among the nations they were in use. Though I could almost say in one word that they were received everywhere. The East, at least for the most part, used them, and that from of old. Of the Syrians it is written in Esther: Haman was hanged on the gallows which he had prepared for Mordecai. Of the Jews, in Joshua: who hanged their king (of Ai) on a tree until evening. Likewise in Numbers: Take all the princes of the people, and hang them up in the sight of the sun on gibbets. And in the sacred books often. I find that the Egyptians also used them, as Thucydides says of King Inaros: [προδοσία ληφθεὶς ἀνεσταυρώθη] taken by betrayal, he was put on a cross. And Justin, in the same Egypt: Agathocles is killed, and the women are fastened to gibbets in revenge for Eurydice. And the Persians often. Herodotus on Polycrates: [Ἀποκλείνας δὲ μὲν οὐκ ἀξίως ἀπηγγέλη καὶ Οροίτης ἀνεσαύρωσε] Killing him (which is unworthy to relate), Oroetes fixed him to a cross. Ammianus of his own age: Aelianus the Count and the tribunes, wickedly fixed to gibbets, taken, of course, by the Persians. But the Africans, most frequently of all, who used them not only on base men but on the most distinguished persons. And by the Senate of Carthage even generals who waged war with a bad plan were fastened to the cross, even if good fortune had followed. I see that the Greeks too used them. Certainly Alexander the Macedonian crucified Glaucus the physician, and Tyrians, and several others. Xanthippus of Athens also crucified the Persian Artayctes, of whom you may read at the end of Herodotus in the Calliope. Now among the Romans the ancient and most ancient punishment of gibbets (I shall use Victor's words) was in use. If we trust Livy, they were used at once under the first kings, and there is an example in Horatius, for whom it was being prepared under Tullus. Although Cicero seems to disagree, and to refer that dreadful sentence to Tarquin the Proud as its author: Lictor, he says, bind his hands. These are not the words of that gentleness and liberty, nor of Romulus or Numa, but are the torturing verses of Tarquin, the proudest and most cruel king: cover his head, hang him on the unlucky tree. Whether Cicero said this for popular effect and to serve his cause, or whether he meant it sincerely, and it was not from that Tarquin's time but was most worthy of him and common under him: either way, I see that crosses were in use at once even under a free republic. Dionysius on the conspiring slaves: [Καὶ αὐτίκα ἀ μὲν ἐξ οἰκιῶν συλ-ληφθέντες, ἢ δ' ἐν τῶν ἀγρῶν ἀχθέντες ἀνεσκολοπίσθησαν ἅπαντες.] And at once some were seized from their houses, others led from the fields, and all were put on the cross. Line [8] above should end at the start of the marginal note; the remaining text follows in [9].

units.la: In Thalia. Lib. ii. cap. vii. Plutarch. in Alexan. In Constantino. Lib. i. Orat. pro Rabir. {a}sam Cicero dixerit, aut hoc sentiens, non ab auctore illa Tarquinio fuisse, sed illo maximè digna, & apud eum crebra. Vtrum horum est, video etiam liberâ rep. statim in vsu cruces. Dionysius de seruis coniuratis: Καὶ αὐτίκα ἀ μὲν ἐξ οἰκιῶν συλ-ληφθέντες, ἢ δ' ἐν τῶν ἀγρῶν ἀχθέντες ἀνεσκολοπίσθησαν ἅπαντες. Et ilico alij quidem è domibus extracti, alij è foris abducti, omnes in Crucem acti sunt. & deinceps ψαμμαχόσοι, vt cum Graecis dicam, testes. Quid Germani? nunquid & illi vsi? distrahor. Tacitus videtur dicere: Proditores & transfugas arboribus suspendunt. sed fortassis ad laqueum & suffocationem hoc aliquis trahat. Tamen idem Patibula etiam attribuit: Quot patibula captiuis, quas scrobes: quo nisi suo & Romano, sensu?
units.tr: In Thalia. Lib. ii. cap. vii. Plutarch. in Alexan. In Constantino. Lib. i. Orat. pro Rabir. (the rest of the text follows) Dionysius on the conspiring slaves, and so on; and the [ψαμμαχόσοι], as countless as the sand, to use the Greek phrase, bear witness. What of the Germans? Did they also use them? I am torn. Tacitus seems to say: They hang traitors and deserters on trees. But perhaps someone may take this to mean a noose and strangling. Yet the same writer also attributes gibbets to them: How many gibbets for captives, how many pits, which, unless in his own and the Roman sense, what could it mean?

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CAP. XII.

units.la: Apud Romanos vile fuisse hoc supplicium, & plurimum seruorum. Quas ob causas ij affecti.
units.tr: That this punishment was common among the Romans, and mostly for slaves. The causes for which such people were punished.

units.la: PLVRIFARIAM igitur receptæ Cruces, sed vix tamen nisi in homines viliores, Romano quidem ritu. Atque apud eos seruorum ferè hoc supplicium, aut plebeiorum qui iuxta seruos. De seruis mulier apud Iuuenalem: Pone Crucem seruo.
units.tr: Crosses were therefore used in many ways, but hardly ever except for baser people, and in the Roman manner. Among them this punishment was mostly for slaves, or for commoners who were little better than slaves. On slaves, a woman in Juvenal says: "Put a slave on the cross."

units.la: Et alia apud Petronium: Nec Dij sinant, ut amplexus meos in Crucem mittam. Ita enim venustè seruum cruciarium appellat, quâ facie sermonis
units.tr: Petronius has another instance: "May the gods not allow me to send my embraces to the cross." He calls the slave who is to be crucified by a fine phrase, using the figure of speech that Cicero explains, "a criminal for a criminal."

units.la: Cicero explicatus. nis Scelus pro scelesto. Seruus ipse apud Plautum comiter fatetur.
units.tr: Plautus's slave himself speaks with humour:

units.la: Noli minitari, scio crucem futuram mihi sepulcrum,
units.tr: "Don't threaten me. I know the cross will be my tomb,

units.la: Ibi maiores mei siti sunt, pater, auus, proauus, abauus.
units.tr: There my ancestors are buried, father, grandfather, great-grandfather, great-great-grandfather."

units.la: Atque adeo peculiare hoc seruis, vt nomine Seruilis supplicij Crux veniat capienda. In Tacito: Asiaticus (enim is libertus) malam potentiam seruili supplicio expiauit. Iterum: Sumptum de eo supplicium in seruilem modum. In Vulcatio explicatiùs: Centuriones rapi iussit & in crucem tolli, seruilíque supplicio affici. In Capitolino: Nam & in crucem milites tulit, & seruilibus supplicijs semper affecit. Ergo Liuium sic euolues: De captiuis, vt quisque liber, aut seruus, sua fortuna à quoque sumptum supplicium est. Suae fortunae: nempe Crux seruo reposita, gladius aut securis libero. Ipsum hoc ita in Hirtio legas: Prehensi serui tres, & vnus e legione vernaculâ. Serui sunt in crucem sublati, militi ceruices abscisa. Seruile igitur hoc supplicium, sed non ob leuem aut cottidianam noxam. Horatius indicat:
units.tr: So peculiar is this to slaves that the cross is named as "the servile punishment." In Tacitus: "Asiaticus (for he was a freedman) paid for his wicked power with a servile punishment." Again: "A punishment was inflicted on him in the servile manner." In Vulcatius, more fully: "He ordered the centurions seized, hanged on a cross, and subjected to a servile punishment." In the Capitoline: "For he both carried soldiers to the cross and always punished them with servile punishments." So you will read in Livy: "Concerning captives, each man was punished according to his lot, whether he was free or a slave." According to his lot: namely, the cross was kept for a slave, the sword or axe for a free man. You may read this exact thing in Hirtius: "Three slaves were seized, and one man from the native legion. The slaves were lifted up on crosses, the soldier had his neck cut off." This punishment was therefore servile, but not for a slight or everyday offence. Horace shows this:

units.la: Si quis eum seruum, patinam qui tollere iussus Semesos pisces, tepidúmque ligurrierit ius, In cruce suffigat; Labeone insanior inter Sanos dicatur.
units.tr: "If anyone, a slave ordered to carry the dish, has licked up the half-eaten fish and the lukewarm broth, let him be fixed to a cross; he would be called more mad than Labeo among sane men."

units.la: Indicat, inquam, graues fuisse & in extremo supplicio extremas caussas. Sed quas illas? ægrè vniuersas dixerim: quasdam adnumerabo. Delatura domini. Pertinax apud Capitolinum, eos qui calumniis appetiti per seruos fuerant, damnatis seruis delatoribus, liberauit, in Crucem sublatis talibus seruis. Sic Macrino iam Principe, συκοφάντας τε ἠδοῦλοι, ὅσοι δεσπότας κατήγγειλαν, ἀνεπολόπιστοι ἦσαν: Sycophanta, aut serui, quicunque dominos detulerant, in crucem sunt acti. Et in genere, omnis machina contra dominicam salutem. Paulus: Si serui domini salutem consuluerint (Mathematicos, intelligé:) summo supplicio, id est Cruce, afficiuntur. Item Fuga, sed (vt opinor) diuturna, aut repetita. Cicero tangit: Qua Crux huic fugitiuo potest satis supplicij adferre? Et Valerius: Cruce dignissimi sugitiui. Quin Scipio, apud eundem, trasfugas Romanos, tanquam patria fugitiuos, Crucibus affixit. Simile sub Augusto, in Sexti milite puniendo, qui fere e fugitiuis: Τὸ μὲν δεδεσμένος, ait Dio, τῆς δεσπότας τοῖς τιμωρίαν ἀπεδόθη· εἰ δὲ τὸν μηδεὶς κύριος δυνάμενος, ἀνεπολόπιστος: Seruitia dominis reddita ad poenam, quorum domini non exstarent, Cruci sunt fixa. Quanquam hic & alia causa suberat, Hostilitas in rem Romanam. Haec & plura in seruis: quos mitiores duriorésve domini, grauius, mitius, pro arbitrio sunt puniti.
units.tr: He shows, I say, that these were grave matters and that the most extreme causes led to the extreme punishment. But what were those causes? I can hardly list them all; I will name some. Informing against one's master. Pertinax, in the Capitoline, "freed those who had been attacked by false accusations through slaves, when the slave informers had been condemned, the slaves having been raised on crosses." So also under Macrinus, already emperor, "Sycophants and slaves who had informed against their masters were not without blame: sycophants, or slaves, whoever had informed against their masters, were put on the cross." And in general, every plot against the safety of the master. Paulus: "If slaves have plotted for their master's safety (understand: mathematicians), they are punished with the highest punishment, that is, the cross." Likewise flight, but (as I think) a long or repeated flight. Cicero touches on it: "What cross can bring enough punishment to this runaway?" And Valerius: "Runaways most deserving of the cross." Indeed Scipio, in the same author, "fixed Roman deserters to crosses as fugitives from their country." Something similar under Augustus, in the punishment of a soldier of Sextus, who was nearly a runaway. Dio says: "Slaves who had been bound were given over for punishment to their masters; but those whose masters could not be found were fixed to the cross." Yet here another cause also lay underneath: hostility against the Roman state. These and more causes concern slaves, whom their masters punished more severely or more mildly, according to their own judgment.

units.la: Vt Delatio.
units.tr: As informing.

units.la: Machinatio.
units.tr: Plotting.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CAP. XIII.

units.la: Etiam liberi quidam in Crucem dati, sed viliores aut nocentiores: ut Latrones, Sicarij, Falsarij, atque alibi & Fures.
units.tr: Some free men too were given to the cross, but they were the baser or the more guilty: such as robbers, assassins, forgers, and elsewhere thieves.

units.la: QVID autem in liberis? Rara crux, ut prædi-xi. Quin remouere prorsus ab hoc genere Lactantius videatur, vbi de Christo: Cur si Deus fuit, & mori voluit, non saltem aliquo honesto genere mortis affectus est? cur potissimum Cruce? cur infami genere supplicij? quod etiam homine libero, quamuis nocente, videatur indignum. Sed frænanda ea assertio est: & ciue quidem indigna Crux, nec credo vsurpatam in eos nisi præter leges, & per sæuitiam: viliores liberi, & prouinciales, non ab eâ profecto immunes. Atque hæc crimina in ijs cruciaria: primùm, Latrocinium. Se-neca: Latrocinium fecit aliquis. quid ergo meruit? ut suspendatur. Caue de alio suspendio interpretêre. Petronius: Imperator prouincia iussit latrones Crucibus affigi. Apuleius: Latronem istum, miserorum pignorum meorum peremptorem, Cruci affigatis. Callistratus Ictus: Famosos latrones, in his locis vbi grassati sunt, furcâ figendos compluribus placuit. Scripserat ille, Cruce, vt pòst docemus. Cum ipso Seruatore vtrimque secus latrones duo fixi: quos duo Euangelistæ diserte λησὰς appellant, Lucas paullò communiùs ληστὰς. Deinde Sicariatus. Paulus: In honestiores (sicarios) pœna capitis vindicari placuit, humiliores vero in Crucem tolluntur, aut bestiis subijciuntur. Tertio, crimen Falsi. Firmicus: Facient in crimine falsi comprehensos in Crucem tolli. Anne & furtum? ita, sed non Romae. Lampridius: Cum quaereretur a regibus, quid apud eos fures paterentur? illi responderunt, Crucem. Et mirum ni è Gallis Germanisue isti reges, quorum moribus etiam nunc Fures ad furcam. Alia etiam crimina in hanc poenam, ne ambigas: sed ego sileo, quae testibus aut tabulis non consigno.
units.tr: But what of free men? Crucifixion was rare, as I said above. Indeed Lactantius seems to exclude this class altogether, where he speaks of Christ: Why, if he was God and willed to die, was he not afflicted with some more honourable kind of death? Why especially the cross? Why the infamous kind of punishment, which seems unworthy even of a free man, however guilty? But that assertion must be qualified. Crucifixion was indeed unworthy of a citizen, and I do not believe it was inflicted on such men except against the law and out of cruelty. The baser free men and the provincials were certainly not exempt from it. And these are the crimes for which people were crucified. First, robbery. Seneca: Someone committed robbery. What then did he deserve? To be hanged. Take care not to interpret this as some other kind of hanging. Petronius: The emperor ordered the robbers of the province to be fixed to crosses. Apuleius: Nail that robber, the destroyer of my dear children, to a cross. The jurist Callistratus: It has been decided by many that notorious robbers, in the places where they have roamed, are to be fixed to a gallows. He had written to a cross, as we shall show later. With the Saviour himself, two robbers were fixed, one on either side. The two evangelists plainly call them robbers [ληστάς]; Luke uses the more common word [ληστάς]. Next, assassins. Paulus: It has been decided that the more honourable assassins are punished by capital punishment, but the humbler ones are raised on the cross or thrown to the beasts. Third, the crime of forgery. Firmicus: They shall have those caught in the crime of forgery lifted onto the cross. And theft too? Yes, but not at Rome. Lampridius: When kings were asked what thieves suffered among them, they answered: the cross. And it would be no surprise if those kings were Gauls or Germans, whose customs even now hang thieves on the gallows. Other crimes too were punished with this penalty, do not doubt it; but I say nothing of those I cannot confirm by witnesses or documents.

units.la: CAP. XIIII. Quae causa falsò assignata in Cruce Christi? videri Innouationem & Seditionem esse.
units.tr: CAP. XIIII. What cause was falsely assigned for the cross of Christ? That it was seen as innovation and sedition.

units.la: CVM haec vidimus, pie non curiose quaero, in Seruatore nostro quis praetextus (nam causa nunquam fuit) ad Crucem? Blasphemiam aliquis dixerit, ex vocibus aut judicijs Iudaeorum. Atque ipsi sane ita apud Pontificem accusant, & huic noxae testes quaeruntur, & ipse denique Pontifex eius damnat. Attamen, si legem spectes, hi tales lapidibus, non cruce puniti. An non verius ac simpliciius, totum illud judicium, etsi judicij dissimile, Romanis moribus legibusque directum? Mihi videatur. & respondeam damnatum innoxium nostrum agnum, quasi Seditionis nomine & Regni affectati. Certe Romana lege, auctores seditionis aut tumultus, pro quali-
units.tr: When we have seen these things, let me ask, piously and not curiously, what pretext there was for the cross in our Saviour (for there was never any cause). Someone might say blasphemy, from the words or judgments of the Jews. Indeed they accuse him of this before the High Priest, witnesses are sought for this offence, and the High Priest himself condemns him. Yet if you look to the law, such men were punished by stoning, not by the cross. Is it not truer and simpler that the whole of that trial, though unlike a proper trial, was conducted according to Roman customs and laws? So it seems to me. And I answer that our innocent lamb was condemned under the name of sedition and of aspiring to kingship. Certainly under Roman law, the instigators of sedition or tumult, according to the rank-

units.la: Christus non ob blasphemiam fixus. Potius ob regni cupidinem. qualitatis dignitate, aut in Crucem tolluntur, aut bestiis obijciuntur. Quod autem sic etiam apud Pi-latum accusatus, Lucas clarè: Hunc inuenimus subuertentem gentem nostram, & prohibentem tributa dare Cesari, & dicentem se Christum regem esse. Credidit, nec credidit Pilatus: & Titulum tamen caussamq; mortis inscripsit, Rex Iudaeorum. Ex Iudaeorum quidem libris si rem decidimus, intricamur. nec vsquam traditum clarè quae noxa ad crucem, nisi quod Philo prodidit de Homicidis. contrà quos ait Legislatorem mille mortis genera, si potuisset, dilecturum fuisse: cum non potuit, ... poenam aliam adjunxit, jubens homicidas & sicarios crucifigi.
