Sed tuâ pace Philo, vbi hoc Legislator? nusquam expresse. hoc tantùm vniuersè: Quando peccauerit homo, quod morte plectendum est, & adjudicatus morti appensus fuerit in patibulo. Peccatum non designat: & frustrà credo fore, si quis nunc quaerat. Tamen Theologi vidento. ego
units.tr: Christ was fixed not for blasphemy but rather for ambition to be king. ...by the dignity of their station, they are either raised on the cross or thrown to the beasts. That he was accused in this way before Pilate too, Luke makes clear: We found this man subverting our nation, forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ the King. Pilate believed it, and yet did not believe it; still he inscribed the title and the cause of death: King of the Jews. If we try to settle the matter from the books of the Jews, we become entangled, and nowhere is it clearly handed down what offence merits the cross, except what Philo reports about homicides: Against whom he says the Lawgiver would have chosen a thousand kinds of death, had he been able; since he could not... he added another penalty, ordering homicides and assassins to be crucified. But with respect, Philo, where is this Lawgiver? Nowhere expressly. Only this in general: When a man has sinned in a way that must be punished by death, and having been condemned to death, he shall be hanged on a gibbet. It does not name the sin, and I think it would be in vain if anyone sought it now. Still, let the theologians look into it. I...

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: Crux interdum liberè & laxè vagata: in hostes, in seditiosos, in Christianos, in feminas denique.
units.tr: The cross sometimes wandered freely and loosely: against enemies, against seditious persons, against Christians, and finally against women.

units.la: IN hos ergo tales ex ordine & more Crux vsurpata. Interdum regnum ei largius, & praesertim apud reges. nam hi ex libidine saepe ita saeuierunt in hostes aut rebelles, & vno tempore multos. Alexander Magnus vt supra tetigi, duo millia Tyriorum, capta eorum vrbe, crucifixit. Alius minutus Alexander in Iudæa, ἐσπώμψ⊗ ἐν πόλῳ μὴ τῶν παλμαχίδων, ἀνεσαύρωσε περὶ ... Conuiuans in publico & conspicuo loco vnà cùm pellicibus, iussit in Crucem dari Iudæorum ad octingentos. Quinctilius etiam Varus, ex eâdem gente, ob nescio quem motum, ἀνεσαύρωσε περὶ διχιλίας: crucifixit circiter bis mille. At Titus in obsidione illâ exitiali, quingenos, & plures, in singulos dies Crucibus affixit: καὶ διὰ τὸ πλῆθος χώρας τε ἐνελείπετο τοῖς Σταυροῖς, καὶ Σταυροὶ τοῖς σώμασι: & ob multitudinem terra Crucibus, & Cruces corporibus deerant. Nota, nota. historicâ hæc fide, non attollendi causâ dicuntur, & ab eo qui vidit, Iosepho. Nec ego miseror. abi pessima natio, hæc præmia Crucis illius, quam impiè posuisti nostro & tuo (voluisses modò) Seruatori. Iam & Augustus confecto bello Siculo, * sex millia seruorum, quorum domini non exstabant, in Crucem egit. Et in Christianos Tyranni crebrò adhibuerunt, atque eos numerosos. Lego vno tempore, vno loco, ad millia decem sic interfecta. Atqui nec à fœmineo sexu abstinuerunt hoc supplicium. & Tiberius, ob adulteratam in templo Isidis Paulinam, Τὺς τε ἱερέας ἀνεσαύρωσε, καὶ τὼ Ιδνυ ὀλέσης ... & Sacerdotes crucifixit, & Idam (ancillæ nomen) quæ corruptela causa fuerat. E Christianis etiam Beata
units.tr: So the cross was used in this order and manner against such people. Sometimes its use was more widespread, especially among kings, for they often raged out of lust against enemies or rebels, and against many at one time. Alexander the Great, as I touched on above, after capturing the city of Tyre, crucified two thousand Tyrians. Another, lesser Alexander in Judea, [ἐσπώμψ⊗ ἐν πόλῳ μὴ τῶν παλμαχίδων, ἀνεσαύρωσε περὶ ...] feasting in a public and conspicuous place with his concubines, ordered about eight hundred Jews to be put on crosses. Quinctilius Varus too, from the same nation, on account of I know not what disturbance, [ἀνεσαύρωσε περὶ διχιλίας] crucified about two thousand. But Titus, during that deadly siege, fixed five hundred and more to crosses each day: [καὶ διὰ τὸ πλῆθος χώρας τε ἐνελείπετο τοῖς Σταυροῖς, καὶ Σταυροὶ τοῖς σώμασι] and because of the multitude there was a lack of ground for the crosses and of crosses for the bodies. Note, note. These things are related with historical fidelity, not for the sake of exalting anyone, and by one who saw them, Josephus. Nor do I pity them. Go, most wicked nation; these are the rewards of that cross which you impiously set up against our Saviour and yours (if only you had wished it). Likewise Augustus, when the Sicilian war was finished, put six thousand slaves to the cross, whose masters could not be found. And tyrants have often applied it against Christians, and in large numbers. I read that at one time, in one place, some ten thousand were so killed. Yet they did not refrain from this punishment even for the female sex. And Tiberius, on account of Paulina, who had been corrupted in the temple of Isis, [Τὺς τε ἱερέας ἀνεσαύρωσε, καὶ τὼ Ιδνυ ὀλέσης ...] crucified the priests, and Ida (the name of a maidservant), who had been the cause of the corruption. Among Christians too, Blessed

units.la: {*} Est idem quod ex Dione supra cap. xii. Beata Eulalia, vngulas flammásque perpessa, demum cruci affixa martyrij coronam accepit. Sed & in Corsica, sancta Julia virgo crucis supplicio coronata est. Plura in Martyrum historijs exempla reperies, &, si voles, addes.
units.tr: This is the same as what is taken from Dio above, chap. xii. Blessed Eulalia, having endured claws and flames, was at last fixed to a cross and received the crown of martyrdom. But also in Corsica, the holy virgin Julia was crowned by the punishment of the cross. You will find more examples in the histories of the martyrs, and, if you wish, you may add them.

units.la: I. LIPSI DE CRVCE LIBER II. Cap. I.
units.tr: I. Lipsius, On the Cross, Book II, Chapter I.

units.la: Transitio ad Modum figendi praemissum de atrocitate huius supplicij, quod Summum & Extremum dictum.
units.tr: Transition to the method of fixing, previously announced, and on the atrocity of this punishment, which was called the highest and extreme.

units.la: IXI satis Quid Crux & Cuiusmodi fuerit, Vbi & Quare vsurpata: pergo longius, & vniuersum hoc poenale aedificium exstruo, per singula etiam membra. Dicam enim Quomodo vsurpata: & non animis solùm, sed paene oculis subijciam saeuitiam & foeditatem ejus supplicij: quae sane magna. Nec temere Cicero crudelissimum teterrimumque appellauit: & poëta Nonnus ἐλέγχισον ἵνα πολμόν: damnatissimum quod- Edam fatum. Quin etiam Iurisconsulti, nomine Summi supplicij, velut ob eminentiam, designant istud. Paulus: Summo supplicio, id est Cruce, afficiuntur. Ab eadem mente Supremum Vlpianus dixit: Si liberi sint, ad bestias dari; si serui, supremo supplicio affici. cum enim aliud non exprimat, & de seruis responsum sit, jure capio Crucem. Cur non ignem? inquies: cum Tertullianus etiam dixerit & censuerit, Summam ignium poenam? Quia ex Iurisconsultorum mente, Crux etiam supra ignem. Certè Paulus hoc ordine Summi supplicij tria genera recensetr: Crucem, Crematonem, Decollationem. Praeit, vt vides, Crux: & cum causa, si infamiam, magnitudinem, & praesertim diuturnitatem poenarum in ea attendis. Dicta haec ipsa Extrema poena. vt in Apuleio de seruo cruciando: Certum extremae poenae, quae more maiorum in eum competit. An & sic Arnobius? Crucem mereatur extremam, quisquis vobis dominis supplicarit. Quod tamen etiam laxè, & de peste aut pernicie capit interpretari.
units.tr: I have now said enough about what the cross was, what sort it was, where it was used and why. I will go further and build up this whole penal structure, down to its individual parts. For I shall explain how it was used, and I shall set before the eyes, almost, as well as the mind, the cruelty and foulness of this punishment, which is certainly great. Cicero did not call it most cruel and most horrible without reason, and the poet Nonnus called it the most shameful [ἐλέγχισον ἵνα πολμόν] of fates, one most damned. Indeed, the jurists also use the name of the highest punishment for it, as if by way of eminence. Paulus says: They are punished with the highest punishment, that is, the cross. With the same meaning Ulpian called it the supreme: If they are free, they are to be given to the beasts; if slaves, they are to be punished with the supreme punishment. Since he names no other, and the answer concerns slaves, I rightly take the cross. Why not fire, you will ask, since Tertullian also called and judged fire the highest punishment? Because in the jurists' view the cross stands above fire. Certainly Paulus lists the three kinds of highest punishment in this order: the cross, burning, beheading. As you see, the cross comes first, and with reason, if you consider the infamy, the severity and especially the long duration of the pains in it. These same words name it the extreme punishment, as in Apuleius on torturing a slave: the certain extreme punishment which, after the manner of our ancestors, falls upon him. And does Arnobius use it so? Whoever has pleaded against you, his masters, deserves the extreme cross. Yet this may also be taken loosely, of any plague or ruin.

units.la: CAP. II. Duplex figendi Modus, Vulgaris & Rarus. In illo Flagellatio ex more semper anteiuit.
units.tr: CHAP. II. The two ways of fixing, the common and the rare. In the common way, scourging always went before.

units.la: SED saeui foediique quid in hoc supplicio fuerit, Modusipse dixerit: quem graphicè imus repraesentatum. Vt magis possit; partimur,& duplicè eum facimus: Vulgarem, & Rarum. Illum, qui receptissimus & quo vulgò vtebantur. Alterum, qui magis sepositus, nec in tam assiduo vsu. De illo priùs: & quidem ordine hæc tria, Qua ante fixionem, Qua in ipsâ, Qua post ipsam. Ante Fixionem duo adhibita: Flagellatio & Deductio. Flagellatio quidem sollennis antecessor, & raro in crucem dati nisi sic purpurati. Apud Liuium, de seruis coniuratis: Multi occisi, multi capti, aliý verberati crucibus affixi. Verberatos ecce prædixit. Alexander apud Curtium, moris huius retinens, eos qui Petram obstinatè defenderant, omnes verberibus affectos, sub ipsis radicibus Petra crucibus iussit affigi. Iudæi, apud Iosephum, flagellati & præcruciati ante mortem omne genus verberibus, crucifigebantur. Philo item narrans Iudæos Alexandriæ in crucem actos à Flacco, hoc addit: postquam flagellati fuissent in theatro. Sollennis ergo mos, imò lex: & horrendum Carmen diserte canebat: Verbera intra aut extra pomœrium: & tum denique succinebat, Arbori infelici suspendito.
units.tr: BUT what was cruel and foul in this punishment, the method itself will show, and we have set it out here in a picture. So that it may be better understood, we divide it and make it twofold: the common and the rare. The first is the most usual, and the one commonly used. The other is more remote, and not in such constant use. Let us deal first with the common one, and in order these three parts: what comes before fixing, what happens in the fixing itself, and what follows after. Before fixing, two things were applied: scourging and leading out. Scourging was the solemn forerunner, and men were seldom given to the cross unless they had first been so reddened. In Livy, about the conspirators among the slaves: Many were killed, many captured, and others, scourged, were fixed to crosses. Here he foretold the scourging. Alexander, in Curtius, keeping this custom, ordered those who had stubbornly defended the Rock, all of them flogged, to be fixed to crosses at the very foot of the Rock. The Jews, in Josephus, scourged and tortured beforehand with every kind of blow, were crucified before death. Philo too, telling how the Jews of Alexandria were led to the cross by Flaccus, adds this: after they had been scourged in the theatre. So it was a solemn custom, indeed a law, and a dreadful song openly sang: Blows inside or outside the pomerium, and then at last they answered: Hang him on the unlucky tree.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: Flagellorum & Virgarum discrimen. Illa magis vilia, & magis acerba esse. solere & talis asperari.
units.tr: The difference between whips and rods. That the former are cheaper and more cruel, and that they were commonly made harsher with knucklebones.

units.la: VERBERATI igitur: sed vtrum virgis an flagellis? Illas interdum reperio: sed magis crebrò ista. Discrimen enim esse scimus: & quia Virgæ honestiores, inhonestissimo huic supplicio adtributa Flagra. Cicero illudens & cauillans in Labienum: Porcia lex virgas ab omnium ciuium corpore amouit; hic misericors flagella retulit. Quomodo retulit? vna cum Cruce, cui hæc adiuncta. Dixi inhonestiora fuisse. Ita, & propriè seruorum. Sic apud Terentium
units.tr: Were they beaten then with rods or with whips? I find both at times, but the whip more often. We know there was a difference, and rods were regarded as more honourable, while whips were assigned to this most dishonourable punishment. Cicero, mocking and jeering at Labienus, says: "The Porcian law removed rods from the body of every citizen; this merciful man has brought back whips." How did he bring them back? Together with the cross, to which they were attached. I have said they were more dishonourable, and indeed they were properly for slaves. So in Terence:

units.la: ad necem operiere loris. S A N. loris liber?
units.tr: "You will wait to be killed with thongs." SAN. "Thongs, for a free man?"

units.la: Exclamat & indignatur, vt in re insolenti, quòd libero intentata lora. Et ab hac notâ seruilem conditionem Menæ Horatius opprobrat:
units.tr: He cries out and is indignant, as at something unheard of, that thongs were threatened against a free man. And Horace reproaches Menas with this mark of servile condition:

units.la: Sectus flagellis hic triumuiralibus Præconis ad fastidium.
units.tr: "Here he is, cut with the triumvirs' whips, to the disgust of the herald."

units.la: Significata a Triumuiris (Imperium ijs & animaduersio in seruos) cæsum flagris publicè, idque sub præconis voce. Itaque & Macer Ic.tus scripsit, Ex quibus caussis liber fustibus, ex his seruum flagelis cadi. Et Impp. rescripserunt, mulierem habere iustas diuortij causas, si se verberibus, quæ ingenuo aliena sunt, afficientem maritum probauerit. Flagra hæc ipsa intelligunt: quæ cùm ab ingenuis, tum à fæminis remota maximè. Atque vt nouum & seuerum in Licinio Pontifice narrat Valerius: quòd ei virgo Vestalis, quia parum diligens ignis æterni custos fuisset, digna visa est, quæ flagro admoneretur. Flagella autem hæc aspera. adeò vt Vlpianus scripserit, ministrorum immanitate, multos sub eiusmodi flagellis interijsse. Et Horribile etiam id Horatio visum agnominare: Nec scutica dignum, horribili sectere flagello. Quod magis fuit, cum ea insitis talis aut officiculis exasperabant. Factum Romæ, atque alibi. Eustathius dici notat ἀσεφγαλῶϊὰς μαστίγας, τὰς ἐξ ἀσεφγάλων ενεινεφμένων καταχεστωμένας: Flagra talaria, qua talis insertis involutisque confecta sunt. Apud Athenæum quispiam recensét, in Parthis optimates quoque & Satrapas, vbi visum Regi, ῥάβδοις & ἰμάτων ἀσεφγαλῶϊς μαστιγοῦς: virgis & loris taxillatis cædi. Apuleius agnoscit, & Flagrum pecuinis ossibus cathenatum, scitè appellat. Ille idem Gallis Matrisdeûm adscribit. Arrepto flagro, inquit, quod semiuiris illis proprium gestamen est, contortis taeniis lanosi velleris prolixè fimbriatum, & multiugis talis ouium tessellatum, indidem sese multimodis commulcant ictibus. Et Plutarchus apposité ad eius lucem: Οὐδὲ μαστιγ& ἐλαυνέσεας δεόμεν&, ἀλλὰ ἀσεφγαλωτῆς ἐκείνης, ἢ σὺν Γάλλους πληθμελωδίας ἐν τοῖς μητρῴοις κολάζεται: Nec qui libera verberationis egeat, sed flagri illius taxillati, quo Gallos aliquid offendentes in sacris Magnæ matris coercent. An tale aliquod flagri genus, quo Christus etiam noster caesus? imaginantur, aut pingunt per pietatem nonnulli. Haud ego assero: sed illud Euangelistæ, cæsum esse & quidem flagro. Sic enim Matthæus, corruptâ ipsâ Latinâ voce: Τὸν δὲ Ἰησοῦν φραγελλώσας παρέδωκεν ἵνα σταυρωθῆ. Jesum cùm flagellasset, tradidit vt crucifigeretur. Ιμάτην, id est, lorum, flagellū appellat Nonnus. {y} Contra Coloss.
units.tr: That is, he was flogged publicly by the triumvirs (who had authority over slaves and their punishment), and this was announced by the voice of a herald. Hence the jurist Macer also wrote: "For those offences for which a free man is beaten with clubs, a slave is beaten with whips." And the emperors replied that a wife has just grounds for divorce "if she proves that her husband treats her with blows that are foreign to a freeborn person." They understand these to be whips, which were kept especially far from freeborn men and from women. And Valerius relates as something novel and severe against the pontiff Licinius that a Vestal virgin, "because she had been too careless a guardian of the eternal fire, was thought worthy to be admonished with a whip." These whips were harsh, so much so that Ulpian wrote: "through the savagery of the attendants, many died under whips of this kind." Horace also thought it a terrible thing to call them: "Nor are you worthy of the lash; you are cutting me with a dreadful whip." This was worse when they made the whips harsher with knucklebones inserted or attached. This was done at Rome and elsewhere. Eustathius notes that they are called "whips with knucklebones, those made of knucklebones fastened and covered in": "heel-bone whips, made with knucklebones inserted and wrapped in" [ἀστραγαλωτὰς μαστίγας, τὰς ἐξ ἀστραγάλων ἐνειλουμένας]. In Athenaeus someone recounts that among the Parthians even the nobles and satraps, when the king so decided, were beaten "with rods and with thongs weighted with knucklebones" [ῥάβδοις καὶ ἱμᾶσι ἀστραγαλωτοῖς μαστιγοῦσθαι]. Apuleius knows this too, and aptly calls it "a whip of knucklebones, chained with sheep bones." The same author ascribes it to the Galli, the priests of the Mother of the gods: "Seizing the whip, which is the particular equipment of those half-men, long-fringed with twisted woollen ribbons and studded with many knucklebones of sheep, they lash themselves in many ways with blows." And Plutarch, to the same point, says: "Nor does he need a whip that drives on freely, but that knucklebone-studded one with which the Galli are punished in the rites of the Great Mother when they offend in any way." Some people in their piety imagine or paint some such kind of whip with which our Christ too was struck. I do not assert this; but the Evangelist says that he was struck, and indeed with a whip. Thus Matthew, using a corrupted form of the Latin word: "When he had scourged Jesus, he handed him over to be crucified" [Τὸν δὲ Ἰησοῦν φραγελλώσας παρέδωκεν ἵνα σταυρωθῇ]. Nonnus calls the thong or whip [ἱμάς] by the name of a lash [μάστιξ]. Against the Colossians:

units.la: Ριγέδαιν Χεῖσοῖο δέμας φοίνιξεν ιμάσθλη.Horribili Christi corpus rubefecit habenâ.
units.tr: "Blood-red the body of Christ made the dreadful lash" [Ῥιγέδανον Χρίστοιο δέμας φοίνιξεν ἱμάσθλη].

units.la: CAP. IIII.
units.tr: CHAP. IIII.

units.la: Solitos ad Columnam verberari; atque aliàs per viam. De ipsâ columnâ cui sacrum corpus annexum.
units.tr: Those who were customarily scourged at the Column, and at other times along the way. Of the column itself, to which the sacred body was tied.

units.la: SED obserua. Flagellatio hæc non vno semper loco, aut tempore. Aut enim ante Deductionem vtebantur, idque domi: quod in Seruatore factum. Aut in ipsâ Deductione, per viam: quod moris fuit magis prisci. Si domi, ligabant ferè ad columnam. Firmamenta huic ritui, non tam multa reperio, reperio tamen. Artemidorus vbi somnium narrat serui, qui visus sibi ab hero δ\έφεδαι, deglubi & turpiter tangi: addit, ὣς οδεῖς νίου πολλὰς ἔλαβε πληγάς: columna alligatus, multas accepit plagas. Phileas etiam apud Eusebium, sæuitiam in Martyres, qui Alexandriæ, referens: Ἄλλοι δὲ ὡς τῆς νίοσιν αὐτοσφάγπου ἐδοῦν: Alij autem ad columnas vultibus inter se aduersis, astringebantur: & de flagellatione sentit. An & Plautum sic accipimus?
units.tr: But observe: this flogging did not always take place in one spot or at one time. Either it was inflicted before the Condemnation, and then at home, as was done to the Saviour; or it was inflicted during the Condemnation itself, along the way, which was the more ancient custom. If it was at home, they usually bound the victim to a column. I find not many, but still some, testimonies for this practice. Artemidorus, in relating a dream in which a slave seemed to his master to be flayed and foully handled [δέρεσθαι], adds that bound to a column, he received many blows. Philea also, in Eusebius, when recounting the cruelty toward the martyrs at Alexandria, says: Others, however, were bound to the columns, facing one another [Ἄλλοι δὲ πρὸς τοὺς κίονας ἀντιπρόσωποι ἐδέοντο]; and he means a flogging. Or do we understand Plautus in this way?

units.la: —Abducite hunc
units.tr: Take this man away,

units.la: Intrò, atqʒ adstringite ad columnam fortiter.
units.tr: Inside with him, and bind him fast to the column.

units.la: Ego quidem: etsi ad custodiam modò id factum aliquis pertendat. Sed de Seruatore nostro non ambiguum, piis quidem & in religione antiquis. Etsi enim Euangelia non exprimunt: tamen secuti Patres. Prudentius clarè, & cum ritus quo-que prisci attestatione: ——atque columna Annexus, tergum dedit, ut seruile, flagellis.
units.tr: For my part, though someone may argue that this was done only for custody. But concerning our Saviour there is no doubt, at least among the pious and those who are ancient in religion. For although the Gospels do not express it, the Fathers followed it, and Prudentius clearly, and with the attestation of the ancient rite as well: —bound to a column, he offered his back to the whips, as a slave would.

units.la: Hieronymus & suo æuo exstitisse commemorat: Ostendebatur illi (Paulæ) Columna, Ecclesiæ porticum sustinens infecta cruore Domini, ad quam vinctus dicitur & flagellatus. Indicat fulcri vsum habuisse in ædificio tepli: quod ipsum Prudentius. Perstat adhuc, templumq; gerit veneranda columna. Etsi Bedæ tempore in medio Ecclesiæ fuisse, ipse testatur. Meminit huius quoque, & miraculorum per eam, Gregorius Turonensis. Hæc domi flagellatio, & ad columnam: quid per viam sub furcâ id factum, de quâ in * loco dicam.
units.tr: Jerome also records that it still existed in his own age: There was shown to her (Paula) a column, supporting the portico of the Church, stained with the blood of the Lord, to which he is said to have been bound and scourged. He indicates that it served as a support in the building of the temple; Prudentius himself says as much: The venerable column still stands and bears the temple. Bede testifies that in his time it stood in the middle of the Church. Gregory of Tours also mentions it, and the miracles wrought through it. This flogging at home, at the column: as for what was done along the way, under the yoke, I shall speak of it in its own place (*).

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CAP. V.

units.la: Crucem suam tulisse, aut totam, aut ejus partem.
units.tr: That he carried his cross, either the whole of it or a part of it.

units.la: AD Deductionem venio, in quâ duo obser-uo, Ludibrium & Tormentum. Ludibrium, quòd ipsi coacti crucem suam ferre, aut certè eius partem: ut verè esset illud quod dicitur, Suo sibi iumento malum. Artemidorus: βασάζειν ὑπὸ τῶν δαιμόνων χθονίων κακύργῳ μὲν ἰδόντι Σταυρὸν αὐτῷ σημαίνει. ἔοικε γὰρ καὶ ὁ Σίσυφος θανάτῳ, ὡς ὁ μέλλων ἀποθνήσκειν ... ἀπολύσας ... βασάζει: ferre aliquem Deorum inferorum, malefico quidem id videnti Crucem prodicit. Similis enim & Crux morti; & qui in eâ figendus, prius eam portat. Plutarchus etiam comparatione quadam vtili: Καὶ τὰ μὲν σώματα τῶν κολαζολαζομένων ἕκαστος τῶν κακούργων ἐπφέρει τὸν αὐτῷ Σταυ-ρὸν, ἡ ἡ κακία τῶν πολασηείων ἐφ' ἑαυτῷ ἕκαστον ᾧ αὐ-τῆς τεκτάινε̈): Et corpore quidem quisque malefico-rum suam effert Crucem: malitia autem cruciatuum quemque in se, ex se, gignit & fabricatur. Benè hoc & salubriter Plutarchus: & Dij de eq (ait quispiam) quàm malè est extrà legem viuentibus? quidquid meruerunt, semper expectant. Sed repono me in gradum. Ferebant Crucem. Atque ita Iohannes de Christo: βασάζων τὸν Σταυρὸν αὐτὸς ἐξ-ἠλθεν εἰς τὸν λεγόμενον κεφαλίου τόπον: baiulans suam Crucem, exiuit in locum Caluariae dictum. Quâ solâ causâ veteră quædam vaticinia aut imagines Doctores nostri ad Christum trahunt. Vt Ter-tullianus hoc de Isaaco. Cùm, inquit, Isaac à patre hostia ducereture, & lignum ipse sibi portaret, Christi exitum jam tunc denotabat, in victimam concessi a Patre, lignum passionis suæ baiulantis. Idem in Isaiæ verbis istis: Cuius imperium factum est super humerum ipsius. Solus, ait, novus rex Christus novæ gloriæ potestatem & sublimitatem in humero extulit, id est Crucem. Et Christus sanè totam plenamque Crucem tulit. Ni fecisset, quid opus erat auxiliatore & subsequâ, qui adleuâsset? Alij non semper totam: atque ideò caute prædixi, ejus partem. Nam qui ritu veteri sub furcâ cæsi ducebantur, ferebant non nisi istam. Imò interdum nec istam. Pone in arbore aliquâ crucifixum, & subitò: profectò, præter se, nihil tulit.
units.tr: I come now to the Leading-out, in which I observe two things: Mockery and Torment. Mockery, because they were forced to carry their own cross, or at least part of it, so that the saying was truly fulfilled: Evil to him from his own beast of burden. Artemidorus: To carry (a cross) is signified by the demons of the underworld; for a criminal who sees it, it foretells a cross for him. For Sisyphus too is like death, as one who is about to die ... having released ... carries: to carry something belonging to the gods of the underworld, for a wrongdoer seeing it, betokens a cross. For the cross is like death, and the one who is to be fastened to it carries it first. Plutarch also makes a useful comparison: Indeed, the bodies of the wrongdoers who are punished each bear the cross for himself, while the wickedness of the tortures each one creates and fashions in himself, out of himself. Plutarch says this well and wholesomely: And the gods, (someone says) how wretched it is for those who live outside the law! Whatever they have deserved, they always await. But I return to my point. They carried the cross. And so John says of Christ: Bearing his own cross, he went out into the place called Calvary. For this reason alone our teachers draw certain ancient prophecies or images to Christ. As Tertullian does with Isaac: When Isaac, he says, was led by his father as a victim, and carried the wood himself, he was already then foreshadowing Christ's departure, given up by the Father as a victim, carrying the wood of his passion. The same writer, on those words of Isaiah: His rule was made upon his shoulder. The new king Christ alone, he says, bore the power and the loftiness of his new glory upon his shoulder, that is, the cross. And Christ surely bore the whole and entire cross. If he had not, why would there have been need of a helper and a follower to lift it with him? Others did not always carry the whole; and so I carefully said part of it. For those who were led to be beaten under the gallows, according to the old custom, carried only this, and sometimes not even this. Put someone crucified on some tree: and suddenly, surely, he carried nothing but himself.

units.la: * Vide lib. iii.
units.tr: * See book iii.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: Deductos cum vexatione, Stimulis etiam actos.
units.tr: Led away with harassment, driven also with goads.

units.la: TORMENTVM etiam in Deductione: quia trahere, diuexare, & stimulis agere per viam solent. Dionysius de tractione: διʼ ἀλοεγὶς αὐτὸν μαστιγούμενον ἐπέλασεν ἔλκειν: per forum flagellatum ipsum, trahere eos iussit. Nec dubium est quin impulerint, deiecerint, erexerint, per saeuitiam aut per lusum. De Stimulis etiam non temere addo. & aperte auctor adfirmandi Plautus, apud quem conseruo seruus:
units.tr: There is also Torment in the Leading-out, because they are accustomed to drag, harass and drive with goads along the way. Dionysius on the dragging: having had him scourged through the marketplace, he ordered them to drag him. Nor is there doubt that they pushed, threw down, and raised them up again, through cruelty or as sport. About the goads I do not add lightly, and the writer Plautus is a clear witness to what I affirm, where a slave speaks to a fellow slave:

units.la: O carnificinum cribrum! quod credo fore, Ita te forabunt patibulatum per vias Stimulis, si noster huc reuenerit senex.
units.tr: O sieve of the executioner! I believe it will be so: they will pierce you through the streets with goads, as one hung on the gibbet, if our old master comes back here.

units.la: Habes Stimulos, idque in Patibulato (ad furcam astricto) & per vias. Iungit iterum cum Cruce Plautus: Stimulos, Laminas, Crucesque. & alias meminit, sed sic vt seorsim eos fuisse sciamus inter cruciatus & tormenta, sicut laminas & ignes. Pictores nostri (nec heri, aut hodie) asserculum siue tabellam imae Christi vesti appingunt, quae clauis praeacutis confixa pedibus calcibusq; euntis illidatur: nunquid alludentes ad hanc Destimulationem? quae tamen stimulis aliis facta. quos oblongos, siue e sudibus praeacutis, siue & ferro praefixis gestabant ad hunc vsum. Sumptum a bubus, quos sic exstimulabant. Sed nisi ea Pictorum mens, ipsi vidento: ego inuenticulae eius nec auctor sim, nec interpres.
units.tr: You have goads, and that in the case of one hanged on the gibbet (bound to the fork) and through the streets. Plautus again joins them with the cross: Goads, plates, and crosses. He mentions them elsewhere too, but in such a way that we know they were separate among the torments and tortures, just as the plates and fires were. Our painters (not only yesterday or today) paint on the lowest part of Christ's garment a little board or tablet, which is struck against his feet and heels as he walks, fixed with very sharp nails: can they be alluding to this Driving-on-with-goads? Yet that was done with other goads, which they carried for this use, long ones, made either of sharpened stakes or with iron points fixed on. Taken from the oxen, which they goaded in this way. But unless that is the painters' intention, let them see to it themselves: I am neither the author nor the interpreter of this little invention of theirs.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: In ipsa Fixione nudi in crucem dati: an altam, an in terrâ depositam? id quaesitum, & utrumque firmatum.
units.tr: In the fixing itself, the men were laid naked on the cross: was the cross raised up, or lying on the ground? This is asked, and both are affirmed.

units.la: {a}ISTA sunt quae Ante fixionem: nunc quae In ipsâ. Tria considero, Suspensionem, Astrictionem, Inscriptionem. Suspensio praeit, & ante illam etiam Nudatio. quia simul ad crucem ventum, spoliabant hominem, & sic in eam dabant. Receptum hoc in plerisque supplicijs, velut Naturae suasu, quae nudos induxit in vitâ & educit: etiam in isto. Artemidorus: Σταυρῳδῆται ἀγαθὸν τὰ πένητα. ἡ γὰρ ὕψηλὸς ὁ σαωρωδείς. οὓς δὲ πλουσίους βλάπτει. γυμνοὶ γὰρ σαυροῦνται. Crucifigi bonum pauperi, quia sublimis est crucifixus: noxium vero diviti, quia nudi crucifiguntur. In Christo factum hoc observes: quem Euangelistae narrant recepisse vestes post flagellationem jam deducendum, & posuisse iterum deductum. Ergo nudi dati in crucem: sed Iacentem an Erectam? Pro Iacente, Acta vetera de Pionio Martyre: Ultro se vestimentis spoliavit, & in caelum suspiciens ac Deo gratias agens, super lignum seipsum extendit, militique tradidit ut clavis configeretur. Satis clare: atque etiam mox clarius: Eum igitur ligno fixum erexerunt. Dici nihil potest, quin fixio hic in Iacente facta fuerit, quae post erecta. Et ratio etiam aliqua suadet. Nonne enim facilius hominem sic affigere supinum & inclinatum...
units.tr: These are the things that come before the fixing; now I consider what happens in it itself. I consider three things: the suspension, the fastening, and the inscription. Suspension comes first, and before it the stripping. For as soon as they came to the cross, they stripped the man and so gave him over to it. This was customary in most punishments, as if by the prompting of nature, which brought us into life naked and brings us out so; and it held in this one too. Artemidorus: To be crucified is good for the poor, for the one who is crucified is raised high; but it harms the rich, for they are crucified naked. You will notice this was done to Christ, whom the Evangelists tell us had his garments taken off after the scourging, and had them put back on when he was led away. So they were given to the cross naked. But was he laid down or raised up? For the laid-down position, there are the old Acts concerning the martyr Pionius: He stripped himself of his garments of his own accord, and looking up to heaven and giving thanks to God, he stretched himself upon the wood and handed himself to the soldier to be nailed with spikes. That is clear enough, and what follows is clearer still: So they raised him, fixed to the wood. Nothing can be said more plainly than that the fixing here was done with him lying down, and that he was raised up afterwards. And some reason also seems to support it. For is it not easier to fasten a man in this way, lying on his back and bent back...

units.la: {b} Pro Iacente. inclinatum: quàm tollere in erectam, pendulum, labentem, fortasse & reluctantem? Videtur. Tamen quòd in Erectam, plusculi adfirmant testes. Cicero in Gauiana cruce describenda: Quid attinuit, cum Mamertini more atque instituto suo Crucem fixissent post urbem in via Pompeia, te iubere figere in via quae Rhegium spectat? Et verba & rei seriem vide, obseruabis fixam primò crucem, & tum in eam datum. Idem in Rabiriana: In campo Martio Crucem ad ciuium supplicium defigi & constitui iubes. Stabat iam defixa, dum caussa diceretur, & cruciarium suũ exspectabat. Galba apud Suetonium, cuidam inclamanti se ciuem Romanum esse, multo prater ceteras altiorem & dealbatam crucem statui iussit. Statui, acrum suffigi. Iosephus de Iudaeo quodam a Ro-manis capto: O ὁ βασιλεὺς ὠργίσθη ... Bassus iussit defigi crucem, tanquam statim suspensurus in eâ Eleazarum. Denique & libro Esdrae: Ut omnis homo qui hanc mutauerit iussionem, tollatur lignum de domo ipsius, & erigatur, & configatur in eo. Vtrobique hîc erectio, fixionem antecedit. Nec video quid obduci possit: nisi istud infirmum, statutas quidem, sed sub aduentum noxij iterum demissas. Quis credat? aut irriti laboris quae ratio? Abnuunt etiam phrases veteres, quas scimus plerumque adsimiles rebus ipsis: Dicunt enim Tollere, Agere, Ferre, Dare in crucem: quae omnia elationis sunt aut molitionis. Item in ipsis fontibus, Excurrere, Ascendere, Salire in crucem: quae mihi videntur convenire non nisi in Erectam. Priorum phrasium exempla nota atque obvia sunt: posteriorum cape ista. Plautus:
units.tr: ...bent back, than to lift him up upright, hanging, sliding, and perhaps resisting? It seems so. Yet several witnesses affirm that it was done with him upright. Cicero, in describing the cross of Gavius: Why was it necessary, when the Mamertines had fixed their cross, in their own custom, outside the city on the Pompeian road, for you to order it to be fixed on the road that looks toward Rhegium? Look at both the words and the sequence of events, and you will observe that the cross was first fixed, and only then was the man given to it. The same in the speech for Rabirius: You order the cross to be driven in and set up in the Campus Martius for the punishment of citizens. It was already standing fixed while the case was being argued, and it awaited its victim. Galba, according to Suetonius, when a certain man kept shouting that he was a Roman citizen, ordered a cross to be set up for him, much higher than the rest and whitewashed. It was set up, that is, fixed upright. Josephus, of a Jew captured by the Romans: The king was angry... Bassus ordered a cross to be fixed, as if he were about to hang Eleazar on it at once. Finally, in the book of Ezra: That any man who shall change this decree, let a beam be taken from his house, and let it be raised up, and let him be fastened upon it. In both places here the raising precedes the fixing. Nor do I see what can be objected, except this weak point: that the cross was indeed set up, but was lowered again when the condemned man arrived. Who would believe that? Or what reason would there be for such useless labour? Ancient phrases also oppose it, and we know they usually match the things themselves. For they say to lift, to drive, to carry, to give someone to the cross; all of which imply raising or effort. Likewise in the sources themselves: to run out, to climb, to leap onto the cross; which seem to me to fit only an upright cross. Examples of the former phrases are familiar and common; take these of the latter. Plautus:

units.la: Ego dabo ei talentum primus, qui in crucem excucurrerit.
units.tr: I will give him a talent, the first one who has run out to the cross.

units.la: Crux illa nostra est, nos patibulum ascendimus.
units.tr: That cross is ours; we climb the gibbet.

units.la: Credo hercle adveniens nomen mutabit mihi, Faciet quoque extemplo Crucisalum me ex Chrysalo.
units.tr: By Hercules, I think, when he comes, he will change my name too, and he will make me a Crucisalus instead of a Chrysalus at once.

units.la: Sed & testes, in ipsa narratione, pro Erecta. Nonnus de Christo:
units.tr: But the witnesses also favour the upright cross in the narrative itself. Nonnus, on Christ:

units.la: Εἰς δόρυ τετραπλευρον, ἐπήορον, ὑψόθε γαίηςΟρθιον ἐξετάνυσσεν.
units.tr: Εἰς δόρυ τετράπλευρον, ἐπήορον, ὑψόθε γαίης ὄρθιον ἐξετάνυσσεν.

units.la: In lignum quadratum, altum, terráque levatum,Rectum extenderunt.
units.tr: Onto a four-sided wood, hanging high above the earth, they stretched him out upright.

units.la: Extentum manifesto ait sublimem, & super terram.
units.tr: By stretched out he plainly means raised up, and above the earth.

units.la: De eodem eadem Nazianzenus versibus lucu-lentis: Αὐτίχ' ὁμιλῶς ἱερανοδρόμῳ ξύλῳ Ἀνῆγον, ἦγον, ἦγον εἰς ἄκρον τέλος. Ορθὸς δ' ἐς ὀρθὸν αἰθέρ' ἐπρίζετο. Ἐ'σκλίνα δ' ἐγκάρσιον ἄλλον διὰ ἀὐθέως Ἐ'τειναν, ἐξέτειναν, ἡλωσαν χειρας, Πόδας δ' καθήλωσαν ἐν πηκτῷ ξύλῳ.
units.tr: Gregory Nazianzen says the same of the same thing in clear verses: at once they drove him up with the crowd onto the wood that runs up to heaven, up, up, up to the highest end. Upright he was fastened to the upright, reaching for the sky. Then they bent a cross-beam across, and stretched and stretched out his hands, and they nailed his feet to the wooden post.

units.la: Quorum versuum (haud sane * optimorum, liberè dicam) haec sententia. Ductum & subductum in altam crucem, ad ultimum eius finem: rectum ita statutum: tum ad transversarium lignum manus fixas: denique & pedes ad stipitem defixum.
units.tr: The sense of these verses (not, I will freely say, the best of verses) is this: He was led up and lifted onto the tall cross, to its very top; so he was set upright; then his hands were fixed to the transverse beam; and finally his feet were nailed to the upright stake.

units.la: Atque
units.tr: And

units.la: * Neque scio an ipsa Tragedia Germana Nazianzeni, Atque ista pro Erecta. In dissensu autem nos quid definimus? consensum, quâ licet. Dicimus vtrumque vsurpatum, sæpiùs tamen hoc postremum. Imò interim necessario hoc postremum. Pone enim in arbore suspensos (sæpe factum:) quomodo demitti ea potuit, & tunc attolli?
units.tr: * I do not know whether the German tragedy of Nazianzen itself is also for the upright cross. But in this disagreement what do we settle? We seek agreement as far as we can. We say that both were used, though the latter more often; indeed, at times the latter is necessary. For suppose men hanging on a tree (which often happened): how could they have been let down and then raised up?

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Clauis figi solitos, interdum funibus adstringi.
units.tr: That they were usually fixed with nails, and sometimes bound with ropes.

units.la: SED jam ad Adstrictionem transeo; quæ facta clauis, aut funibus, sed plurimùm illis. Seneca nominat: Cum refigere se crucibus conentur, in quas vnusquisque vestrum clauos suos ipse adigit. Ita legendum, non adiycit. Illi, inquit, conantur tollere se de crucibus suis: vos contrà, magis magisque affigitis, & clauos adigitis in lignum. Meminit & Apollo in oraculo quopiam, de Christo:
units.tr: But now I pass to binding, which was done with nails or ropes, but mostly with ropes. Seneca names it: When they try to pull themselves back off the crosses, on which each one of you drives in his own nails. Thus it should be read, does not add. He says: they try to lift themselves from their crosses; you, on the contrary, fix yourselves ever more firmly and drive your nails into the wood. Apollo too mentions it in some oracle about Christ:

units.la: Clauisq; & palis mortem exantlauit acerbam.
units.tr: And with nails and stakes he endured a bitter death.

units.la: Loquitur de hac eius morte per crucem: quia, vt Artemidorus ait, ἐκ ξύλων καὶ ἥλων γέγονεν ὁ σαυρὸς: ex lignis & clauis crux confecta est. Atque ab hac re Græcis passim ipsa crucifixio, σταυρώσεις dicta: quasi dicas clavi-fixio. Vlpianus in Demosthenem explicat σταυροῦσθαι, Σταυρῷ σταυροῦσθαι τῆς ἥλοις: cruci affigi clauis. Et fortasse eò respexit Strabo cùm de Cantabris dixit, ἀναπεπηγότας ἐπὶ τῶν Σταυρῶν: suffixos in crucibus. Ergo de clauis cer- rum tum: an etiam de funibus? sunt exempla. Ausonius suum Cupidinem facit
units.tr: He speaks of this death of his by the cross, because, as Artemidorus says, the cross was made of wood and nails [ἐκ ξύλων καὶ ἥλων γέγονεν ὁ σταυρός]. From this the Greeks commonly call the crucifixion itself staurōseis [σταυρώσεις], as if you were to say "nail-fixing." Ulpian, in his commentary on Demosthenes, explains staurousthai [σταυροῦσθαι] thus: to be fixed to a cross with nails [Σταυρῷ σταυροῦσθαι τῆς ἥλοις]. Perhaps Strabo had this in mind when he spoke of the Cantabrians as fixed on crosses [ἀναπεπηγότας ἐπὶ τῶν Σταυρῶν]. So much for nails, as a certainty. But what of ropes? There are examples. Ausonius portrays his Cupid thus:

units.la: Deuinctum post terga manus, substrictaq; plantis Vincula morentem.
units.tr: With his hands bound behind his back, and cords drawn tight about his feet, holding him back.

units.la: Et communi ligandi verbo in hac re Artemidorus vsus: Σταυροῦσθαι, inquit, ἀνδρὶ ἀγαμῷ γάμον ςαυροσλοφεῖ διὰ τὸν δέσιν: Crucifigi (in somnis) viro calibi nuptias designat, ob ligaturam. quia scilicet ligno jungitur copulaturque. Plinius inter magicas ineptias Spartum etiam e cruce numerat, id est sparteos funes. Quid, quod D. Andreas ita alligatus? Abdias aperte,& caussam etiam addit: Proconsul mandat quaestionariis, ut ligatis manibus & pedibus, non clauis affixus suspenderetur, quo diutino cruciatu deficeret. Ex quo colligas, habitum id magis saeuum. Etsi prima fortasse crucifixio talis,& in Liuij priscis scriptisque libris legas: Arbori infelici reste suspendito. Reste, inquam, additur: quod tamen heri ac nuper ejecerunt correctores. An sic quoque appensi latrones bini, qui cum Christo? Vulgo sentiunt, nec aliter pingunt. Tamen falsò: quia illi, pariter ac Christus, fixi. Nonnus adfirmat.
units.tr: Artemidorus also uses the common verb for binding in this connection: To be crucified [σταυροῦσθαι], he says, in a dream signifies marriage for an unmarried man, because of the binding [ἀνδρὶ ἀγάμῳ γάμον σημαίνει διὰ τὸν δέσμον], of course because he is joined and coupled to a wood. Pliny, among magical nonsense, also counts spartum taken from a cross, that is, ropes of esparto. What of St Andrew, bound in this way? Abdias states it plainly and adds the reason: The proconsul orders the torturers that he be hung up, with his hands and feet bound, not fixed with nails, so that he would die of a long torment. From this you may gather that this form was the crueller one. Yet perhaps the earliest crucifixion was of this kind, and in the old manuscripts of Livy you may read: Hang him by a rope on an unlucky tree. "By a rope," I say, is added; yet the editors of our own day and of late have removed it. Were the two thieves who were hung with Christ also fastened in this way? People commonly think so, and paint them no other way. Yet this is false, because they, like Christ, were nailed. Nonnus affirms it:

units.la: κέντροις ἀντιτύποιον ἐπὶ Σταυροῦ λεξέντες:
units.tr: Having been fixed with nails [κέντροις ἀντιτύπον ἐπὶ σταυροῦ λέξαντες] on the cross.

units.la: In cruce praduris clauis fixi, inque ligati.
units.tr: Fixed on the cross with hard nails, and also bound.

units.la: Et magis Historia prisca, quae est de Helena Constantini matre. Ea cùm venisset sacra & Deo homini trita loca, cupidine visendi & venerandi: de cruce etiam inquisiuit nostrâ illâ seruatrice. Fodit, tres reperit, ac diu animi anceps hæsit quæ esset illa vera. Nam Titulus, quo dignosci potuisset, jacebat seorsim disiectus. Denique miraculo & diuina indicatione opus fuit ad discernendum. Quid autem opus, si vestigia clauorum modo in vna? Argumentum certum est, & res ipsa per Ecclesiæ annales.
units.tr: The older story about Helena, Constantine's mother, is more to the point. When she came to the holy places trodden by the God-man, out of desire to see and venerate them, she also inquired about the cross of our Saviour. She dug, found three, and for a long time hesitated in doubt which was the true one. For the title, by which it could have been recognised, lay apart, thrown aside. In the end a miracle and a divine indication were needed to tell them apart. But what need would there have been, if the traces of nails were on one only? The proof is certain, and the matter stands as recorded in the annals of the Church.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: In quibus partibus clavi, & quo numero?
units.tr: On which parts were the nails, and in what number?

units.la: CLAVOS autem istos, sive & funes, in manibus pedibusque fuisse satis notum. Nonnus de Seruatore: κραὶ ποσὶ καὶ παλαμῆσι σιδήρεα κέντρα κομίζων:
units.tr: That these nails, or perhaps cords, were in the hands and feet is well enough known. Nonnus, speaking of the Saviour, says: bearing iron goads in his feet and hands [κραὶ ποσὶ καὶ παλαμῆσι σιδήρεα κέντρα κομίζων].

units.la: Et pedibus manibúsque ferens stimulos ferratos.
units.tr: And bearing iron-shod goads in his feet and hands.

units.la: Tertullianus de veteri vaticinio: foderunt manus meas & pedes, quæ propria atrocitas crucis. Habent atrocia libri scripti: & recte, vt amat loqui ille scriptor. At quam multi isti clavi? enimuero dissident. Alij de ternis asserunt. vt Nonnus, qui Christum depingit ——ἀμετρήτῳ ὃ πεπαρμένον ἄζυγι γομφῳ Διπλοοῦ ἠτορ ἔχουσα μὴ τεθεσμένον ὁρμῇ, Ποσὶν ὁμοπλεκέεσιν.
units.tr: Tertullian, on the ancient prophecy: they pierced my hands and feet, which is the peculiar atrocity of the cross. Habent atrocia the written books have "atrocia", and rightly so, as that writer likes to speak. But how many nails were there? The authorities disagree. Some assert three, as Nonnus does, who depicts Christ as pierced by an immeasurable, unyoked bolt, his heart held fast with a double stroke, with his feet interlaced [ἀμετρήτῳ ὃ πεπαρμένον ἄζυγι γομφῳ Διπλοοῦ ἠτορ ἔχουσα μὴ τεθεσμένον ὁρμῇ, Ποσὶν ὁμοπλεκέεσιν].

units.la: Facit ecce magno & singulari clauo pedis vtriusque pectusculum transfigi, & quidem vno ictu, idque pedibus mutuo impositis & complicatis. Clarum est. etiam illud Nazianzeni, pariter de Christo, vbi cruce deponitur:
units.tr: This seems to show that the little breast was pierced by one large and single nail through both feet, and indeed with one blow, the feet being laid one upon the other and crossed. That is clear. The saying of Gregory Nazianzen about Christ also agrees, where he is taken down from the cross: taking down the naked one from the wood fixed with the three-nail [Γυμνὸν τειςπήλῳ κείμϱιον ξύλῳ λαβὼν].

units.la: Γυμνὸν τειςπήλῳ κείμϱιον ξύλῳ λαβὼν:
units.tr: Γυμνὸν τειςπήλῳ κείμϱιον ξύλῳ λαβὼν

units.la: Nudum triclaui repositum ligno auferens.
units.tr: Taking down the naked one from the wood fixed with three nails.

units.la: At contrà tamen tendunt alij, & suggerunt quaternos. De eodem Christo Gregorius Turonus: Clauorum dominicorum, quòd quattuor fuerint, hæc est ratio. Duo sunt affixi in palmis, & duo in plantis. Sed & Cyprianus melior maiorque auctor πληθυντικῶς scripsit: Clauis sacros pedes terebrantibus. Quid, quod Plautus ex more astruere videtur tantos?
units.tr: But on the other hand others contend for four, and put forward four. Of the same Christ Gregory of Tours writes: The reason that the Lord's nails were four is this: two were fixed in the palms, and two in the soles. But Cyprian, the better and greater author, also wrote in the plural: piercing his sacred feet with nails. What of the fact that Plautus, following custom, seems to presume so many?

units.la: Ego dabo ei talentum, primus qui in crucem excucurrerit.
units.tr: I will give him a talent, the first who runs out to the cross.

units.la: Sed eâ lege, vt affigantur bis pedes, bis brachia. Nisi is tamen ibi sensus. vt seruulus ad maiorem quasi cautionem, & ne facilè se refigeret, voluerit non semel manus pedesque, sed bis singula figi: ita inquam, vt bini in quoque membro essent claui. Quàm magis considero, tam magis hoc dictum censeo: cùm id quoque reperiam, per sæuitiam multiplicatos alibi clauos. Vt in Martyrologio: Agricolam plurimis clauis Cruci affigentes interemerunt. Interdum & in aliâ corporis parte. In eodem Martyrologio: Philomenus manibus pedibúsque, ac demum capite clauis confixo, martyrium consummauit. Itaque si morem veterem vides; arbitrarium fuit de clauis, & frustra litigemus. Si de Christo tamen quæritur; nescio, & in dissensu Patrum non est meum arbitrari.
units.tr: But on this condition, that his feet be fixed twice and his arms twice. Unless the sense there is that the slave, for greater security as it were, and so that he could not easily unfasten himself, wanted hands and feet fixed not once but twice each; so that, I say, there were two nails in each limb. The more I consider it, the more I think this is what the saying means, since I also find elsewhere that nails were multiplied out of cruelty. As in the Martyrology: they killed a farmer by fixing him to the cross with many nails. Sometimes also in another part of the body. In the same Martyrology: Philomenus, with nails fixed in his hands and feet and finally in his head, completed his martyrdom. So if you look at ancient custom, the matter of the nails was a matter of choice, and we would quarrel in vain. If the question is asked about Christ, I do not know, and where the Fathers disagree it is not for me to judge.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Ordo & modus affigendi. An lignum aliquod in Cruce suppedaneum?
units.tr: The order and manner of fixing. Was there some wooden footrest on the Cross?

units.la: ADDO magis de figendi modo. Is fuit, vt manus primùm figerent, inde pedes. Graphicè Lucianus in Dialogo vbi Prometheus figitur. Vulcanus Mercurio loquitur: Ἀνασαυρώσω, ἐμπεπλαδεὶς τὰ χεῖρε ἀπὸ τουτοῦ πρὸς τὸ ἐναντίον: Crucifigatur, extensus ambas manus ab hac parte in adversam. Atque initium à manu dextrâ. Ibidem Mercurius Prometheo: Ἀλλ' ὅρεγε τὴν δεξιάν. σὺ δ' ὦ Ἥφαιστε, καταλλφε, καὶ ταῖς σφύραν ἐρρωμένως καλάφεσε· δὸς καὶ τὴν ἑτέραν, καταληφθῶ δὲ μάλα καὶ αὐτή: Sed prabe dexteram. tu autem Vulcane, astringe, & confige, & malleum fortiter demitte. Da & alteram, quò illa etiam rectè astringatur. Tum itum ad pedes. Sed ambigas, Manusne fuerint toti moli ferendae? Apparet enim corpus omne (praesertim si quis pedes inflecteret) pependisse à manibus solis. Ego ita arbitror. Quidni? Durae & neruosae illae partes, & lentae frangi. Fortasse nec in media semper manus volâ claui fixi, sed superius paullò quàcum brachio coit, id est circa carpum. Plautus facit suspicari, qui diserte scribit brachia offigi, non manus. Sed puto equidem amplius. si corpus grauius, aut manus tenuior; adminiculum saepe fuisse funes. Illos quoque additos, & circa humeros aut pectus {ctus} medium, ad crucem astrictos. Hoc malim, quàm cum alijs asserculum siue tabellam inducere, in quâ innixi & fixi simul pedes. Nimis accurata ea fabrica, imò delicata. Tamen in Christi cruce Gregorius Turonicus agnoscit; quiâne fuit, an quia pie imaginatus est? Ipse quidem sic: In stipite erecto foramen factum manifestum est. pes quoque parua tabula in hoc foramen insertus est: super hanc vero tabulam, tanquam stantis hominis, sacra affixa sunt planta. Nec scio an illuc Innocentij hæc referenda: fuerunt in Cruce dominicâ ligna quattuor, stipes erectus, & lignum transuersum, truncus suppositus, & titulus superpositus. Nam vidi qui de Trunco sic acciperent: etsi vox videtur abnuere: quæ parùm apta ad minutam illam tabellam. Verba etiam plura & sequentia Innocentij cum examino, sentire eum dixerim non de hac imposita, sed vere (vt loquitur) supposito trunco, è quo ipsa crux surgat. Itaque enim sensisse videtur: truncum aliquem fuisse, siue fulciendæ cruci in imo appositum (ἀνλεπιδιον Græci id genus obliqui sustentaculi vocant;) siue sub ipso recto stipite in terra, cui ille immissus, vt firmior staret. Neque ego assero id factitatum: sed mentem scriptoris pono. Trahunt etiam Irenæum istuc, qui crucem sic deformat: Ipse habitus crucis fines & summitates habet quinque, duos in longitudinem, & duos in latitudinem, & vnum in medio vbi requiescit qui clauis configitur. En,
units.tr: I will add more about the manner of fixing. It was this: they first fixed the hands, and then the feet. Lucian describes it vividly in the dialogue in which Prometheus is nailed to the rock. Vulcan says to Mercury: Stretch him out, and fix both hands from this side to the other; let him be crucified. [Ἀνασαυρώσω, ἐμπεπλαδεὶς τὰ χεῖρε ἀπὸ τουτοῦ πρὸς τὸ ἐναντίον] And the beginning was made with the right hand. Mercury says to Prometheus in the same passage: But hold out your right hand. And you, Vulcan, fasten it and nail it firmly, driving the hammer down hard. Give me the other as well, so that it too may be firmly bound. [Ἀλλ' ὅρεγε τὴν δεξιάν. σὺ δ' ὦ Ἥφαιστε, καταλλφε, καὶ ταῖς σφύραν ἐρρωμένως καλάφεσε· δὸς καὶ τὴν ἑτέραν, καταληφθῶ δὲ μάλα καὶ αὐτή] Then they went on to the feet. But you may ask whether the hands alone were meant to bear the weight of the whole body. For it seems that the whole body (especially if someone bent the feet) hung from the hands alone. That is my view. Why not? Those parts are hard and sinewy and slow to break. Perhaps the nail did not always pass through the middle of the hand, but a little higher up, where it joins the arm, that is, near the wrist. Plautus suggests this, for he expressly writes that the arms, not the hands, were fastened. But I think more: if the body was heavy, or the hand slender, cords were often an aid. These were added too, and tied to the cross around the shoulders or the middle of the chest. I would prefer this to supposing, with others, a little board or tablet on which the feet rested and were fixed together. That contrivance is too precise, indeed too delicate. Yet Gregory of Tours recognises it in the cross of Christ. Was it so, or did he merely imagine it devoutly? He himself says: In the upright post a hole is plainly visible. A small plank was also inserted into this hole, and the sacred feet were fixed upon this plank, as if of a standing man. Nor do I know whether Innocent's words should be referred there: There were in the Lord's Cross four pieces of wood: an upright post, a crossbeam, a trunk placed beneath, and a title placed above. For I have seen people take the word "trunk" in this sense, although the word seems to reject it, as it hardly suits that little tablet. Also, when I examine Innocent's further and following words, I would say he did not mean this added board but, as he says, a truly placed trunk, from which the cross itself rises. So he seems to have meant that there was some trunk, either placed at the foot to support the cross (the Greeks call such a slanting support hypopedion), or sunk into the ground beneath the upright post itself, so that it stood more firmly. I do not assert that this was commonly done, but I set out the writer's meaning. They also drag Irenaeus into this, who describes the cross in this way: The very shape of the cross has five ends and extremities: two in length, two in breadth, and one in the middle where he rests who is fixed with nails. Look,

units.la: De tabellâ suppedaneâ.
units.tr: On the footrest tablet.

units.la: De Glor. Mart. cap. vi.
units.tr: On the Glory of the Martyrs, ch. vi.

units.la: Serm. i. de vno Mart.
units.tr: Sermon i, on the one Martyr.

units.la: Lib. ii. cap. xlii. En, inquiunt, mediusille finis tabella est in quâ corpus requiescit. Fateor verba huc ire, nec temere contenderim de alienâ mente. Tamen Iustinus martyr, è quo sumpta haec videntur, sic de isto fine: Καὶ τὸ ἐν τῷ μέσῳ πεπηγνύμενον ξύλον ὡς κέρας ἔχον ἐστὶν, ἐφ' ᾧ ἐπονχοιῶνται ⓐ σαυρούμενοι: Et illud in medio desixum lignum, ut cornu ipsum etiam eminet, in quo feruntur & quasi inuebuntur, qui crucifiguntur. Cornu id appellat, & notare vult: quomodo aptè in planâ hac tabellâ? Videndum ne vterque ille scriptor aliud intellegat à iam dicto sensu. Diuidunt crucem in quinque fines (Apices Tertullianus scitè appellat) quattuor illos, qui noti sunt & incurrūt: quintum, quem in media cruce collocant, vbi lignū transuersum scindit transitque stipitem desixum. Hac consideratione, quinque sunt fines: & vnus ille stipes (sed sectus) facit ternos. Quod autem aiunt inuehi & requiescere: verum est. corpus acclinatur ei & quasi
units.tr: Book ii, ch. xlii. "Look," they say, "that middle end is the tablet on which the body rests." I admit the words seem to point that way, and I would not rashly argue about another's mind. Yet Justin Martyr, from whom these words seem to be taken, says of that end: [Καὶ τὸ ἐν τῷ μέσῳ πεπηγνύμενον ξύλον ὡς κέρας ἔχον ἐστὶν, ἐφ' ᾧ ἐπονχοιῶνται ⓐ σαυρούμενοι] And the wood fixed in the middle juts out like a horn, on which those who are crucified are carried and, as it were, borne up. He calls it a horn, and wishes to indicate something: how would that fit aptly on this flat tablet? We must see whether both writers meant something other than the sense just stated. They divide the cross into five ends (Tertullian neatly calls them apices): the four well-known ones that run out at the extremities, and a fifth, which they place in the middle of the cross, where the crossbeam cuts across and passes over the fixed upright. By this reckoning there are five ends, and that single post (though divided) makes three. As for their saying that the body is carried up and rests, that is true. The body leans against it, and as it were

units.la: Engraving: crucifixion scene, a figure on a cross with a stake; towns in the background. quasi innititur à tergo. Augustinus hoc sensu scripsit, Longitudinem crucis à terrâ surgentem, cui corpus erat infixum. An totum corpus? imò pedes tantùm, quod liquet: sed adfixum innixumque intellegit, nec scio an innixum scripsit. Tamen in picturis sculpturisque etiam priscis vestigium tabellae huius exstare audio: non ergo temerè spreuerim. non certè à Christi cruce: de aliis, audacius. Quod enim vestigium in scriptoribus antiquis?
units.tr: Engraving: crucifixion scene, a figure on a cross with a stake; towns in the background. As it were, it rests on its back. Augustine wrote in this sense: The length of the cross, rising from the earth, to which the body was fixed. Does he mean the whole body? No, only the feet, which is clear; but he means that the body was fastened to it and leaned upon it, and I do not know whether he wrote leaning. Yet I hear that a trace of this tablet survives in paintings and sculptures, even ancient ones, so I would not rashly reject it. Certainly not from the cross of Christ; about others I would speak more boldly. For what trace of it is there in the ancient writers?

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CAP. XI.

units.la: De Titulo, quid is Latinis? quomodo affcriptus, aut prælatus.
units.tr: On the title: what it is in Latin, and how it was fixed on or carried before the condemned man.

units.la: POST Astrictionem Inscriptio. Quid ea est? Caussa supplicij, & ipsum crimen, & Romanâ voce Titulus: quâ & Iohannes est visus. Atque item Nonnus:
units.tr: AFTER the scourging comes the inscription. What is it? The cause of the punishment, and the charge itself, and in Latin the word titulus, by which John is also rendered. So too Nonnus: [Γεγραμμα, τῆς καλέσαι Λαλυιδὶ Τίτλου ἰωῆ].

units.la: Γεγραμμα, τῆς καλέσαι Λαλυιδὶ Τίτλου ἰωῆ.
units.tr: Γεγραμμα, τῆς καλέσαι Λαλυιδὶ Τίτλου ἰωῆ.

units.la: Mathæus Αἰτίαν benè & signanter dixit. Glossæ Græcanicæ veteres: Αἰτία, caussa, materia, titulus. Eædem Latinæ, Titulus, ἐλέγχον. Latini etiam passim pro causâ. Vt poëta:
units.tr: Matthew rightly and pointedly says "accusation" [Αἰτίαν]. The old Greek glosses: "accusation" [Αἰτία] means cause, matter, title. The same glossaries give for the Latin titulus the Greek "proof" [ἐλέγχον]. Latin writers too often use the word for cause. Thus a poet:

units.la: Et poteris titulum mortis habere meæ?
units.tr: And will you be able to have a title of my death?

units.la: Valerius: Fine vitæ nostræ variis & occultis caussis expositò, interdum quædam immerentia supremi fati titulum occupant. Atque hic Titulus præferri aut apponi solet damnatis. Præferri, vt in Suetonij Caligulâ: Præcedente titulo qui caussam pœnæ indicat. indicaret, per cœtus epulantium circumducitur. Epistola Lugdunensium, de Attalo Martyre: Πε-ριαχθεὶς κύκλῳ τοῦ ἀμφιθεάτρου, πίναχα αὐτὸν προ-γοντος, ἐν ᾧ ἐγέγραπτο ῥωμαϊστί, Οὗτός ἐστιν Αττάλος ὁ χριστιανός: Circumactus per Amphitheatrum, tabellâ ipsum præeunte, in quâ Latinè scriptum, Hic est Attalus Christianus. Sed & appendi, aut apponi damnatis solet. Suetonius Domitiano: Patremfamiliâs detractum è spectaculis in arenam canibus obiecit cum hoc titulo, Impiè locutus parmularius. Quinctilianus ostendit Gladiatores quoque sic productos: Quidam ut patrem sepeliret, auctorauit se. Die muneris productus sub titulo caussa, rudem populo postulante accepit. Sed facit propriè ad Crucem Dionis locus, de seruo, quem Dominus agi in crucem, idque per forum iussit: μὴ γραμ-μάτων τὴν αἰτίαν τ̃ θανατώσεως δηλούντων: Cum litte-ris (siue Titulo) qua caussam mortis aperirent. Sæpe etiam neglecto aut spreto titulo contenti Superdictione fuerunt, id est ut Præconis præeuntis voce populo id nunciaretur: de quo more alij, & ego alias.
units.tr: Valerius: When the reasons for the end of our life are set out, various and hidden, sometimes some undeserved cases seize the title of the last fate. This title is usually carried before the condemned or fixed to them. Carried before, as in Suetonius's Caligula: with the title going before, which indicated the cause of the punishment, he is led around through the gatherings of diners. The letter of the Lugdunese about the martyr Attalus: [Περιαχθεὶς κύκλῳ τοῦ ἀμφιθεάτρου, πίναχα αὐτὸν προ-γοντος, ἐν ᾧ ἐγέγραπτο ῥωμαϊστί, Οὗτός ἐστιν Αττάλος ὁ χριστιανός]: He was led round the amphitheatre, a placard going before him, on which was written in Latin, This is Attalus the Christian. But it was also usual to hang or attach the title to the condemned. Suetonius on Domitian: He had a man of good family dragged from the spectacles into the arena and thrown to the dogs, with this title: "Shield-bearer who spoke impiously." Quintilian shows that gladiators too were presented in this way: Someone, in order to bury his father, sold himself as a gladiator. On the day of the show he was brought out under a title stating the cause, and when the people demanded it he received the wooden sword. But the passage in Dio about the cross bears most directly on this, concerning a slave whom the lord ordered to be led to the cross, and through the forum: [μὴ γραμμάτων τὴν αἰτίαν τῆς θανατώσεως δηλούντων]: with letters (or a title) that made the cause of death plain. Often, too, with the title neglected or set aside, they were content with the proclamation, that is, with the announcement to the people by the voice of a herald going before. Other writers, and I elsewhere, have treated of this custom.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: Post fixionem, quomodo mortui in cruce? languore, aut fame. Vitalitas quorumdam.
units.tr: After fixing: how did the dead die on the cross? From weakness or hunger. The vitality of some.

units.la: BENE iam & fideliter fiximus: quid Post fixionem? hæc tria, Mors, Corruptio, Custodia. Mors, lenta, molesta, & vel à stillante paulatim sanguine, vel à fame. Quid si etiam ab auium ferarumque laniatu? videbimus,& singillatim diducemus. De sanguine quem demittebant fixi, clarum est, nec testimonij eget: & tum eâ caussâ, tum ex acri verberatione quæ præiuerat, credo inualidiores multos obijsse. At de fame, Eusebius vbi Martyres narrat crucifixos in Ægypto: Τηρέμενοί τε ζῶντες, εἰσόπε ἐπ᾽ ἀυτῶν ἰκείων λιμῷ διαφθαρείεν: & seruati sunt viui, donec in ipsis patibulis fame morerentur. Itaque legas quosdam diu in crucibus vixisse, vt ingenitum scilicet robur erat, aut vires. Beatus Andreas in Cruce suspensus, in eâ populum docens, (ô athletam Deo dignum!) biduo superuixit. Victorinus sub Neruâ, iussus suspendi capite deorsum, ita per triduum vixit. Quod sanè miror in schemate illo minimè apto ad longam vitam. Magis etiam istud: quòd Timotheus & Maura in Cruce nouem diebus viui pendentes, ac seipsos in fide corroborantes, martyrium consumpserunt. Vnde hæc vis aut vitalitas, nisi a vitæ ipso fonte? Quamquam & alij quidam animosè egisse in extremissimis istis rebus legantur. velut Bomilcar ille apud Iustinum: qui patibulo suffixus in foro medio, magno animo crudelitatem ciuium tulit: adeo vt de summâ Cruce, veluti de tribunali, in Pœnorum scelera concionaretur. Quidam etiam petulanter: vt proteruuli apud Senecam, qui ex patibulo spectatores suos conspuunt. Atque etiam adnotaui, quosdam miseratione Prin-
units.tr: Well and faithfully have we fixed them so far. What follows fixing? Three things: death, decay, and guarding. Death is slow and painful, coming either from blood dripping away little by little or from hunger. What if it also comes from the tearing of birds and wild beasts? We shall see, and we will take these one at a time. About the blood that the fixed men let out, the matter is clear and needs no witness, and I believe that for this reason, and because of the harsh scourging that came before, many of the weaker ones died. But about hunger, Eusebius, where he tells of the martyrs crucified in Egypt, says: "They were kept alive until they died of hunger upon the very gibbets" [τηρούμενοι τε ζῶντες, ἕως ἐπ' αὐτῶν τῶν σταυρῶν λιμῷ διαφθαρεῖεν]. So you may read of some who lived a long time on the crosses, evidently because they had innate strength or stamina. Blessed Andrew, "hanging on the cross, teaching the people from it" (O athlete worthy of God!), survived for two days. Victorinus under Nerva, "ordered to be hanged head downwards, lived in this way for three days." I marvel at this, since that posture is by no means suited to a long life. Even more remarkable is this: Timotheus and Maura, hanging alive on the cross for nine days and strengthening themselves in the faith, completed their martyrdom. Whence this force or vitality, unless from the very fount of life? Yet other men too are read of as having acted with courage in those extreme circumstances, such as that Bomilcar in Justin, who, fastened to a gibbet in the middle of the forum, bore the cruelty of his fellow citizens with great spirit, so that from the top of the cross, as if from a tribunal, he harangued them about the crimes of the Carthaginians. Some even behaved wantonly, like the saucy boys in Seneca, who spat at their spectators from the gibbet. And I have also noted that some, taken down from the cross through the pity of a prince or magistrates, afterwards lived.

units.la: Lib. VIII. cap. VIII. Principis, aut Magistratuum è Cruce ablatos, post vixisse. Iosephus in vitâ suâ recitat: Redibam, inquit, è vico quodam, & vidi multos ex hostibus (Iudæis) crucifixos: & tres ex ijs adagnoscens, cum quibus antè mihi consuetudo, valdè in animo dolui, & cum lacrimis progressus, dixi Tito. Ille autem statim depositos eos mandat diligentissimè curari, atque ex ijs duo inter ipsam curam obierunt, tertius superuixit.
units.tr: Book VIII, chap. VIII. Josephus recounts in his Life: "I was returning," he says, "from a certain village, and saw many of the enemy (the Jews) crucified. Recognising three of them, men with whom I had formerly been acquainted, I was deeply grieved in mind, and going forward with tears I said to Titus. He at once ordered them taken down and most diligently cared for; and of these, two died in the very course of the care, but the third survived."

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CHAP. XIII.

units.la: Quosdam à volucribus, aut feris etiam viuos laceratos, & plerosque omnes mortuos. interdum & lanceis interfectos.
units.tr: Some were torn alive by birds or even by wild beasts, and most were mangled after death; sometimes they were also killed with spears.

units.la: AT de laniatu etiam addidi, & caussam illam quoque feci mortis. Haud temerè, quia sic ligati, & cùm se non commouerent, dati reuera * ἐλωέα, vt cum poetâ dicam, νὺν ὀσιν Οιωνοῖσί τε πᾶσι. Atque id etiam viui. Prudentius: Crux illum tollat in auras, Viuentésque oculos offerat alitibus.
units.tr: But I have also added the mangling, and made that too a cause of death. Not rashly, since, bound thus and unable to move, they were in truth given as prey, as I may say with the poet: "for dogs and for all birds" [νῦν ὀσιν Οιωνοῖσί τε πᾶσι]. And this was done while they were still alive. Prudentius: "Let the cross lift him up into the air, and offer his living eyes to the birds."

units.la: Horatius aspexit:
units.tr: Horace looked upon this:

units.la: Non hominem occidi. non pascas in cruce corvos, quia sicarij scilicet & homicidæ dari solent in crucem. Item Iuuenalis: Vultur iumento, & canibus, crucibúsque relictis Ad fœtus properat, partémque cadaueris affert.
units.tr: "I have not killed a man; do not feed the crows on the cross," since assassins and murderers are usually given to the cross. Likewise Juvenal: "The vulture, leaving the beast of burden, the dogs and the crosses, hastens to its young and brings them a part of the carcass."

units.la: Quin reperio in sententiâ iudiciali quoq; id aliquando expressum. Actis Martyrum: Claudius, Asterius, Neon, cruci affigantur, & corpora eorum avibus laceranda relinquantur. Itaque Apuleius proprium hunc refert Patibuli cruciatum, cum canes & vultures intima protrahunt viscera. Addit autem & Canes: & discas licet cruces non semper fuisse per-altas. Quomodo enim, si canes attingerent, atque etiam lupi? Nam & hos Catullus addit in Epigrammatio, quod mihi quidem non nisi circumlocutio videtur cruciariae huius mortis.
units.tr: Indeed I find that this was sometimes also expressed in a judicial sentence. In the Acts of the Martyrs: Claudius, Asterius and Neon are to be fixed to the cross, and their bodies left to be torn by the birds. So Apuleius mentions this as the particular torment of the gibbet, when dogs and vultures drag out the entrails. He also adds dogs; and you may learn that crosses were not always set very high. For how could they reach them if dogs could not, and even wolves? Catullus also adds wolves in an epigram, which seems to me nothing but a circumlocution for this kind of death by crucifixion.

units.la: Si Comini arbitrio populi, tua cana senectus Spurcata impuris moribus, intereat: Non equidem dubito, quin primum inimica bonorum Lingua * exsecta avido sit data vulturio: Effossos oculos voret atro gutture corvus, Intestina canes, cetera membra lupi.
units.tr: "If at the will of the people your grey old age, defiled with impure morals, should perish, I do not doubt that first your tongue, the enemy of good men, will be cut out and given to the greedy vulture; the crow will devour your eyes with its black throat, the dogs your entrails, the wolves the rest of your limbs."

units.la: Istae mortes. nisi quod interdum lanceis etiam transfuerberatos lego, an ad accelerandum fatum, an explorandum? Illud fuit in Marcelliano & Marco: quibus ad stipitem ligatis in pedibus eorum affixi sunt clavi; cumque transfisset unus dies & nox, iussit ambos (Fabianus iudex) lanceis per latera verberari. At istud in nostro Domino; cui miles iam mortuo lancea latus aperuit, scilicet periculum an bona fide obijssent.
units.tr: These are the deaths. Except that sometimes I read of men pierced through also with spears: was this to hasten their fate, or to make sure of it? That was done to Marcellianus and Marcus: with them bound to a post, nails were driven through their feet; and when one day and one night had passed, the judge Fabianus ordered both to be pierced through the sides with spears. But in the case of our Lord, to whom a soldier opened the side with a spear when he was already dead, the purpose was surely to test whether they had died in good faith.

units.la: * Fortasse exserta.
units.tr: Perhaps exserta.

units.la: CAP. XIIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: Crurifragium à Cruce remotum. Quid fuerit, in quos receptum, & quomodo?
units.tr: Breaking of the legs, removed from the Cross. What it was, among whom it was received, and how?

units.la: NON autem & crura ijs fracta, inquies, atque ita interempti? Vulgò inualuit hæc opinio, sed vulgò. Qui penetrant & examinant, vident disparata hæc supplicia & seorsim fuisse. Induxit vulgum, quòd in sacra historia latronibus duobus crura fracta leguntur. Atqui sciant pro moribus Iudæorum id fuisse: atque illic fortasse tantum. Lactantius monuit: Suffixus itaque Christus cum spiritum deposuisset, necessarium carnifices non putauerunt ossa eius suffringere, sicut eorum mos ferebat. Ait caute eorum mos: nempe Iudæorum. Et cur hoc Iudæi? ne fraus legi fieret, quæ iusserat ad Solem occasum suspendiosos deponi. At deponi nisi mortui non debebant: diutius autem plerique viuebant: ergò hac, aut aliâ via mors festinanda. Aliâ etiam dico viâ: nec crediderim fuisse hanc solam. Lex quam tango, est in Deuteronomio, & vertit sic doctor Afer: Si autem fuerit in aliquo delicto, itâ ut iudicium mortis sit, & morietur, & suspendetis eum in ligno, sed & sepultura â sepelietis eum ipsâ die. Ergò Crurifragium proprie nihil ad Crucem: tamen quia se ingerit, & vile, atque item sæuum est iuxtà crucem, breuiter de eo dicam. Vox ipsa proba & vetus. Glossæ priscæ: Crurifragium σκελοκοπία. atqui alibi Crurifrangium rectè etiam scribunt. Nam Tago & Tango, & Frago & Frango, dixerunt: sed prior scilicet scriptio magis pro archaismo. Diuisit elegantiæ gratiâ Apuleius: Vxor diras in eum deuotiones deprecata, & crurum ejus fragium abominata. vbi adominata pro vero magis & pro sensu. Ipsa res antiqua, & jam Plauti, & antè æuo, passim Crurifragium minati seruis. In ejus Asinariâ:
units.tr: But, you will say, were their legs not broken too, and so they were killed? This opinion has gained wide currency, but only among the common people. Those who examine the matter closely see that these punishments were distinct and carried out separately. What led the common people astray is that the sacred history records that the legs of two robbers were broken. But let them know that this was done according to the customs of the Jews, and perhaps only there. Lactantius gave the warning: So when Christ was hung up and had given up his spirit, the executioners did not think it necessary to break his bones, as their custom required. He says carefully "their custom," namely the Jews'. And why did the Jews do this? So that the law would not be broken, which had ordered that those hanged be taken down at sunset. But they could be taken down only if dead, and many lived for a long time. So death had to be hastened by this means or another. I say "another means," and I do not believe this was the only one. The law I am touching on is in Deuteronomy, and the teacher Aquila renders it thus: If, however, there is a sin in someone such that the judgment is death, and he dies, and you hang him on a tree, you shall bury him on the same day. So breaking of the legs has no proper connection with the Cross. Nevertheless, since it thrusts itself upon us, and is both base and cruel in the manner of the cross, I shall say a little about it. The word itself is sound and old. The ancient glosses have: Crurifragium [σκελοκοπία]. Elsewhere they also write Crurifrangium, correctly. For they said Tago and Tango, and Frago and Frango; but the former spelling is naturally the more archaic. Apuleius varied it for the sake of elegance: His wife, having begged that curses be heaped upon him, and having cursed the breaking of his legs, where adominata is more correct and suits the sense better. The thing itself is ancient: already in Plautus and earlier, masters everywhere threatened slaves with the breaking of their legs. In his Asinaria:

units.la: Asinar.
units.tr: Asinaria.

units.la: —Crura herclè offringentur, Age impudice, nisi istum percies.
units.tr: By Hercules, your legs will be broken! Come on, shameless fellow, unless you strike that man.

units.la: Et credam, vt crucem ipsam, peculiare fuisse seruis. Seneca: Magnam rem sine dubio fecerimus, si seruulum infelicem in ergastulum miserimus. Quid properamus verberare statim, crura protinus frangere? Suetonius Augusto: Thallo à manu, quod pro epistolâ prodità denarios quingenos accepisset, crura effregit. Idem in Tiberio: Utrique mox (ministro cuipiam, & tibicini) quod mutuo flagitium exprobrâssent, crura fregisse. Ergo in seruis: sed ita, vt liberi non immunes. siue in crimine, siue potius per sævitiam vindicantis. Ita M. Mario Gratidiano Cornelius Sulla perfringi crura, erui oculos, amputari manus jussit. Et Spendiani rebelles in Africâ, cum Pœnorum optimates cepissent, Κολοβώσαντες, καὶ ζωντες τὰ σκέλη, ἐπὶ ζῶντας ἐρριψαν εἰς τινα τάφρον: admutilantes, & crura conterentes, adhuc viuos projecerunt in foueam aliquam. Et in Martyres nostros plurifariâm sic sæuitum. Eusebius de his quae in Arabia aut Cappadocia: τῶν Μαρτύρων τὰ πέλυξιν ἀναιρεθυμένων, τὰ δὲ τὰ σπέλη καταγνυμένων: Martyribus aliás securibus interfectis, aliás Crurifragio punitis. Martyrologium memorat Hadrianum Nicomediae, cum aliis vigintitribus, omnes sub Diocletiano martyrium crurifragio consummâsse. Idem de pluribus, atque innominatis: Commemoratio SS. Martyrum, qui in persecutione Maximini fractis cruribus necati sunt. Et saepius: Modus hujus supplicij, ut incus cum malleo, vel vecte ferreo inferretur, ac tibias incudi imponerent, validis ictibus sic frangendas. Colliges ex Actis Martyrum priscis, quae Surius vulgavit. Sublatum hoc supplicium a Constantino Victor asseuerat, de quo in * loco.
units.tr: I believe, as with the cross itself, that this was a punishment peculiar to slaves. Seneca: Undoubtedly we would be doing a great thing if we sent the unhappy slave to the workhouse. Why do we hurry to beat him at once and break his legs straightaway? Suetonius, in his life of Augustus: He had Thallus, his secretary, have his legs broken, because he had leaked a letter and accepted five hundred denarii.
