The same, in his life of Tiberius: Both of them (a certain servant and a flute-player) had their legs broken soon after, because they had reproached each other with their disgrace. So it was inflicted on slaves; but not in such a way that free men were exempt, whether for a crime or rather through the cruelty of the one exacting vengeance. Thus Cornelius Sulla ordered that the legs of Marius Gratidianus be broken, his eyes torn out, and his hands cut off. And when the Spendian rebels in Africa had seized the leading men of the Carthaginians, [they had them maimed and] with their legs broken while they were still alive, they threw them alive into some ditch: mutilating them and crushing their legs, they cast them, still alive, into a pit. [Greek: Κολοβώσαντες, καὶ ζωντες τὰ σκέλη, ἐπὶ ζῶντας ἐρριψαν εἰς τινα τάφρον.] And in our Martyrs such cruelty was shown in many places. Eusebius, on those in Arabia or Cappadocia: [Greek: τῶν Μαρτύρων τὰ πέλυξιν ἀναιρεθυμένων, τὰ δὲ τὰ σπέλη καταγνυμένων] Some martyrs were put to death with axes, others were punished by the breaking of their legs. The Martyrology records that Hadrian at Nicomedia, together with twenty-three others, all completed their martyrdom under Diocletian by the breaking of their legs. The same is said of several, and of unnamed ones: A commemoration of the holy martyrs who were killed with their legs broken in the persecution of Maximinus. And more often: The manner of this punishment was that an anvil with a hammer or an iron bar was brought in, and they placed the shins on the anvil, to be broken by strong blows. You may gather this from the ancient Acts of the Martyrs, which Surius published. Victor asserts that this punishment was abolished by Constantine, about which I will speak in the * place.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CAP. XV.

units.la: Corrumpi in cruce passi sunt, & nefas sepelire.
units.tr: Those who were crucified were left to rot, and it was wrong to bury them.

units.la: CORRVPTIO jam post Mortem. Quam sic intellego, quod nec mortuos deponerent, sed tabo illic passi sunt diffluere, & a Sole ac pluuiâ corrumpi. Valerius impresse hoc narrat de Polycrate, qui ab Oroete cruci affixus: E quâ, inquit, putres ejus artus, & tabido cruore manantia membra, atque illam laevam, cui Neptunus annulum manu piscatoris restituerat, situ marcidam, Samos laetis oculis aspexit. De quo ipso Afer noster, ut solet, succinctè: Polycrati Samio filia Crucem pro-
units.tr: Corruption already after death. I understand this to mean that they did not take the dead down, but that those who had suffered there dissolved into putrid matter and were rotted by sun and rain. Valerius relates this plainly of Polycrates, who was fixed to a cross by Oroetes: From it, he says, his rotting limbs and members dripping with putrid blood, and that left hand, to which Neptune had restored the ring by the hand of a fisherman, now withered with decay, Samos looked upon with joyful eyes. Of this same man our African, as is his habit, says briefly: The Samian daughter of Polycrates looks out from the cross

units.la: Corrupti in Crucibus. prospicit de Solis unguine & lauacro Iouis. Tangit historiam, & somnium quod in Herodoto, & tu ab eo pete. Sed haec mens somnij, sublimem in cruce madidandum a Ioue cùm plueret, a Sole unģedum cùm is calidus e nudo corpore saniem eliceret adipemque. Hanc in cruce putrefactionem intellexit Theodorus Cyrenæus, cùm Tyranno minanti eam respondit: Suâ nihil interesse, humni, an sublimi putresceret. Neque aliam Artemidorus, cùm malum diuitibus ominatur à somniatâ cruce: τὰς γὰρ σαρκας ἀπολλύσιν ἐξ σαρκωθέντες: Carnes enim amittunt qui in cruce fixi. Itàinquam, amittunt, siue tempore & defluxu: siue & lanienâ volucrum ferarumque, de quâ dixi.
units.tr: Bodies corrupted on crosses. She looks out on the ointment of the sun and the bath of Jove. He touches on the history and the dream that is recounted in Herodotus; seek that from him. But the meaning of the dream is that the man lifted up on the cross was to be soaked by Jove when it rained, and anointed by the sun when, being hot, it drew out the matter and fat from his naked body. Theodorus of Cyrene understood this putrefaction on the cross, when he answered the threatening tyrant that it made no difference to him whether he rotted on the ground or on high. Artemidorus too, when he foretells evil for the rich from a dreamed cross, says: For those who are fixed to a cross lose their flesh [τὰς γὰρ σάρκας ἀπολλύσιν ἐξ σαρκωθέντες]. Yes, I say, they lose it, either through time and decay, or also through the mangling of birds and beasts, of which I have spoken.

units.la: CAP. XVI. Custodia & miles ad Crucem, ne quis detraheret.
units.tr: CAP. XVI. A guard and soldiers at the cross, lest anyone take the bodies down.

units.la: ITAQVE hoc fine asseruati in Cruce, & deponi rarum omninò fuit. Nisi quod Philo tamen notat, receptum moribus fuisse in Natali Imperatoris, aut simili die festo quosdam e crucibus deponi, & permittiad sepulturam: at Flaccum contrà, novos etiam tum ijs affixisse. Ne quis autem deponeret, miles & custodia asedit. Petronius: Miles cruces asseruabat, ne quis corpora ad sepulturam detraheret. Plutarchus in Cleomene: Ὀλίγας δὲ ὑςερον ἡμέρας τὸ σῶμα ἐκ κλεομένους ἀνεσταυρωμένον φυλάττοντες, εἶδον ἀμφιεγέτη ... ὀγυέον ὄρνεον ἐφίπταδς σαρκοφάγον: Paucis post diebus, ij qui Cleomenis cruci affixum corpus custodiebant, viderunt magnum serpentem capiti ejus circumplexum, & faciem velantem tegentémque, ne qua carniuora auis attingeret. Vbi utrumque habes, & custodiri solitos mortuos; & aues faciem in primis inuolasse. Possis ad hanc Custodiam illud Euangelistæ referre: Ἔχετε κυστωδίαν, ἀπάγετε: Habetis custodiam, abite. Quæ Pilati vox fuit ad Iudæos petentes asseruari monumentum. Videtur autem intelligere custodiam, quæ paullo ante ad crucem. nisi quis malit, Habete custodiam; quasi ab imperante, & indignanter dante. Vox enim Græca in utrumuis valet.
units.tr: SO, kept under guard in this way on the cross, it was very rare for anyone to be taken down. Philo does note, however, that it was the custom, on the emperor's birthday or some similar festival day, for some to be taken down from the crosses and permitted burial; but Flaccus, on the contrary, even then fixed new ones up. To prevent anyone from taking them down, a soldier and a guard sat by. Petronius: The soldier kept watch over the crosses, lest anyone should take the bodies down for burial. Plutarch in the Life of Cleomenes: [Ὀλίγας δὲ ὑςερον ἡμέρας τὸ σῶμα ἐκ κλεομένους ἀνεσταυρωμένον φυλάττοντες, εἶδον ἀμφιεγέτη ... ὀγυέον ὄρνεον ἐφίπταδς σαρκοφάγον] A few days later, those who were guarding the body of Cleomenes, fixed to the cross, saw a great serpent coiled round his head and covering and shielding his face, so that no flesh-eating bird might touch it. Here you have both facts: that the dead were customarily guarded, and that birds especially attacked the face. You could refer to this guard that passage of the Evangelist: [Ἔχετε κυστωδίαν, ἀπάγετε] You have a guard; go, make it as secure as you can. That was Pilate's word to the Jews who asked for the tomb to be kept under guard. But he seems to mean the guard which had just been posted at the cross, unless one prefers Have a guard, as if said by a commander and in irritation. For the Greek word can mean either.

units.la: Ambiguus intellectus in Euangelista.
units.tr: An ambiguous meaning in the Evangelist.

units.la: I. LIPSI DE CRVCE LIBER III. Cap. I.
units.tr: I. Book III of Lipsius's De Cruce, Chapter I.

units.la: Transitio ad Rarum figendi Modum. Furca diuisa, & hic de Ignominiosâ dictum.
units.tr: Transition to the rare mode of fastening. The fork divided; and here, on the ignominious kind.

units.la: BVNDE, quæ ad Vulgarem crucifigendi modum, diximus: Rarus superelt, quem ipsum pari curâ imus expunctum. Eum supra descripsimus (& vox præfert) sepositum, & minus in assiduo vsu. Sepositum œuo, Inusitatum vel Schemate vel Fine. De his tribus ordine & partitè dicam (iuuat in his talibus) & in lucem fortasse protraham, quæ vsque adhuc parum claro oculo conspecta. Æuo seposita Furca est: olim quidem in creberrimo vsu, sed quæ paulatim desijt atque aboleuit. Mentio crebra non in historijs solùm, sed Comœdijs priscis: mentio tamen magis, quàm explicatio. ego hic faciam, & pro copiâ ingenij dabo in splendorem. Vt possim, duplicem illam facio, Veterem & Nouam. Priorem, quæ priscis Romanis (non enim apud alias gentes legi) visitata: atque hanc iterum duplicem. Ignominiosam & Pœnalem. Illa est,
units.tr: What I have said about the common mode of crucifixion is now done. What remains is the rare mode, and I shall take it in hand with the same care and dispatch it. I have already described it above, and its very name shows that it is set apart, and less in constant use. What is set apart is set apart either by age, as the Unusual form, or by Shape or by End. I shall take these three in order and one by one (such matters are a pleasure to me), and perhaps bring into the light things that have so far been seen only with a dim eye. The fork is set apart by age. Once it was in very frequent use, but gradually it fell out of use and disappeared. It is often mentioned, not only in the histories but in the old comedies, though mentioned more than explained. I shall do the explaining here, and I shall make it as bright as my wit allows. To make the matter clearer, I divide it into two kinds, the Old and the New. The former was used by the early Romans (I have not read of it among other peoples), and this too I divide again into two: the Ignominious and the Penal. The first is:

units.la: Quid Rarus modus.
units.tr: What the rare mode is.

units.la: Is diuisus.
units.tr: How it is divided.

units.la: Furca duplex.
units.tr: The fork is double.

units.la: Iterum duplex. est, quâ collo impositâ serui circumduci solent ob culpam aliquam, ostentui & ad irrisum. Isidorus: Furcifer dicebatur olim, qui ob leue delictum cogebatur a dominis, ignominiae magis quam supplicij caussa, furcam circa vrbem ferre, praedicans peccatum suum, & monens ceteros ne quid simile peccarent. Plutarchus in Coriolano, Humane habitos seruos a prisцis dominis notat, & addit: ὢ ἡ μεγάλη κόλασις οἰκέτας πλημμελήσαντας, εἰ ξύλον ἀμάξης ὥσπερ τὸν ῥυμὸν ὑπεῖδσον ἀφαιρῶ[?], διεξελθοι τῶν γειτνιάσων. ὁ γὰρ τοῦτο παθὼν καὶ ὀφθεὶς, ὑκέτι πίστιν εἶχεν, ἐμαλεῖτο δὲ Φερκίφες: Erat autem magna castigatio serui delinquentis, si lignum currus, quo temonem sustentant, tollens & ferens exiret circa viciniam. Id enim passus, & sic conspectus, non vltra fidem habebat, & vocabatur Furcifer. Talia idem in Quaestionibus Romanis Glossae veteres: Furcifer, σανεχμίς, διχεγνοφόρος. Ο παιονίες ἀνὴ ὑμωείας δίκεγνον ἐν τῖς τεχνήλοις ἔχοντες ᾠκονομιζον, διὰ τ πολέως ᾠκαγό- μενοι: qui patibulum fert, qui furcam. Qui peccaue- rant, pro poena furcam in collo habentes circuibant, per urbem undique ducti. Atque haec illa prima est, ab ipsa re & fine ignominiosa à me dicta: quæ origo aut exemplar tamen Pœnalis.
units.tr: Again, it is double. The first is that in which a man is led about with a fork placed on his neck, as slaves were commonly paraded for some fault, for display and for ridicule. Isidore: A furcifer was the name once given to one who, for a slight offence, was compelled by his masters to carry a fork about the city, more for shame than as a punishment, proclaiming his sin and warning the others not to commit the same. Plutarch, in the Life of Coriolanus, notes how slaves were treated by their old masters, and adds: It was a great punishment for a slave who had done wrong, if, taking the wooden piece of a cart, the one that supports the pole, he was made to carry it round the neighbourhood. For a man who had suffered this, and was seen so, no longer had credit, and was called a Pherkiphes [Φερκίφες]. The old glosses in the Roman Questions say much the same: Furcifer: one who carries a cross-beam, a yoke-bearer. Among the Romans, slaves who had done wrong were made to wear a fork on their neck as a penalty, led about through the city on every side. This, then, is the first kind, which I have called ignominious from its very nature and purpose. The origin or model of the Penal kind lies here.

units.la: CAP. II. De Furcâ Pœnali, & casos sub eâ ad mortem.
units.tr: CHAP. II. On the Penal Fork, and the cases under it that ended in death.

units.la: Ea est, quâ item collo impositâ circumducti, sed cum verberibus & pœna caussâ. Atque adeò mors plerumque huic consequa~: siue sub ipsâ Furcâ ad necem caesis, siue cum eâ in crucem latis. Seorsim vtrumque explicabo, & firmabo. Sub eâ ad mortem caesi: ex Suetonio, qui poenam more maiorum interpretatur, nudi hominis ceruicem inseri furca, corpus virgis ad necem cadi. Atque idem etiam Victor: Senatus sententiâ constitutum, vt, more maiorum, collo in furcam coniecto, virgis ad necem caderetur. Ac reperio exempla etiam in historiâ, etsi haud crebra. Liuius* incestum cum Vestale sic punitum ostendit: L. Cantilius scriba Pontificum, quos nunc minores Pontifices appellant, qui cum Floroniâ stuprum fecerat, a Pontifice Max. eousque virgis in Comitio caesus, vt inter verbera exspiraret. Dionysius in culpâ simili, & de ijs qui Vrbiniam stuprarant: τῶν ὁ διαπεξαμένων τὴν ἀνοσίαν φθορὰν, ὁ μὲν ἑτερόφ ἑαυτὸν διεχειρίσατο, τὸν δ᾽ ἕτερον ἐπὶ τῶν ἱερῶν ἱεροποιοὶ συλλαβόντες, ἐν ἀγορᾷ μαστιγωσάμενοι, καθάπερ ἀνδραπόδου, ἀπέκτειναν: Ex ijs autem qui illicitam corruptionem patrauerant, alter seipsum interemit, alterum ij qui sacris praerant (ij sunt Pontifices) comprehendentes, in foro flagris secantes tanquam mancipium, interemerunt. Nam etsi neuter furcae hîc mentionem faciat, tamen cum verberibus ad necem datos denarrent, probabile id ita ritu prisco factum: hoc magis, quòd Dionysius quasi indicans addidit, καθάπερ ἀνδραπόδου, seruilem in modum. Quòd autem liberi etiam sub furcâ interdum caesi, exemplum in Epitoma Liuij clarum, de C. Matieno: qui accusatus apud Tribunos quòd exercitum in Hispania deseruisset, damnatúsque, sub furcâ diu virgis cæsus, & sestertio nummo venit. Nam etsi ille non ad veram mortem cæsus, tamen ad ciuilem, & libertatem ciuitatemque pariter amisit. Atque ideò dixi plerumque mortem consequam: cùm & in Plauto legam:
units.tr: This is the kind in which, likewise, a man is led about with a fork on his neck, but for the sake of punishment and with blows. And so, for the most part, death followed. This happened either when men were beaten to death under the fork itself, or when they were carried with it to the cross. I shall explain and establish each separately. Men beaten to death under it: Suetonius, who explains the penalty according to the custom of our ancestors, says that the bare neck of the man was put into the fork, and his body was beaten with rods until he died. Victor too: By the decision of the Senate it was ordained that, according to the custom of our ancestors, the man should have his neck put into the fork and be beaten with rods to death. I also find examples in history, though not many. Livy shows an incestuous act with a Vestal punished in this way: Lucius Cantilius, a clerk of the Pontiffs, whom they now call the lesser Pontiffs, who had committed fornication with Floronia, was beaten with rods in the Comitium by the Chief Pontiff until he expired under the blows. Dionysius, in a similar crime, speaks of those who had defiled the Vrbinia: Of those who had committed the unlawful defilement, one killed himself, and the other was seized by those who presided over the sacred rites (these are the Pontiffs), and was flogged in the forum and put to death, as if he were a slave [καθάπερ ἀνδραπόδου]. For although neither of these writers mentions the fork here, since they describe men put to death with blows, it is probable that this was done in the old manner, the more so because Dionysius, as if to indicate it, added as if he were a slave, that is, in the manner of slaves. That free men too were sometimes beaten under the fork is shown clearly in the Epitome of Livy, concerning Gaius Matienus: He was accused before the Tribunes of having deserted his army in Spain, and when condemned was beaten with rods for a long time under the fork, and was sold for a sestertius. For although he was not beaten to true death, he lost by it both his civil standing and his liberty together. And so I said that death for the most part followed. I find also in Plautus:

units.la: Et ob eam rem in carcerem tedesse compactum scio,Et postquâ es emissus, casum virgis sub furcâ scio. Quæ obijciuntur seni viuo etiam & videnti.
units.tr: And for that reason I know that you were thrown into prison in chains, and after you were released, I know that you were beaten with rods under the fork. These charges are brought against an old man who is still alive and sees.

units.la: CAP. III. Ligatos ad Furcam in crucem solere tolli, Furcam & patibulum videri eadem, aut haud longe dissita.
units.tr: CHAPTER III. That those bound to the furca were usually lifted up onto the cross, and that the furca and the patibulum seem to be the same, or not far apart.

units.la: SED cum Furcâ in crucem latos etiam dixi: quod rei nostræ facit. atque id tale fuit. Ligati ad Furcam, & sub eâ cæsi, per viam ducebantur; fixi deinde ad eam, tollebantur in crucem. Firmamus veterum scriptis. Arnobius: Seruum pessime meritum per Circi aream mediam traduxisse casum virgis, &, ex more, multasse post patibuli pœnâ. Ita legimus, non pœnam. Et quod ait, ex more, huic rei seligimus: quasi receptum videlicet & tralaticium post cæsionem hanc, suspendi. Nam etsi Arnobius non expressit sub Furcâ cæsum: tamen ita fuit, & in ipsâ hac narratiunculâ alij omnes consensu produnt. Liuius: Seruum quidam paterfamilias nondum commisso spectaculo, sub Furcâ casum, medio egerat Circo. Cicero: Seruus per Circum, cùm virgis caderetur, Furcam ferens ductus est. Valerius: Cùm seruum suum verberibus multatum sub Furcâ, ad supplicium egisset. Denique Lactantius, qui & Patrisfamiliæ nomen expressit: Antonius Maximus (potius Autronius, ex Macrobio) diuerberatum seruum sub Furcâ, medio Circo ad supplicium egerat. Ergo sub Furcâ ad supplicium acti: sed nunquid in eâ appensi? Ita. quia hæc Furca non aliud quàm Patibulum fuit. Certa auctoritas Macrobij: qui de illoipso facto. Autronius, inquit, Maximus quidam seruum suum verberatum, patibuloque constrictum, per Circum egit. Quid hoc est, patibulo constrictum, nisi quod alij omnes Furcam dixerunt, & Liuius de Horatio, sub Furcâ vinctum? Nam ita res fuit. Alligari brachia manusque ad hanc furcam solent: atque ita circumduci, mox in eâ attolli. In Plauto legis, Dispessis manibus patibulum habere. item: ire patibulatum per vias. Et quod Nonius ex eo citat: Patibulum ferre per urbem, deinde affigi cruci. Nota verba & seriem: Ferre, deinde Affigi. Quæ ipsa in Licinij historici fragmeto apud eundem Nonium: Ad patibulos (ita mutato genere, pro patibula) deligantur, & circumferuntur, cruci defigantur. Clarè omnia. Habes, ut in Macrobio, ligari constringiqueae ad patibulum, habes, circumferre; habes defigi. Circumferre inquam. nam quod vulgò
units.tr: But since I have also said that men were lifted onto the cross from the furca, which serves my purpose, here is how it went. Men were bound to the furca and beaten beneath it while being led along the road; then they were fastened to it and hoisted onto the cross. Let me confirm this from the writings of the ancients. Arnobius: "He had led a slave who had deserved the worst through the middle of the Circus, beaten him with rods, and, as was customary, punished him with the gibbet afterwards." We read it thus, not "punishment." And when he says "as was customary," I take that to mean this practice: clearly it was the accepted and traditional thing that, after this flogging, the man was hanged. Although Arnobius does not state that the beating took place under the furca, it was so, and all the others agree on this very point in their short accounts. Livy: "A certain master, before the show had begun, had beaten his slave under the furca and led him through the middle of the Circus." Cicero: "A slave was led through the Circus, being beaten with rods, carrying a furca." Valerius: "When he had driven his slave, punished with blows, under the furca to execution." Finally Lactantius, who also gives the master's name: "Antonius Maximus" (rather Autronius, according to Macrobius) "had led his slave, severely beaten, under the furca through the middle of the Circus to execution." So they were taken under the furca to execution. But were they also hanged on it? Yes, because this furca was nothing other than the patibulum. Macrobius is a reliable authority, and he speaks of this very deed: "Autronius Maximus, so he says, had driven his slave through the Circus, beaten, and bound to a patibulum." What is "bound to a patibulum," if not what all the others called the furca, and what Livy says of Horatius, "bound under the furca"? For that is how it was done. The arms and hands were usually tied to this furca, and the man was then paraded around, and soon afterwards raised up on it. In Plautus you read, "to carry the patibulum with arms outstretched," and likewise, "to go along the streets as a patibulatus." And Nonius cites from him, "to carry the patibulum through the city, and then to be fastened to the cross." Note the words and their order: "to carry, then to be fastened." The same appears in a fragment of the historian Licinius, in the same Nonius: "They are bound to the patibula (the gender changed, for patibula) and carried around, and are fixed to the cross." Everything is clear. You have, as in Macrobius, being bound and fastened to the patibulum; you have being carried around; you have being fixed. I say "carried around," for what is commonly printed

units.la: De Diuinat. I. ; Lib. I. cap. VII. ; Lib. II. cap. VIII. ; Lib. X. Saturn. cap. X. ; Mostell. ; In patibul. vulgò est circumferuntur, vereor vt rectum sit. quia non profectò circumlati, sed ipsi pedibus suis ibant: nisi tamen capias quasi circumductos. Sed ego malim, circumferunt reponi, vt sit ligatos ad patibula, eaipsa circumtulisse. Ita Plautus: Tu quidem hodie canem & furcam feras. Nam ibi Furcam, quod patibulum alias dixit. sicut & hic: Cum furca in urbem, tanquam Carbonarium. Atqui docendum etiam est, inquies, in eâ appensos. Nónne res clamat? Si enim Furca idem quod patibulum: quid ambigas? Constat certè in patibulo suspensos. Sed firmo & testibus. Festus; Furcilla sive furcilla, quibus homines suspendebant. Cedò, de quibus alijs hoc accipies? Plinius: Supplicia annua canes pendunt, inter adem Juuentutis & Summani, furcâ sambucea, arbore fixi. Vix est vt aliter intelligas, quàm in furca ad arborem fixos. At clarissimè iam Firmicus: Seuerâ animadvertentis sententiâ patibulo suffixus, in crucem crudeliter erigetur. En, primò patibulo suffigitur, deinde tollitur in crucem. Atque hinc illa phrasis, Patibulo crucis affigi: quia patibulum scilicet, hoc sensu, pars crucis. Distinguit & Tacitus: Patibula, ignes, cruces. & quod patens hæc transuersaque pars sic dicta, Seneca indicat: Alij brachia patibulo explicuerunt. sicut inferior defixusq; stipes, Crux propriè dictus.
units.tr: (De Divinat. I.; Lib. I. cap. VII.; Lib. II. cap. VIII.; Lib. X. Saturn. cap. X.; Mostell.; In patibul.) as "they are carried around" I fear may not be correct, since they were certainly not carried round but walked on their own feet. Unless you take it as "led round." But I would prefer that "carried" be restored, so that the sense is that they carried the patibula themselves while bound to them. Thus Plautus: "You, today, shall carry the dog and the furca." There he uses furca for what elsewhere he called the patibulum, as here too: "with a furca into the city, like a charcoal-seller." But you will say that it must also be shown that they were hanged on it. Does the matter not speak for itself? If the furca is the same as the patibulum, what is there to doubt? It is certain that they were hung on the patibulum. But I confirm it also by witnesses. Festus: "Furcilla, or furcilla, the things by which men were hanged." Come now, from which other sources will you take this? Pliny: "Each year dogs hang as punishment, between the temple of Youth and that of Summanus, fixed to an elder-wood furca, to a tree." You can hardly understand it otherwise than as men fixed to a tree on a furca. But Firmicus says it most clearly: "Fastened to the patibulum by a severe sentence of the judge, he shall be cruelly raised up onto the cross." See, first he is fastened to the patibulum, then he is lifted onto the cross. Hence also the phrase "to be fastened to the patibulum of the cross," because the patibulum, in this sense, is a part of the cross. Tacitus also distinguishes: "Patibula, fires, crosses." And that this transverse part, which projects, is so called, Seneca shows: "Others have stretched their arms out on the patibulum." Just as the lower, fixed upright post is properly called the cross.

units.la: CAP. IIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Qua forma Furca fuerit, obscure traditum in vete- rum scriptis.
units.tr: What shape the furca was, as handed down obscurely in the writings of the ancients.

units.la: SED qualis haec suspensio, & qua vera germanaque facie ipsa Furca, vt ingenue dicam, haereo, & velut inter Solem & Orcum erro. Video, non video; probo, improbo; & plane quod Graeci dicunt, τῷ γνώμῳ ζαλαντᾶω. Suidas Furcam sic describit: Φῦρκα δὲ ῥωμαιοῖς ξύλον δίδυμον: Furca Romanis est lignum duplex siue geminum. Plutarchus paullo magis videtur aperire: δίπλεῦν ξύλον, ὁ ταῖς ἁμάξαις ὑφίσταον: duplex lignum quod curribus subiiciunt. Tamen hoc ipsum satis γλωσσ& & αἰσίσως. itaque distinctius alibi: ξύλον ἁμάξης εἰς τὸν ῥυμὸν ὑπερείδεσι: lignum currus, quo temonem sustentant. Atque addit: ὁ γὰρ Ἕλληνες ὑποστάτων ἢ σημεῖον, τοῦτο ῥωμαῖοι φῦρκαν ὀνομάζουσι: quod enim Graeci Hypostaten & Sterigma (suffulcimentum & sustentaculum) id Romani appellarunt Furcam. Bene & clare pro suis Graecis: nos an scitiores? In Hesychio hoc saltem reperio: σπείγσας (idem quod σπείγματα) dici a quibusdam, τὸ διπλοῦν ὅπως ὑπολιθέσαι τῷ τῆς ἁμάξης ζυγῷ: illud biceps aut furcatum, quod subiiciunt currus iugo. Iuuat, an moratur? istud potius, quoniam Ζυγὸν scribit sive Jugum, quod Plutarchus Temonem & ῥυμὸν. Vtri accedimus? Plutarcho magis, nec video quid Iugo fulciendo subieceris, quod dependet & fertur collo boum. Ergo, me quidem arbitro, Hesychius, in vicinis voculis, sic corrigatur. Atque ex istis rem factam habeamus, si nota veterum curruum membra. Nescimus, & aliunde, si potest, lucem etiam mutuemur. In Dionysio, vbi poena describit serui illius Autronij Maximi (de quo plusquam supra) haec lego: Ἀνὴρ Ῥωμαῖος οὐκ ἀφανὴς θεραπόντα ἴδιον ἐπὶ πυρωσίᾳ ἐκδοῦναι... [?]ομοδούλοις ἄγειν, ἵνα δὴ περιφανὴς ἡ ἱμωσία τοῦ ἀνθρώπου [?], δι' ἀγορᾶς αὐτὴν μαστιγούμενον ἐξέλουσεν ἐλκειν, καὶ εἶπεν ἄλλος ἐν τῇ πόλεως τόπος ἐπιφανής. [?]ἄγοντες τὸν θεραπόντα ἐπὶ τὴν πυρωσίαν τὰς χεῖρας ἀπο-τεινάντες ἀμφοτέρας, καὶ ξύλῳ προσδήσαντες περὶ τὰ σέγνα τὲ καὶ τοὺς ὤμους, ἐμέχει τῶν καρπῶν διηνοῦλι, παρηκολούθουν ξαίνοντες μάστιξι γυμνὸν ὄντα: Vir Romanus haud ignobilis, seruum suum ad mortis supplicium tradens conseruis aliis ducendum, vt conspicua & illustris poena hominis eius fieret, per forum verberibus affectum trahere ipsos iussit, & si quis alius in vrbe locus celebris. Qui autem ducebant eum ad poenam, manus eius ambas extendentes, & ad lignum alligantes, quod circa pectus et humeros ad manuum volam pertingeret, sequebantur flagris cadentes sic nudum. Iam Plautus imagine etiam videtur voluisse expressam: — ego remittam ad te virum Cum furca in vrbem, tanquam carbonarium.
units.tr: But what this suspension was, and what the true and genuine form of the furca itself was, I frankly confess I am at a loss over. I wander as if between the Sun and Orcus. I see, I do not see; I approve, I disapprove; and I am plainly in the position the Greeks describe as [τῷ γνώμῳ ζαλαντᾶω, "my judgment is tossed about"]. Suidas describes the furca thus: [Φῦρκα δὲ ῥωμαιοῖς ξύλον δίδυμον]: "Among the Romans the furca is a double or twin piece of wood." Plutarch seems to explain it a little more fully: [δίπλεῦν ξύλον, ὁ ταῖς ἁμάξαις ὑφίσταον]: "a double piece of wood which they place under carts." Yet even this is quite [γλωσσ& & αἰσίσως, obscure in its wording]. So elsewhere he is more distinct: [ξύλον ἁμάξης εἰς τὸν ῥυμὸν ὑπερείδεσι]: "a piece of wood of a cart, by which they prop up the pole." And he adds: [ὁ γὰρ Ἕλληνες ὑποστάτων ἢ σημεῖον, τοῦτο ῥωμαῖοι φῦρκαν ὀνομάζουσι]: "for what the Greeks call a hypostates or sterigma (a support or prop), this the Romans called a furca." Well and clearly, for the Greeks at least; but are we the more learned? In Hesychius I find at least this: [σπείγσας, the same as σπείγματα]: some say this means [τὸ διπλοῦν ὅπως ὑπολιθέσαι τῷ τῆς ἁμάξης ζυγῷ], "the double or forked piece which they place under the yoke of a cart." Does this help, or does it hinder? The latter, I think, since he writes [Ζυγὸν], "yoke" or "jugum", where Plutarch has [Temon and ῥυμὸν], "pole" and "shaft." Which of the two do we follow? I incline to Plutarch, nor do I see what you would prop up under a yoke, which hangs from and is carried on the necks of oxen. So, in my judgment, Hesychius should be corrected in the neighbouring words, and then the matter is settled, provided we know the parts of ancient carts. We do not know them; so let us borrow light from elsewhere, if we can. In Dionysius, where he describes the punishment of that slave of Autronius Maximus (of whom more above), I read these things: "A Roman of no little standing, wishing to hand over his slave to execution, ordered others of his slaves to lead him, beaten with rods, through the forum, so that the man's punishment might be conspicuous and notable, and through any other famous place in the city. And those who led the slave to punishment stretched out both his hands and tied them to a piece of wood which reached across his chest and shoulders to the palms of his hands, and they followed, lashing the naked man as he went." Indeed, Plautus seems to have wished to express the very picture: "I will send you back to the city to your master, with a fork, like a charcoal-burner."

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Ex ijs tres sententiæ erutæ, & singulæ explicatæ. Tertiam πιθανοτάτην videri.
units.tr: Three opinions are drawn from these and each is explained. The third seems the most plausible [πιθανοτάτην].

units.la: HÆC sunt quæ apud veteres quidem legerim rei huic illustrandæ. Nos ex ijs sententias, an somnia nostra? proponemus: impetrabili tamen veniâ, sicubi in antiquitatis illis tenebris subsistemus, aut labemur. Sententias, dixi. nam tria sunt quæ ex descriptiunculis elicio iam dictis. Primùm, Furcam potuisse esse facie quâ nostrum hodie Patibulum: atque idipsum reliquias & exemplar esse à pœnâ priscâ. Ait Plutarchus, currui aut temoni subiectum fuisse. quid olim, nescio: tale aliquid in nostris curribus supra ipsum axem. Ait Dionysius, per humeros, per pectus ijsse: hoc in isto, si collo imponas. Obstat tamen huic, quod diserte aiunt ξύλον δίπλῶν, διχρῶν, δίδυμον: lignum duplex, biceps, geminum. Nam certè hoc triplex lignum est: etsi ista quoque forma Furca olim dicta. Sententia altera, Lignum fuisse geminum, quod à tergo per humeros, & ante per pectus, hominem medium includeret; atque ita rectum ad expansas vtrasque manus iret. Forma, quam Dionysius ingerere videtur & suadere. Quid tamen hic simile Furcæ? quomodo in vtroq; isto ligno homo suspensus? Nam anterius illud incommodauerit, imò ad guttur strangularit. Sed nec in curribus quid simile, scio. Sententia tertia. Furcam, veram esse furcam: quam hodieque dicimus, & quam Varro indicat, ubi Valkum ἐνμολογεῖ: quod singula ibi extrema bacilla furcillata figuram habeant litera v. Pro hac sententia multa sunt. Primum quod Furca διχέγνος in bonis priscisque Glossis. item Furcifer, διχεγνοφόρος. Atqui διχεγνος Hesychius describit τὰς ἀπὸ μιᾶς ἀρχῆς εἰς δύο συνδυάσας, οἷον δύο τέλη ἐχόντας: quae ab uno initio & capite in duo desinunt, tanquam duos fines habentes. Est plane figura Varroniana, & litterae iam dictae. Quid, quod in curribus hodie, qua Temo cum axe coit, Furca est sustentando illi aut fulciendo? Denique cum descriptione Dionysij mihi conuenire videtur examussim. Da Furcam istam paulatim diuaricantem; ab humeris per pectus, & inde manus veniat; est illud ipsum lignum quod descripsit. Iam Plauti Carbonarium, quo nisi huc referas? Ecce qui lignarios fasces aut carbonum saccellos hodieque ferunt, furcam iungunt. cuius caput cum exstantia aliqua bacillorum a tergo est; longiores duo fines diversi per pectus descendunt, & manu utraque (quasi ad contranixum) sustentantur. Atqui, inquies, manus hic non in alto expansae. Fateor non in alto expansae tamen: & cum funibus traherentur, ligatis ad extremas manus, etiam protendebantur tollebanturque. Quin alius locus Plauti est, qui videatur ab hac modesta expansione, si attendis. Nam in Milite, seruus quispiam in ostio stabat, mulierculam redituraм exspectans, & nequa elaberetur. Ad eum seruus alter:
units.tr: These are the things I have read among the ancients to illustrate this matter. From them I shall put forward some opinions, and you may judge whether they are my own dreams. I beg indulgence in advance wherever I wander or stumble in the darkness of that antiquity. I say opinions, because I draw three points from the short descriptions cited above. First, the furca may have been shaped like our present patibulum, and this itself may be a remnant and copy of the ancient punishment. Plutarch says that it was fitted under a chariot or pole. What it was in his day I do not know; something of the kind exists in our carts, above the axle itself. Dionysius says that it went through the shoulders, through the chest; this fits well if you place it on the neck. Yet against this is that they expressly call it double, two-pronged, twin [ξύλον δίπλουν, δίχρων, δίδυμον], that is, a double, two-pronged, twin piece of wood. For that is certainly a three-part piece of wood, although this form too was once called a furca. The second opinion is that the wood was double, one piece behind running over the shoulders and one in front across the chest, enclosing the man in the middle, so that it reached straight out to both outstretched hands. This is the form Dionysius seems to suggest and support. But what here resembles a furca? How could a man be hung on either of those two pieces of wood? The front one would have been an obstacle, and indeed would have strangled him at the throat. Nor do I know of anything similar in chariots. The third opinion is that the furca was a true fork, the one we still use today, and which Varro points out, where he agrees with Valcus [ἐνμολογεῖ]: that each of the extreme little sticks there takes the figure of the letter V. There are many arguments for this opinion. First, the forked [διχέγνος] appears in good and early glosses, and likewise furcifer, bearer of the forked [διχεγνοφόρος]. Hesychius describes the forked [διχέγνος] as those that, joined from one beginning, divide into two, as if having two ends. This is plainly the Varronian figure and the letter mentioned. Moreover, in carts today the fork where the pole meets the axle serves to support and prop it. Lastly, it seems to me to agree exactly with Dionysius's description. Imagine this fork gradually spreading apart, coming from the shoulders across the chest and then to the hands; this is that very piece of wood he described. Now, how else would you refer Plautus's carbonarius to this? Look at those who still carry bundles of firewood or little sacks of charcoal today: they use a fork. Its head has some projecting sticks at the back, and its two longer, diverging ends come down across the chest and are held by both hands (as if pulling against a counterweight). But, you will say, the hands here are not stretched out high. I grant that they are not stretched high, yet when they were dragged with cords tied to the extended hands, they were both stretched out and lifted up. Indeed there is another passage of Plautus which, if you consider it, seems to refer to this moderate outstretching. In the Miles, a slave was standing at the door waiting for a little woman to come back, and lest she slip away. Another slave said to him:

units.la: Credo ego istoc tibi exemplo eundum esse actutum extra portam,
units.tr: I think that for this you will have to go outside the gate at once,

units.la: Dispesis manibus, patibulum cùm habebis. Benè est, inquit. forma & status in te, qui mox erit; cùm herus alligatum te patibulo per vrbem ducet. Atquin stetisse ego eum opinor, manibus ante se proiectis & leuiter diductis, habitu quo solent captantes & apprehensuri.
units.tr: With your hands spread apart, when you have the patibulum. Good, he says. Your posture and stance are already there, for soon your master will lead you through the city bound to the patibulum. But I think he was standing with his hands thrust forward and loosely apart, in the posture that men use when grasping at something and about to seize it.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: Ratio suspendendi per singulas illas formas exposita, atque etiam oculis proposita.
units.tr: The method of hanging, explained through each of those forms and also set before the eyes.

units.la: TRES sententias super Furcæ formâ habes: tu elige: etsi nos ad vltimam vides proclinatos. Quomodo autem nunc Suspensio? Pro formis distinguenda est. Si prima placet, res facilis. in trunco abscisò, in paxillo infixo, imò in fissurâ supernè factâ, potuit firmiter appendi. Imaginem (oculorum enim magis res quàm verborum est) infrà habes. Si altera, tùm sic censeo, ductos quidem cum duplici ligno ad Crucem, sed non cum vtroque in eam actos. Quod ante pectus, depositum putem: manus fixas in altero, atque idipsum in trunco, paxillo, fissurâ (vt prius) firmatum. Imaginem vide. Nec absurda aut vero nimis extranea sententia est: cùm & Patibulum reperiam singularem eiusmodi rectúmque stipitem dictum. Nonius ex Titinio citat: —si quisquam hodie *praeter hanc Posticum nostrum pepulerit, patibulo hoc Ei caput defringam.
units.tr: You have three opinions about the shape of the fork: choose whichever you like, though you see that we lean towards the last. But how was the suspension done in each case? It must be distinguished according to the forms. If the first pleases you, the matter is easy: on a cut-off trunk, on a fixed stake, or even in a cleft made at the top, the man could be fastened firmly. You have a picture of this below, since things are grasped better by the eyes than by words. If the second, then I think this: they were indeed led to the cross with a double piece of wood, but were not fastened to it with both. What lay before the chest, I suppose, was set down; the hands were fixed to the other piece, and that same arrangement was secured on the trunk, stake or cleft, as before. See the picture. Nor is this opinion absurd or truly too far-fetched, since I find that the patibulum was also called a single upright stake of this kind. Nonius cites from Titinius: "If anyone today should push past this back door of ours, I will break his head with this patibulum."

units.la: Et interpretatur Seram, quâ ostia occluduntur, quòd hac remotâ valuæ pateant. Credo eum ex ipso argumento fabulæ sic proferre, & quòd Ianitor aliquis atque ostij custos hæc dicat. Certè quidem Sera est lignum transuersum quod ostijs opponi solet, in postem vtrimq; immissum. Hodie quoq; vsus. Itaque Glossæ: Sera, μοχλὸς ὀψέχς. Et Poeta aliquis ——excute poste seram. Atque ego amplius arbitror. etiamsi olim Furca aliâ facie fuerit: tamen commodi caussâ, & quia pronior faciliorque hæc appensio, successisse singulare hoc rectum〈que〉 lignum, & id tulisse in humeris, manibus inibi reuinctis, in eoque mox figendis. At si tertia sententia sedeat, duplex potuit fuisse suspensio. Prior ista, quòd hominem sic reuinctum clauis in loco fixerint: tum Furcâ sublatum appenderint funibus iisdipsis (siue & alijs, non refert) quibus traxissent. Figuram infrà vide. Posterior, quòd Furcam ipsam, sed inuersam, in trunco, aut paxillo appenderint, facie quam hîc quoq; vides.
units.tr: Nonius explains it as the bar by which doors are shut, so that when it is removed the doors stand open. I believe he gives this sense from the very plot of the play, and that some doorkeeper or gatekeeper says it. Certainly the sera is a transverse piece of wood set against doors, fitted into the doorposts on either side. It is still in use today. So the Glossaries: Sera, a bolt [μοχλὸς ὀψέχς]. And some poet: "shake the bar from the doorpost." I think something more as well, even if the fork was once of another shape: for convenience's sake, and because this kind of hanging was easier and quicker, the single straight piece of wood succeeded it, and the man carried it on his shoulders with his hands bound to it there, and they were soon to be nailed to it. But if the third opinion holds, the suspension could have been of two kinds. The first: they nailed the man, bound in this way, to the place, and then lifted him by the fork and hung him with the same ropes by which they had dragged him (or with others; it does not matter). See the figure below. The second: they hung the fork itself, but inverted, on a trunk or stake, in the shape you see here too.

units.la: Ouid. in Amor.
units.tr: Ovid, in Amores.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: De Noua Furcâ, quae nostrum Patibulum. Tribo- nianum substituisse passim in Legum libris.
units.tr: On the New Gallows, which Tribonian substituted for our patibulum throughout the books of the laws.

units.la: DE veteri Furcâ sic censemus, cum lege resi-piendi & resiliendi, si quis meliora. Mutare in his tabulis non mihi probrum. Noua sequitur quam dixi, quia inferioris ævi inuentum. Ea est instrumentum è ligno triplici, formâ Jugi veteris, cui appensos homines laqueo strangulamus. Hodie quoque vsum & speciem hanc habet in plerâque Europâ. Non & priscis cognita? non arbitramur. Poena quidem laquei Homero expressa, qui facit impudicas ancillas ab Vlysse sic puniri. atque idem infamem καὶ μὴ καθαρὸν θάνατον (ita loquitur) & impuram mortem ostendit: vti & Plinius, qui præposterarum dixit. quia spiritus intercluditur, cui exitus quaerebatur. Sed à Græcis vsurpatam vix reperias: nec à Romanis quidem in publico. etsi ij, in carcere, damnatis gulam * laqueo frangebant. Credo coepisse, cùm Crux desijt, & vicariam illi factam. Isidori quidem ævo nomen hoc & vsum habuit. Patibulum vulgò, inquit, Furca dicitur (ita nunc quoque in Hispania, vbi ille scripsit) quasi ferens caput. Suspensum enim & strangulatum hac exanimat. In libris legum, quas Tribonianus atque eius adiuuæ collegerunt, satis frequens hoc nomen: &, vt opinor, significatione nouitiâ: quia sublato Crucis supplicio, quidni etiam
units.tr: As for the old gallows, we judge thus, with the rule of returning and withdrawing, if anyone has better things to offer. Changing these tables is no disgrace to me. The "new" gallows follows the one I have described, because it is an invention of a later age. It is an instrument of three pieces of wood, in the shape of the old yoke, on which we strangle men hanged by a noose. Today it still has this use and form in most of Europe. Was it unknown to the ancients? I do not think so. Homer describes the punishment of the noose, when he has Ulysses punish unchaste maidservants in this way. The same Homer shows it to be an infamous and "not clean" death (so he calls it), an "impure death." Pliny also calls it "praeposterous," because "the breath is cut off, for which a way out was sought." But you would scarcely find it used by the Greeks, nor indeed by the Romans in public, although in prison they broke the throats of the condemned with a noose. I believe it began when the Cross ceased and this was made its substitute. In the age of Isidore, at any rate, the name and the use existed. "The patibulum," he says, "is commonly called furca" (so it is still called in Spain, where he wrote), "as if carrying the head, for by it the hanged and strangled are killed." In the books of laws which Tribonian and his helpers collected, this name is fairly frequent, and, as I think, in a new sense, since the punishment of the Cross had been abolished. Why not also the old furca?

units.la: Lib. v. Orig. etiam Furca vetus? Itaque ipsos Iurisconsultos {a}vsurpasse, non habet fidem apud iuris & moris antiqui peritos. qui verè notant, substitutum id pro Cruce: caussâ apertâ & liquidâ, quia Constantinus lege latâ sustulerat Crucem. Ergo ipsi quoque, qui leges collectum ibant in ævi illius & sequentis vsum. Exempla plura sunt, & notata alijs: quædam etiam vbi inconspectio. vt in isto Callistrati, de Pœnis: Famosos latrones furcâ figendos placuit. Inconspectè, inquam, imò ineptè. Quid? ad Furcam nouam homines figuntur? certum est astringi. Sed fuerat Cruci figendos: mouerunt alterum, altero retento, quod non debebant. Simile in Vlpiani de Pœnis: quod exscriptor etiam fortasse corrupit. Decuriones in metallum dari non possunt, nec furca subiyci. Cruci in Vlpiano fuerat: sed quis dixerit, Cruci subÿci? Itaque subsigi, vel suffigi, verum censeam, & eamdem ἀπεχθλεψίαν hic agnoscam.
units.tr: Lib. v. Orig. Whether the jurists themselves used the old furca is not credible to those skilled in ancient law and custom, who rightly note that it was substituted for the Cross. The cause is plain and clear: Constantine had abolished the Cross by a law. So those who were collecting the laws were following the usage of that age and the following one. There are many examples, some noted by others, and some where the writer is careless. Take this one from Callistratus, On Punishments: "It has been decided that famous robbers are to be fixed to the furca." Careless, I say, or rather foolish. What? Are men fixed to the new gallows? It is certain they are bound there. But the text must have said "to be fixed to the Cross." They changed one word and kept the other, which they should not have done. Similar is the passage in Ulpian, On Punishments, which perhaps a copyist also corrupted: "Decurions cannot be sent to the mines, nor be placed under the furca." In Ulpian it had been "Cruci." But who would say "placed under the Cross"? So I think subsigi or suffigi is the true reading, and here I recognise the same oversight.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAP. VIII.

units.la: De Raro modo in Schemate. & primùm de Inuer- sâ suspensione.
units.tr: On the rare mode in the scheme, and first on the inverted suspension.

units.la: ADATIM de Furcâ, quæ inter Raros figendi primus Modus fuit. Alter, qui Schemate à vulgari diuersus. Intellego, cùm alio atque alio habitu hominem affigebant. Id quoq; factitatum, vt ingeniosa crudelitas est in pœnas. Iosephus, vbi narrat Iudæos iussu Titi crucifixos: Πεῤῥσπλαν ...
units.tr: I shall go through the cross first, which was the first of the rare modes of fixing a man, and the second, which differed from the common scheme. I know that men were fastened in various postures, one way or another. This too was practised, as cruelty is ingenious in punishments. Josephus, where he tells that the Jews were crucified by Titus's order: ...

units.la: {4} σεφελωσαν δι' ογλω Ꞓ μιΐς ϲθν ἀλνζας, ἀλλον ἀλλῳ χήματι, ϖϱὸς χλαδίλω: Affigebant milites, ab ira & odio, eos quos ceperant, alium alio schemate, ad ludibrium. Hæc schemata varia fuêre; quæ in lectione vidi, tangam. Est illud, quod Inuersum dixeris, cùm hominem in caput suspendunt, pedibus sublatis. Seneca: Alij capite converso interram suspendere. Eusebius ostendit Martyribus in Ægypto id factum: καὶ ἄλλοι πάλιν μὲν ἀναπολο-παθέντες, {4} μὲν κ̣ τ̣ ζωσθεῖς τῖς καχέργοις, {4} ὃ καὶ χειράνως ἀνάπαλιν κατωκαρα ϖϱογπλωθέντες: Atque alij iterum crucifixi. quidam more in maleficis recepto; quidam etiam deterius, inversâ figurâ, & in caput pendentes. Quod ipsum in D. Petro, sed eo rogante, ne assimilaretur Magistro. Abdias: Et accedens ad Crucem, rogavit ut inversis vestigijs figeretur. Chrysostomus: Χαίρεις Πέτρε, ὁ τοῦ ξύλου τοῦ σαυροῦ ἀπολωσας, καὶ καθ' ὁμοιότητα τοῦ διδασκάλου σαυρωθῆναι ὁ ϑελήσας ἐν ὀρθίῳ χήματι, ἀλλα μᾶλλον ἐπὶ κεφαλῆς, ὡς εἰς ϑεὸν τὴν πορείαν ἐπὶ γῆς ποιούμενος: Gaudeas, ô Petre, crucis lignum degustans, & ad instar Magistri crucifigi recusans in recto Schemate, sed magis in caput obuersus, tanquam in cælum viam à terrâ faciens. Et Petrum quidem etiam clauis inibi fixum, idem Chrysostomus restatur: Ω ἀλογημένοι ἥλοι, οἵπνες τὰ ἅγια ἐκεῖνα μέλη διῆλθον: O benedicti Clavi, qui sacra illa membra penetrarunt! Sicut & Calliopius Martyr, post tormenta, verso in terram capite Cruci affixus est. Affixus, non deuinctus. Tamen & funibus adstricti. vt Symeon. Metaphrastes de Philippo Apostolo: Flagris cædunt & verberant, deinde cum funibus a talis vinxissent, sublimem suspendunt præcipitem. In cruce enim aut stipite sic suspensum accipio. Nec aliter Ammianum: Dra-contius & Diodotus, iniectis per crura funibus, exanimati sunt.
units.tr: The soldiers nailed those they had taken, out of anger and hatred, each in a different posture, for mockery. [Josephus, Greek fragment garbled in the scan.] These postures were varied. I will touch on the one that you might call inverted, when they hang a man by the head with his feet raised. Seneca: Others, with the head turned, hang them down toward the ground. Eusebius shows that this was done to the martyrs in Egypt: And others again, crucified, some in the manner customary for criminals, some even worse, with the figure reversed, hanging head downward. [Eusebius, Greek fragment garbled in the scan.] The same was done to St Peter, though at his own request, so that he would not be made like his Master. Abdias: And approaching the cross, he asked that he be fixed with his feet upward. Chrysostom: Rejoice, Peter, you who tasted the wood of the cross, and who, wishing to be crucified in likeness to your Master, refused to be crucified in an upright posture, but rather with the head down, as if making your way to heaven from the earth. [Χαίρεις Πέτρε, ὁ τοῦ ξύλου τοῦ σταυροῦ ἀπογευσάμενος, καὶ καθ' ὁμοιότητα τοῦ διδασκάλου σταυρωθῆναι ἀξιώσας, ἐν ὀρθίῳ σχήματι, ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον ἐπὶ κεφαλῆς, ὡς εἰς οὐρανὸν τὴν πορείαν ἐπὶ γῆς ποιούμενος.] The same Chrysostom also praises the nails that were fixed in Peter there: O blessed nails, which pierced those holy members! Likewise Calliopius the martyr, after his torments, was fixed to the cross with his head turned toward the earth. Fixed, not bound. Yet they were also tied fast with ropes, as Symeon Metaphrastes says of the apostle Philip: They beat him with whips and lashes, and then, having bound him with ropes, hang him up on high, head downward. For I understand this to be a man hanging thus on a cross or a stake. Ammianus likewise: Dracontius and Diodotus, with ropes thrown about their legs, were dead.

units.la: CAP. IX. De obliquâ suspensione, de varicante, & inter ar- bores scissione.
units.tr: CAP. IX. Of the oblique suspension, of the forked cross, and of being split between trees.

units.la: REPERIO & obliquos super crucem crucé ve positos: vt in Plutarchi Artaxerxe: Is narrat Parysatidem regis matrem infensam Eunucho cuipiam, arte redegisse in suam potestatem. tum iussisse ἐνδεῖσθαι ζωὴν, καὶ τὸ σῶμα πλάγιον διὰ τεσσάρων σαυρῶν ἀναπήξαι, τὸ δὲ δέρμα χωρὶς διαπαλαίεσθαι: cutem vivo detrahi, & corpus quidem obliquum iacensque tribus stipitibus sive crucibus infigi, pellem seorsim in palo poni. Video & inter duos palos dispessis manibus pedibusque alligatos, vt in Martyrologio, de Anastasia: Manibus & pedibus extensis ligata est ad palos. Video & inter arbores appensos, & reductis ijs, scissos. De Coronâ Martyre: Ipsa inter arbores scissa, Victor autem decollatus est. Quod ipsum Schema ad Cruces referendum Propertio facilè accredam, qui sic appellat:
units.tr: I also find men fixed obliquely upon a cross or a crossbeam, as in Plutarch's Artaxerxes. He relates that Parysatis, the king's mother, who was hostile to a certain eunuch, got him into her power by a trick, and then ordered that he be bound alive [ἐνδεῖσθαι ζωὴν], and that his body be fixed sideways on four stakes [καὶ τὸ σῶμα πλάγιον διὰ τεσσάρων σαυρῶν ἀναπήξαι], while the skin was pulled off separately [τὸ δὲ δέρμα χωρὶς διαπαλαίεσθαι]: the skin was stripped from him while he was alive, and his body, lying crosswise, was pinned to three posts or crosses, while his skin was hung up separately on a stake. I also see men tied between two stakes with hands and feet spread apart, as in the Martyrology, concerning Anastasia: She was bound to the stakes with her hands and feet stretched out. I also see men hanged between trees and then torn apart when the trees were bent back: in the account of Coronas the martyr: She was split apart between the trees, but Victor was beheaded. I readily agree that this very manner of execution should be referred to crosses, as Propertius calls them:

units.la: Arboreasque cruces Sinis, & non hospita Graïjs Saxa, & curvatas in sua fata trabes.
units.tr: Sinis set up crosses of trees, and rocks that were not hospitable to the Greeks, and beams bent to their doom.

units.la: Senecam etiam huc traham, si fidem libris priscis habeo, qui inter genera Crucium recensset, distracta in diversum actis cruribus membra. Ita libri inquam, quos ego vidi. Est tamen vulgò curribus, bono & suo sensu. ad Metium enim respiciat: etsi vetus desitumque id supplicium, nec inter visitata fortasse ibi referendum.
units.tr: I would also bring in Seneca here, if I may rely on the older books, which in listing the kinds of crosses includes limbs torn apart with the legs driven in opposite directions. So the books I have seen read; but the common text has curribus (chariots), which also makes good sense, for he may be looking at Metius. Yet that punishment is old and now obsolete, and perhaps should not be counted among the ones commonly practised.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CAP. X.

units.la: De Modo qui Fine diuersus. primum de his qui in Cruce vstulati.
units.tr: On the Mode that Differs in Its End. First, of those who were burned on the cross.

units.la: TERTIVS figendi modus Rarior, qui Fine diuertit à vulgato. Quem intellego, cùm cruces alio spectant, & hominem capiunt moriturum in ipsis, non per ipsas. In exemplis discès. Tale, cùm appensi flamâ aut fumo necati. Olim factum, ex Cicerone discas: qui fratrem obiurgans, Quid opus fuit, inquit, eiusmodi litteris, quas ad ipsum missisti? Illum crucem sibi constituere, ex quâ tu eum ante detraxisses. te curaturum fumo vt comburatur, totâ plaudente provinciâ. Verba Quinăti & minæ eò spectant, vt homo in cruce fixus vstule-tur fumo. Alexander etiam Imp. quempiam qui fumum vendiderat, quasi compari poenâ affecturus, ad stipitem ligari præcepit, & fumo apposito quem ex stipulis & humidis lignis fieri iusserat, necauit, præcone dicente, Fumo punitur qui vendidit fumum. Atque in Martyribus nostris hoc genus crebrum. Acta vetera de Pionio: Confixus clavus in cruce, aggestis lignis, flamâ combustus est. Nec aliter Polycarpus mortuus, antistes Smymæorum. Ipsi in epistolâ: Μελλόντων ὁ αὐτὸν καὶ ᾠφ-ησθῆναι, εἶπεν, Ἀφετε με ὅτως. ὁ γὰρ διδοὺς ὑπομένειν τὸ πῦρ, δώσει ἐκ χωρὶς τὸ ὑμετερόες ἐν τῷ ἡλωνι ἀσφαλείας ἀσινύλλως ἵπιμεῖναι τῇ πυρᾷ. Οἱ δὲ καθήλωσαν, ᾠφ-σεδήσαν ὁ αὐτὸν: Cùm pararent eum cruci suffigere, dixit, dixit, Relinquite me sic, qui enim dedit exspectare ignem, dabit & sine vestra clauorum firmitate, solutum manere in rogo. Illi autem non confixerunt eum, sed ligarunt. Quin vno etiam tempore plures, appensi pedibus in sublime (nota hic & Schema inuersum) capite verso deorsum, suffocati fumo, & lento igne consumpti sunt. Non ergo iniuria Tertullianus scripsit: Licet nunc Sarmentitios & Semaxios appelletis, quòd ad stipitem dimidij axis reuincti, sarmentorum ambitu exurimur. significat enim adeo crebrum in maiores illos nostros & in religione proceres supplicium hoc fuisse, vt in illudium conuitiumque venerit, & Christiani vulgò Semaxij, à stipite cui astringebantur, & Sarmentitij, à sarmentis quibus vrebantur, sint dicti. Atque hoc est quod Axem vocat alibi incendio constrictum, id est, ad incendium iam cum homine ligatum.
units.tr: The third way of fixing a man is rarer, and it differs from the common one in its end. I mean the kind where the crosses look to another purpose, and take a man who is to die in them, not by them. You will learn this from examples. It is the case when men were hung up and killed by flame or smoke. You may learn that it was done in the past from Cicero, who, rebuking his brother, says: "What was the need for a letter of that kind, which you sent to him himself? He set up a cross for himself, from which you had earlier taken him down. You will see to it that he is burned with smoke, while the whole province applauds." The words of Quintus and his threats point to a man fixed to a cross and burned with smoke. Emperor Alexander also, wishing to punish a certain man who had sold smoke with a like penalty, ordered him bound to a stake, and, when smoke had been set against him, made from straw and damp wood as he had commanded, killed him, while the herald called out, "He is punished with smoke who sold smoke." This kind of death was also common among our martyrs. The old acts concerning Pionius: "He was nailed to the cross, and with wood piled around him, he was burned by flame." Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, died in no other way. In his own letter: "When they were about to fasten him to the cross, he said, 'Leave me as I am; for he who grants me to endure the fire will grant me also to remain in the pyre unmoved, without your security of nails.' But they did not nail him; they only bound him." Indeed, on one occasion several were hung up by the feet, high in the air (note here the inverted figure) with their heads turned downward, and were suffocated by smoke and consumed by a slow fire. So Tertullian wrote not without reason: "Although now you call us Sarmentitii and Semaxii, because we are bound to a stake with half an axle, and are burned by a ring of brushwood." For he indicates that this punishment was so common against our forebears, and among the leaders of the religion, that it came to be a subject of mockery and abuse; and Christians were commonly called Semaxii, from the stake to which they were tied, and Sarmentitii, from the brushwood with which they were burned. And this is what he elsewhere calls the axle bound to the fire, that is, a man already tied to the burning, ready for the fire.

units.la: CAP. XI. De his qui bestijs in Cruce obiecti.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI. Of those who were thrown to the beasts while fixed to the cross.

units.la: {a}CRux & ista Fine alia, cùm homines in eâ fixos bestijs obijciebant. In publicis spectaculis id sæpe factum. Epistola Lugdunensium, de Blandinâ Martyre: Βλανδίνα ἐπὶ ξύλου κρεμαζομένη περιέχεσθαι ...
units.tr: The cross also had another use, when men fixed to it were thrown to the beasts. This was often done at public spectacles. The letter of the Lugdunese about the martyr Blandina says: [Βλανδίνα ἐπὶ ξύλου κρεμαζομένη περιέχεσθαι ...] (Blandina, hanging from a stake, ...).

units.la: Blandina in ligno suspensa prostituta est esca & laniena incurrentium ferarum. Quæ & quòd in specie Crucis videbatur, & ob continuam orationem, multam alacritatem injiciebat certantibus. Sed factum & nō Christianis. ut illi apud Martialem Laureolo: Qualiter in Scythicâ religatus rupe Prometheus Assiduam nimio pectore pauit auem, Nuda Calidonio sic pectora præbuit urso Non falsâ pendens in cruce Laureolus.
units.tr: Blandina was hung on a stake and offered as prey to the attacks of the beasts that rushed upon her. Because she appeared in the form of the Cross, and because of her unceasing prayer, she filled the combatants with great eagerness. But this was also done to non-Christians, as in Martial's lines about Laureolus: "As Prometheus, bound to a Scythian rock, fed the bird that kept gnawing at his breast, so Laureolus, hanging on a cross that was no sham, offered his naked breast to the Caledonian bear."

units.la: Nec satis capiunt, certè non reuelant, interpretes. Vult quempiam sustinuisse velut in fabula personam Laureoli: & cum is pro argumento crucifigendus esset, sed in speciem & moris causâ: rem ex fabulâ Titus fecit, & noxium quempiam ita fixit, & fixum bestijs etiam obiecit. Dico obiecit. atque ita proprie: aliud est, dare ad bestias. Vopiscus in Aureliano: Sanè Mnestheus postea surrectus ad stipitem, bestiis obiectus est. Surrectus, valet rectus ligatus. Hic est stipes, quem Tertullialianus appellat Leoni concessum. Ita lego, non Leone, libello De Pudicitiâ extremo. Atq; ad hunc ipsum morem infamis & infanda illa turpitudo Neronis : quâ viros feminásq; ad stipitem deligatos, ipse ferâ pelle contectus, emissus è caueâ, medios inuadebat. Xiphilinus è Dione : Μαεχῖα νοὶ χοεχας σαωεχις γυμνὰς ᾳεχοδέων, ᾧ μεἰου τέ ἰυ-νος δοεχὶ αὐελαμβανε, ὠ ᾳεχοπίπλων σφισὶν ἠσέλχαυνεν, ὥσπερ τὶ ἐδίων.
units.tr: The commentators do not grasp this, or at least do not explain it. He means that someone played the part of Laureolus in a drama, and that, since he was to be crucified as the plot required, though only in appearance and for the sake of the spectacle, Titus turned the story into a performance: he fixed a condemned man in this way and threw him, once fixed, to the beasts. I say threw to, and I mean it strictly: to give someone to the beasts is one thing, to throw him to them is another. Vopiscus, in his life of Aurelian, writes: Then Mnestheus, afterwards raised upright at the stake, was thrown to the beasts. "Raised" (surrectus) means set upright and bound. This is the stake which Tertullian calls given to the lion; I read it so, not to the lion, in the last part of his book On Modesty. And it was to this same custom that Nero's infamous and unspeakable cruelty belonged: men and women tied naked to stakes, while he himself, covered in a wild beast's skin, let out of a cage, attacked them in their midst. Xiphilinus, from Dio: [Μαεχῖα νοὶ χοεχας σαωεχις γυμνὰς ᾳεχοδέων, ᾧ μεἰου τέ ἰυ-νος δοεχὶ αὐελαμβανε, ὠ ᾳεχοπίπλων σφισὶν ἠσέλχαυνεν, ὥσπερ τὶ ἐδίων.] (Nero, having dressed in a beast's skin, would rush at the naked men and women bound to the stakes, and seize one of them, and drive the rest upon them, as if they were prey.)

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CAP. XII.

units.la: De mortuorum in Cruce suspensione.
units.tr: On the suspension of the dead on the cross.

units.la: AC postremò Crux Fine alia, cùm non viui sed mortui in eâ appensi. Notabis. & quod nobis sollenne in rotâ exponere supplicio iam affectos, ad notam sceleris & infamiam, id olim in Cruce, & Orientalibus præsertim. De Romanis nondum lêgi. nisi quòd Cæsar piratas, à quibus captus esset, cùm in deditionem redegisset, quoniam suffixurum se cruci iurauerat, iugulari priùs iussit, atque atque ita suffigi. Sed id per clementiam, & vt subtraheret diuturnæ pœnæ. Alij per sæuitiam & ad infamiam, vt dixi. Ita Carthaginenses in Hannone. qui captus virgisque casus, effossis oculis, & manibus cruribusque fractis, velut à singulis membris pœna exigerentur, in conspectu populi occiditur: corpus verberibus lacerum in cruce figitur. Idem Parysatis in Eunucho, de quo * supra. Item Ptolomæus Ægypti rex, in Cleomene, qui etsi manu sua animose cecidisset, tamen ἀφαιρέθεις τὸ σῶμα κρεμάσαι καὶ καταβυροῶσαντας: iussit corpus crucifigi, cum cutem prius detraxissent. Vbi obseruo obiter, antiquum hunc morem excoriandi in supplicijs, Ægyptijs Persisque fuisse, quem & hodie Ægyptij tenent. nam grassatores sicariosque ita puniunt, diu viuos, donec ad vmbilicum carnifex perueniat: quod narrat Iohannes Leo, qui cum fide satis & iudicio res Africæ & Ægypti scripsit. Nec cadauer solùm, sed imagines sublatæ in crucem. exemplo in Celso: cuius corpus a canibus consumptum est, & novo iniuriæ genere imago in crucem sublata. Auctor Pollio in xxx. tyrannis.
units.tr: And finally, there is another kind of cross, on which people were hung not while alive but after they were dead. Note this. We are accustomed to expose people already condemned to the wheel as a mark of their crime and a sign of infamy; the same was once done on the cross, especially among the Eastern peoples. I have not yet read of this among the Romans, except that Caesar, when he had forced the pirates who had captured him to surrender, and since he had sworn he would have them nailed to a cross, first ordered them to be strangled and then so fixed. But he did this out of mercy, to spare them a prolonged punishment. Others did it out of cruelty and to inflict infamy, as I said. So the Carthaginians did with Hanno: he was captured, beaten with rods, his eyes gouged out, his hands and legs broken, and as if the punishment were being exacted limb by limb, he was killed in full view of the people, and his body, mangled by the scourging, was fixed to a cross. The same was done by Parysatis to the eunuch mentioned above (see above). Likewise Ptolemy, king of Egypt, with Cleomenes, who although he had bravely fallen by his own hand, nevertheless [ἀφαιρέθεις τὸ σῶμα κρεμάσαι καὶ καταβυροῶσαντας] ordered his body to be crucified after they had first stripped off the skin. Here I observe in passing that this ancient custom of flaying in punishments was practised by the Egyptians and Persians, and the Egyptians keep it even today. For they punish robbers and assassins in this way: they leave them alive for a long time while the executioner works his way up to the navel. John Leo reports this; he wrote about the affairs of Africa and Egypt with reasonable faithfulness and judgement. Nor was it only the corpse that was treated this way; images too were raised on a cross. Example in Celsus, whose body was devoured by dogs, and whose image was raised on a cross as a new kind of insult. The author is Pollio, in his *Thirty Tyrants*.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CAP. XIII.

units.la: E quo ligno Crux fuerit? Item in Monte plerumque defixam, ipsam sæpe altiusculam.
units.tr: Of what wood was the cross? Also, where was it usually fixed, and how high was it?

units.la: PEREGIMVS, de Forma & Modo: duo velut succisiua & extra diuisionem relicta, nunc adiungo Materiam & Locum. E quâ materie Crux?
units.tr: We have treated its shape and manner, two points set aside, as it were, and left outside the division. Now I add matter and place. Of what material was the cross?

units.la: Plerumq; post mutilationem.
units.tr: Usually after mutilation.

units.la: Iustin. lib. xxx.
units.tr: Justin, book 30.

units.la: * Cap. ix. huius libri.
units.tr: See chapter 9 of this book.

units.la: Deglubere olim crebrum Orientalibus. Crux? ex obuio & prompto aliquo ligno. E quâ nostri Seruatoris? censemus è quercu. Primùm quia viri fide digni asserunt, frusta sacratissimi huius ligni quæ hodie exstant, speciē hanc referre. Tum, quia crebra & frequens in Iudæâ olim & nunc quoque illa arbor. Tertiò, quia robustum lignum & fixioni laturæque aptum. Itaque Silius in eo etiam crucifigit.
units.tr: To strip off the bark was once common among Easterners. The cross was made of some common wood that lay ready to hand. Of what wood was our Saviour's cross? We judge it was of oak. First, because trustworthy men assert that the fragments of this most sacred wood which survive today have this appearance. Second, because that tree was and still is common and abundant in Judaea. Third, because it is a sturdy wood, fit to be fixed and to bear weight. So Silius too has him crucified on it:

units.la: Quem postquam diro suspensum robore vidit. Iterum.
units.tr: When he saw him hanging from the dreadful wood. Again:

units.la: —Erecto suffixum robore mastis Ostentabat ouans populus.
units.tr: —The people, exulting, showed him fixed to the upright beam of the mast.

units.la: Nam quòd superioris aliquot æui scriptores tria aut *quatuor genera ligni in Cruce dominicâ agnoscunt, curiosè magis dictum arbitramur quàm verè. At quis Locus cruci? Incertus, & pro arbitrio: tamen plerumque conspectus aliquis, & iuxta vias. Exempla enim exempla esse desinunt, nisi aliorum animum oculosque in se vertant. Quinctilianus: Quoties noxios crucifigimus, celiberrima eligbuntur viæ, vbi plurimi intueri, plurimi commoueri hoc metu possint. Ita Alexander Imp. Eunuchum in crucem tolli iussit per eam viam, quâ erat seruis suis ad suburbana Imperatoria iter frequentissimum. Quinetiam opida, certa loca habuisse videntur, huic rei adtributa. Sic Mamertini, more atque institute, crucem fixerunt in viâ Pompeiâ. Sic Romæ iuxta urbem Tacitus agnoscit Locum seruilibus pœnis sepositum: quod de
units.tr: Some earlier writers of this age recognise three or four kinds of wood in the Lord's cross, but we think this is said more out of curiosity than truth. As for the place of the cross, it was uncertain and chosen at will; yet usually it was some conspicuous spot, beside the roads. For examples cease to be examples unless they turn the minds and eyes of others toward themselves. Quintilian: Whenever we crucify wrongdoers, the busiest roads are chosen, where very many can look on and very many can be moved by this fear. So the Emperor Alexander ordered a eunuch to be raised on a cross along that road which was the most frequented route for his servants to the imperial suburban estates. Indeed, towns seem to have had certain places assigned to this purpose. So the Mamertines, by custom and institution, fixed a cross on the Pompeian road. So at Rome, near the city, Tacitus recognises a place set apart for servile punishments, which we take to refer to

units.la: Annal. xv. de Cruce & Crurifragio interpretamur. Hac ipsâ de causâ posita ea sæpe in monte. Ut Seruatoris nostri, in Caluariæ: ut Polycratis, in excelsissimo Mycalensis montis vertice. Quin ipsa sæpe alta, præsertim in noxio aliquo insigni. Irrisio Galbæ huc pertinuit. qui cuidam imploranti leges & ciuem Rom. se testificanti, quasi solatio & honore aliquo pœnam leuaturus, mutari, multóque præter ceteras altiorem, & dealbatam, statui crucem iussit. Altiorem, vt digniori; albatam, *vt ciui, qui in veste alba. Tale in Iustino, de Carthalone: quem pater, cum ornatu suo, in altissimam crucem, in conspectu vrbis suffigi iussit. Et Pœni fecerunt in Regulo. Apud Silium:
units.tr: the Annals, book 15, and which we interpret as crucifixion and breaking of the legs. For this same reason it was often placed on a hill: as that of our Saviour on Calvary, and as that of Polycrates on the highest peak of Mount Mycale. Indeed it was often high, especially for some notorious criminal. Galba's mockery belongs here: he ordered a certain man who appealed to the laws and declared himself a Roman citizen, as if to lighten his punishment with some consolation and honour, to have a cross set up for him, changed, far higher than the rest and whitened. Higher, as for a more honourable man; whitened, as for a citizen, since he wore white. Similar is what Justin says of Carthalo, whom his father with his finery, ordered to be fixed on the highest cross, in view of the city. The Carthaginians did the same to Regulus. In Silius:

units.la: —— vidi cum robore pendens Italiam cruce sublimis spectaret ab alta.
units.tr: —— I saw him hanging from the beam, raised high on the cross, gazing at Italy from the height.

units.la: Iam illa Amanis præalta: qui Mardochæo crucem quinquaginta cubitorum posuit, sed ipsi ascendendam. Sanè pleræque omnes altiusculæ. atque ideò communiter Tertullianus: Timebit forsitan Caro gladium grauem, aut crucem excelsam. Quam ipsam rationem Lactantius in Dominicâ assignat. Nam quoniam, inquit, is qui patibulo suspenditur, & conspicuus est omnibus, & ceteris altior: crux potius electa est, quæ significaret illum tam conspicuum tamq; sublimem futurum, vt ad eum cognoscendum pariter & colendum cuncta nationes ex omni orbe concurrerent. O inopinatam, sed veram dictionem! cui fides maximè nostro æuo facta: ēta: cùm, virtute & gloriā magnā Hispanicæ gentis, Nouus etiam orbis vēnit in Christianas leges.
units.tr: Then there is that very high cross of Haman, which he set up for Mordecai, fifty cubits long, but on which he himself was to be hanged. Indeed almost all were rather high. And so Tertullian commonly says: Perhaps the flesh will fear a heavy sword or a lofty cross. Lactantius gives this very reason for the Lord's cross: For since he who is hung on the gibbet is visible to all and higher than the rest, the cross was rather chosen, which would signify that he would be so conspicuous and so exalted that all nations from the whole world would flock together to know him and worship him alike. O unexpected but true saying! Which in our own age has been especially confirmed, when, by the virtue and great glory of the Spanish nation, the New World too has come under Christian laws.

units.la: CAP. XIIII.
units.tr: CAP. XIIII.

units.la: Crux sublata, atque etiam Crurifragium fortasse. Quando id factum, quæsitum.
units.tr: The cross abolished, and perhaps also the breaking of legs. When this was done, is inquired.

units.la: NVNC pedem in vltimo velut spatio pono, quod est Quatenus Crux vsurpata. Postquam enim Vitam ipsam interfecit, non diu illi vita: & sustulit ex humanis, aut certè Romanis rebus, Constantinus. Serio iam ille Christianus, noluit salutare signum subseruire ad perniciem; & colendum illud atque eximium pœnis vilescere damnatorum. Ergo sustulit. Victor: Vetus veterrimúmque supplicium patibulorum, & cruribus suffringendis, primus remouit. Cassiodorus: Supplicium Crucis, quod primitus apud Romanos erat in vsu, lege prohibuit. Atque efficaciter etiam sustulit: nec postea reperies reductam. Augustinus: Antea homines cruci figebantur, quod postea edicto prohibitum, manet. Scholiastes Iuuenalis ad illud Partémque cadaueris adfert, notat: Hominum. nam antiqui crucibus figebant. Non ergo eius euo.atq; ex eo discas non nimis antiquum ipsum, etsi antiqua doctum. Quando autem sustulit? sero, nec nisi sub imperij extrema. Colligo, quia illo iam imperante mentio etiam crucium: quid, quod apud ipsum? Lex in eius nomine exstat Theodosij Codice: quâ serui ac liberti, qui dominos
units.tr: Now I set my foot, as it were, on the last stretch, which is how far the cross was used. For after it had put Life itself to death, it did not live long: Constantine removed it from human affairs, or at least from Roman ones. Being now a seriously committed Christian, he refused to let the saving sign serve for destruction, and he refused to let that revered and outstanding thing become cheap through the punishments of the condemned. So he abolished it. Victor: "He first removed the ancient and most ancient punishment of the gibbet and of breaking legs." Cassiodorus: "He prohibited by law the punishment of the cross, which had first been in use among the Romans." And he abolished it effectively: you will not find it brought back afterwards. Augustine: "Formerly men were fixed to the cross, which after an edict was forbidden, remains." The scholiast on Juvenal, on the line "and brings a part of the corpse," notes: "Of men; for the ancients fastened people to crosses." So do not take from this its age, and do not learn from it that the thing itself was not very ancient, although it was learned from antiquity. When did he abolish it? Late, and only at the very end of the empire. I infer this because, even while he was reigning, there is mention of crucifixions. What of the fact that it appears in his own time? A law in his name stands in the Theodosian Code, by which slaves and freedmen who try to accuse or denounce their masters or patrons, with a hearing refused, are fastened to the gibbet.

units.la: In Constant. — Hist. Trip. ix. cap. ix. — Quæst. in Vet. Test. — Lib. 2 x. Tit. v. nos aut patronos accusare aut deferre tentauerint, denegatâ audientiâ, patibulo adfiguntur. Iam Iulius Firmicus, qui eius regno scripsit, non semel Crucis meminit vt recepti supplicij atque visitati. Suprà exempla reperies, atque adde istud de latronibus: Hi, inquit, in crucem tollentur, aut publicâ animaduersione damnati crudelissimâ nece peribunt. Atquin illa ipsa Firmicus scripsit, sub finem eius imperij, & liberis iam adultis. Discès ex fine libri primi. Ergo serò, vt dixi, & sub vitæ finem. Indicat clarè Sozomenus, qui inter omnes ab eo leges hanc recenset postremam. Αμέλει δι, ⟨Greek⟩ ἐγν, inquit, νενομισμένων ῥωμαίοις τὴν ἓ σαῦρας ὑμω-εἶαν νόμῳ ἀναιρεῖ ... ἔ ... καθ'ἡ δικαστηρίων: Denique priùs visitatam Romanis crucis poenam, lege sustulit ex usu tribunalium ac iudiciorum. Ait, δικαστηρίων: an hoc indicans, quod nondum sublata ex visu omni priuato? & quod dominis etiam in seruos vetus suum ius? cogitandum sit. Sicut & illud, satisse Victor ex vero de Crurifragio pariter sublato scripserit, verbis quæ iamanté dedi. Ratio vix esse videtur. Quid enim Cruci aut Christo etiam cum Crurifragio? nisi quia latrones fortasse iuxta Christum. Ridiculum videatur. & si fuit; illud magis sit, quòd martyres multi eo tætro supplicio sint interfecti. Sed profectò sub Constantio eius filio vnum id reperio. Apollinares ambo, ait Ammianus, pater & filius, vt mandatum est, fractis cruribus occiduntur. Nam quod Firmicus etiam agnoscit, abijci elidique potest ratione quam praeiui. Tamen eius verba haec: Hi tales aut in crucem tolluntur, aut illis crura publicâ iudicum animaduersione franguntur. Vbi notabis, palàm, vt diuersum, à cruce seiungi: quod supra monui.
units.tr: In Constant. — Hist. Trip. ix. cap. ix. — Quæst. in Vet. Test. — Lib. 2 x. Tit. v. Moreover Julius Firmicus, who wrote in his reign, mentions the cross more than once as an accepted and customary punishment. You will find examples above, and add this about robbers: "These," he says, "are lifted onto the cross, or condemned by public punishment and perish by the most cruel death." Yet Firmicus wrote this near the end of that reign, when his sons were already grown. You will learn this from the end of the first book. So it was late, as I said, and at the end of his life. Sozomen indicates this clearly, listing this as the last of the laws. Namely, he says, the punishment of the cross, long customary among the Romans, he removed by law from the practice of the courts. He says "of the courts": is this indicating that it was not yet removed from all private use, and that masters still retained their old right over slaves? This must be considered. Likewise, Victor wrote, probably truthfully, that breaking of the legs was abolished at the same time, in the words I quoted above. The reason hardly seems to hold. For what has breaking of the legs to do with the cross or with Christ, unless perhaps because robbers were crucified beside Christ? It may seem ridiculous; and if it was so, it is rather that many martyrs were killed by that foul punishment. But truly under Constantius, his son, I find only this one case. "Both Apollinares," says Ammianus, "father and son, as had been ordered, were killed with their legs broken." For what Firmicus also acknowledges can be set aside and refuted by the reasoning I have set out. Yet his words are these: "Such men are either lifted onto the cross, or their legs are broken by the public punishment of the judges." Here you will note that it is plainly distinguished from the cross as something different, as I warned above.

units.la: CAP. XV. Honores quos Constantinus Cruci habitum iuit. Signis ea & vexillis impositá, aut inserta.
units.tr: CHAP. XV. The honours which Constantine paid to the cross. The cross set on and inserted into standards and banners.
