units.la: HIC exitus Poenalis Crucis fuit: & iam à Constantini primordijs Salutaris nostra coepta honorari. Caussa & origo à victoriâ contra Tyrannum. Nam cùm Maxentium aggressurus esset, ἀγωνιῶντι δὰ ταῦτα, τύπος αὐτῷ σαωεικοὶ μεσούσης ἡμέρας δ' ἀστέρων ἐφάνη κατ' οὐρανὸν, καὶ γεγραφὴ περὶ τὸν σαωέγ ρωμαικοῖς σοιχείοις, Ἐν τούτῳ νίκα. Ἐκ χεύἐσθαι τίνων αὐτίκα ἐκδιάσας σαωέγ τὴν τὸν φανέντα τύπον αὐτῷ, καὶ τοῦτον κελεύσας σεσημειωμένας αὐτὸς ἐπιπορεύεσθαι, τῆς τοῦ Μαξεντίου συρρήγνυ] καὶ ὑπερτερεῖ: ambigenti & animo anxio ob ista, figura ei crucis mediâ die stellis effecta, apparuit in cælo, & scriptura circa eam Romanis litteris, In hoc vince. Igitur ex auro statim subitario opere efformans crucem, iuxta speciem quam apparuisset, & hanc iubens praegredi exercitum, cùm Maxentianis proelium commisit, & superavit. Itaque statim victrix illud signum militaribus signis inseruit,& maximè Labaro quod inter ea primum. Prudentius ad ipsam Romam.
units.tr: Here was the end of the cross as a punishment, and from the beginnings of Constantine our Salvation began to be honoured. The cause and origin was victory over the tyrant. For when he was about to attack Maxentius, and was anxious about these things, a figure of a cross made of stars appeared to him in the sky at midday, and writing around it in Roman letters: "In this conquer" [Ἐν τούτῳ νίκα]. Therefore, immediately forging a cross of gold according to the shape that had appeared to him, and ordering it to go before him, he joined battle with the Maxentians and overcame them. And so at once, victorious, he inserted that sign among the military standards, and especially in the labarum, which was first among them. Prudentius, addressing Rome herself:

units.la: Agnoscas Regina lubens mea signa necesse est, In quibus effigies crucis aut gemmata refulget, Aut longis solido ex auro prefertur in hastis.
units.tr: "You, Queen, must gladly acknowledge my standards, on which the image of the cross shines, set with gems, or is carried on long spears of solid gold."

units.la: Dupliciter Poeta notat Crucem insitam signis, semel in vexillorum purpurâ, gemmis intextam & expressam: iterum in hastarum vertice superstantem, solido auro formatam: Sed, vt dixi, in Labaro maximè ea conspicua. de quo Prudentius:
units.tr: The poet notes in two ways that the cross was set on the standards: once woven into the purple of the banners, set with gems and embroidered, and again standing on the tops of the spears, formed of solid gold. But, as I said, it is most conspicuous on the labarum. Of this Prudentius writes:

units.la: Christus purpureum gemmanti textus in auro Signabat labarum.
units.tr: "Christ was marking the purple labarum, woven with gleaming gold."

units.la: Quomodo Christus? quia & nomen eius in ipso velo expressum, & crux nihilominus in hastâ.
units.tr: How Christ? Because his name was expressed on the cloth itself, and the cross nevertheless was on the spear.

units.la: Eusebius diffusè: Υψηλὸν δόρυ χρυσοῦ καταμφιεσμένον, κεφαλὴν εἶχεν ἐγκάρσιον, σανίδι χρυσῇ πεποικιλμένον, ἄνω ὃ ὡς ἄκρῳ τοῦ παντὸς, στέφανος ἐκ λίθων πολυτελῶν καὶ χρυσοῦ συμπεπλεγμένος κατεσκευάσθαι. καθ' ὃ τὸ σωτηρίας ἐπηγορίας τὸ σύμβολον δύο στοιχεῖα, ἓ Χριστοῦ ὄνομα, διὰ τῶν πρώτων ὑπεσήμαινον χαρακτήρων, χαζομένης τοῦ Ρ πῖ τὸ μεσαίτατον: Sublimis hasta auro circumuestita cornu transuersum habebat effigium in formâ crucis. Supra verò, in ipso culmine omnium, corona è lapidibus pretiosis & auro contexta infigebatur: iuxta quam salutaris appellationis symbolum, duae litterae Christi nomen exprimentes, per primos dumtaxat characteres, litterâ Graecanicâ P scilicet decussatâ & scissâ per medium ipso X. Neque cruces modò signis inseri voluit; sed hoc amplius, solas: ἐκ τῶν χρυσῶν ἀγαλμάτων οἵα πεποίηται τὸ μηδὲν: & aurearum imaginum cuiusmodi antea solebant, nullas. Intellegit aureas imagines vultusque Imperatorum. Forma ecce in Nummis.
units.tr: Eusebius at length: A lofty spear, clothed in gold, had a transverse piece in the form of a cross; and at the top, as the crown of the whole, a wreath of precious stones and gold was fastened. On it, the symbol of the saving name, two letters showing the name of Christ by its first characters, the letter P crossed through its middle by X, was marked. Neither did he wish crosses merely to be inserted into the standards, but moreover, from the golden images, of such kind as had been made, nothing; and of golden images of the kind they used to have, none. He means golden images and the faces of the emperors. See the form on the coins.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: Crux in militum armis: in Imperatorum capite & manibus: in monachorum veste: inseri eam praferunt, & templa.
units.tr: The cross is put on soldiers' arms, on the heads and hands of emperors, and on the garments of monks; and they also display it set into temples.

units.la: NEc vero in Signis solùm Crux expressa, sed etiam ipsorum militum armis. Eusebius:
units.tr: Nor was the cross displayed only on standards, but also on the very arms of the soldiers. Eusebius:

units.la: Ηδη δ' καὶ ἐπ' αὐτῶν τῶν ὅπλων τὸ ξ σωτηρίου τροπαῖον σύμ{a}βολον κατασημαίνεσθαι ἐποίει: Iam vero in armis ipsorum militum salutaris tropæi signum iussit exstare. Quibus armis? duplicibus, Clypeis & Galeis: sed ita, vt Christi quidem ipsum nomen (litteris & notis, quibus in Labaro) clypeis inscriberetur, Galeis autem imponeretur supernè Crux ipsa. Prudentius sic discriminat:
units.tr: He also ordered the sign of the saving trophy to be set on the very arms of the soldiers [Ηδη δ' καὶ ἐπ' αὐτῶν τῶν ὅπλων τὸ ξ σωτηρίου τροπαῖον σύμ{a}βολον κατασημαίνεσθαι ἐποίει]. Which arms? Double ones: shields and helmets. But the name of Christ itself was written on the shields, in the letters and marks found on the standard, while the cross itself was placed above on the helmets. Prudentius distinguishes them thus:

units.la: clypeorum insignia Christus
units.tr: Christ had written the emblems

units.la: Scripserat, ardebat summis crux addita cristis.
units.tr: of the shields, and the cross, added to the topmost crests, blazed.

units.la: Et merito Christus in clypeis, eo ritu quo solent nomina Imperatorum. Atque etiam hodie Constantinopoli sunt columnæ, à Constantino, vt putatur: in quarum basibus clypei cum his notis A ☧ ω.
units.tr: And rightly is Christ on the shields, in the manner in which the names of emperors are usually written. Even today at Constantinople there are columns, thought to be by Constantine, on whose bases are shields bearing these marks: A ☧ ω.

units.la: Sed & crucem in suum caput & ad Diadema Imperator transtulit, hicne, an alius? In Hieronymo quidem lego: Regum purpuras & ardentes diadematum gemmas patibuli Saluatoris pictura condecorat. Et credo ab ipso esse Constantino: qui, & insignurationibus solidorum & in imaginibus propriis signum crucis iussit inscribi. Id Sozomenus quoque asserit: Πλαπομψὼ τὲ ἐν νομίσμασι καὶ εἰκόσι γεγραφομένῳ ἐπέλθοσεν ἀεὶ συγγεγραφέας καὶ συντυπᾶσθαι τοῦτο τὸ θεῖον σύμβολον. καὶ μαρτυρέσθαι εἰς ἔτι νῦν εἰκόνες αὐτῶν ἐπὶ τούτοις ἔσαι ἐ χρήματος: Impresso autem sibi in nummis, aut picto in imaginibus, iussit semper adprimi & adpingi istud diuinum symbolum: & testantur etiamnunc imagines quæ in eo schemate exstant.
units.tr: But the emperor also transferred the cross to his own head and to the diadem. Was it he, or someone else? I read in Jerome: "The purple of kings and the flashing gems of the diadems are adorned with a picture of the Saviour's gibbet." And I believe it was Constantine himself, who "ordered the sign of the cross to be inscribed both on the marks of the coins and on his own images." Sozomen also asserts this: "Having impressed it on the coins, or painted it on the images, he ordered this divine symbol always to be stamped and painted; and the images that still exist in that form bear witness to it" [Πλαπομψὼ τὲ ἐν νομίσμασι καὶ εἰκόσι γεγραφομένῳ ἐπέλθοσεν ἀεὶ συγγεγραφέας καὶ συντυπᾶσθαι τοῦτο τὸ θεῖον σύμβολον. καὶ μαρτυρέσθαι εἰς ἔτι νῦν εἰκόνες αὐτῶν ἐπὶ τούτοις ἔσαι ἐ χρήματος].

units.la: Heraclij Imp. nummus aereus. ΘΗC ΑΕΙ ΑΥΓΥΣΤΟΣ ΗΡΑΚΛΕΙΟΣ ΕΝ ΧΨ ΤΥΦΩ ΝΙΚΗΤΗΣ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΥΣ ΡΩΜΑΙΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΑΛΛΟΣ ΦΙΛΑΝΘΡΩΠΗΤΗΣ ΑΠΟΛΛΙΝΙΟΣ + ILLVMINA VVLTVM TVVM deus SVPER TENEBRAS NOSTRAS MILITATOR SVPER ASPIDEM ET BASILISCVM AMBVLAVIT XOIA EN NVICTIC XV IO OV OTI XIEPPIE CIXI PAC MNAC KAI ELEYOC POCE ATIAN BACI HF CONCVLCAVIT LEONEM ET DRACONEM stant. Statuam etiâ sibi erigi fecit Romæ in urbe media, quæ manu hoc salutare signum teneret, cum inscriptione quam apud Eusebium, qui volet, leget. Et exemplum secuti Imperatores alij, in quorum *Numinis hodieque cruces variè videmus. Alias victoriæ sunt quæ manu eas leuent; alias ipsi, idque dupliciter. aut enim solam eam gestant, aut globulum cui ea infixa. De globulo Suidas etiam tangit, & caussam aperuit, in Iustiniano. Qui, inquit, ἑσπος τὸν ἑαυτοῦ εἰκόνα Φλλίου ἐφ' ἵππου. καὶ τὴν μὲν ἀριστερὰ χεῖρι Φέρει σφαῖραν, ἐμπεπηγότος ἐν σταυροῦ ...
units.tr: Bronze coin of the Emperor Heraclius. Legend: "Augustus Heraclius, ever victorious, conqueror in this sign, king of the Romans, and another Apollinius, lover of mankind" [ΘΗC ΑΕΙ ΑΥΓΥΣΤΟΣ ΗΡΑΚΛΕΙΟΣ ΕΝ ΧΨ ΤΥΦΩ ΝΙΚΗΤΗΣ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΥΣ ΡΩΜΑΙΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΑΛΛΟΣ ΦΙΛΑΝΘΡΩΠΗΤΗΣ ΑΠΟΛΛΙΝΙΟΣ]. Also: "Illumine your face, O God, over our darkness; the warrior walked over the asp and the basilisk; he trampled the lion and the dragon" [ILLVMINA VVLTVM TVVM deus SVPER TENEBRAS NOSTRAS MILITATOR SVPER ASPIDEM ET BASILISCVM AMBVLAVIT XOIA EN NVICTIC XV IO OV OTI XIEPPIE CIXI PAC MNAC KAI ELEYOC POCE ATIAN BACI HF CONCVLCAVIT LEONEM ET DRACONEM]. He also had a statue of himself erected in the middle of the city of Rome, which held this saving sign in its hand, with an inscription that anyone who wishes may read in Eusebius. Other emperors followed his example, and on their coins we still see crosses in various forms. Some are victories who lift the cross in their hands; others the emperors themselves hold, and this in two ways: either they carry the cross alone, or a globe into which it is fixed. Suidas also touches on the globe and explains the reason, in the article on Justinian: "He set up his own image on a column, on horseback. In his left hand he carries a globe, with a cross fixed in it, [the globe signifying the earth] because of its spherical shape. The cross, however, signifies faith, because of God who died in the flesh upon it" [ἑσπος τὸν ἑαυτοῦ εἰκόνα Φλλίου ἐφ' ἵππου. καὶ τὴν μὲν ἀριστερὰ χεῖρι Φέρει σφαῖραν, ἐμπεπηγότος ἐν σταυροῦ ... ἐν τῇ γῆ, διὰ τὸ σφαιροειδὲς αὐτῆς χῆμα. πίστις δὲ ὁ σταυρός, διὰ τὸν ἐν αὐτῷ σαρκὶ ἀποθανόντα θεόν]. Yet Justinian was not the author of this invention: coins so marked by Theodosius and others exist long before his time. Indeed, I observe that the Byzantine princes carried this cross in their own hands in public processions. John Curopalates: "Of the other insignia the emperor carries whatever he pleases, but he always carries the cross in his right hand" [Ἀπὸ μὲν οὖν τῶν ἄλλων φορημάτων φορεῖ ὁ βασιλεὺς οἷα ἂν βέλτιστον, τὸ δὲ γε σταυρὸν ἐν δεξιᾷ φέρει αἰεί].

units.la: ἐν τῇ γῆ, διὰ τὸ σφαιροειδὲς αὐτῆς χῆμα. πίστις δὲ ὁ σταυρός, διὰ τὸν ἐν αὐτῷ σαρκὶ ἀποθανόντα θεόν: Iustinianus imaginem suam posuit super columnam in equo. Ea sinistra manu fert globum, cruce in eo infixa: significante quod per fidem in crucem, terra dominus sit factus. Globus enim terra est, ob hanc eius rotundam formam: fides autem crux, ob Deum qui carne in eâ affixus. Nec tamen Iustinianus inuenti eius auctor: exstant Theodosij aliorumq; nummi sic insigniti diu ante illum. Quin observuo Principes Byzantinos in progressibus publicis crucem hanc prætulisse suâptè manu. Ioannes Curopalates: Ἀπὸ μὲν οὖν τῶν ἄλλων φορημάτων φορεῖ ὁ βασιλεὺς οἷα ἂν βέλτιστον, τὸ δὲ γε σταυρὸν ἐν δεξιᾷ φέρει αἰεί. E reliquis gestaminibus gestat Imperator quæ voluerit cunque: Crucem autem dexterâ semper gestat.
units.tr: In the earth, because of its spherical shape. The cross is faith, because God died in the flesh upon it [ἐν τῇ γῆ, διὰ τὸ σφαιροειδὲς αὐτῆς χῆμα. πίστις δὲ ὁ σταυρός, διὰ τὸν ἐν αὐτῷ σαρκὶ ἀποθανόντα θεόν]: Justinian set up his own image on a column, on horseback. In his left hand he holds a globe with a cross fixed in it, signifying that through faith in the cross he has become lord of the earth. For the globe is the earth, because of its round form; and the cross is faith, because God was fixed to it in the flesh. Yet Justinian was not the author of this invention: coins of Theodosius and others marked in this way exist long before him. Indeed, I observe that the Byzantine emperors used to carry this cross in their own hand in public processions. John Curopalates: Of the other ornaments the emperor wears whatever is most fitting, but he always carries the cross in his right hand. [Ἀπὸ μὲν οὖν τῶν ἄλλων φορημάτων φορεῖ ὁ βασιλεὺς οἷα ἂν βέλτιστον, τὸ δὲ γε σταυρὸν ἐν δεξιᾷ φέρει αἰεί.]

units.la: Atque infrà: Καὶ τῇ μὲν δεξιᾷ χρεὶ κατέχει τὸν σαυ-ρὸν, ὡς Σιβυλλης ἐστι νεκρλεῖν τὸν βασιλέα ὅταν Ꞓ τὸ σῆμα φορεῖ: Et dextrâ quidem manu tenet crucem, sicut solenne est teneri ab Imperatore, quoties & Stemma fert, id est diadema. Ab hoc ritu etiamnunc crucifer ille globus inter Sacri illius Imperij insignia: quod tu nunc Rudolphe Caesar per tot inclytos maiores ad te missum tenes, tenebisq; diu (ita voueo) bono Christiani orbis.
units.tr: And further on: "And in his right hand he holds the cross, as it is customary for the emperor to hold it whenever he wears the Stemma, that is, the diadem" [Καὶ τῇ μὲν δεξιᾷ χρεὶ κατέχει τὸν σταυρὸν, ὡς Σιβυλλῆς ἐστι νεκρλεῖν τὸν βασιλέα ὅταν τὸ σῆμα φορεῖ]. From this custom the cross-bearing globe still survives among the insignia of that holy empire, which you, Emperor Rudolf, now hold, sent down to you through so many illustrious ancestors, and which you will hold for long (so I pray) for the good of the Christian world.

units.la: Quod his elogijs cum Damasceno lubens merito afficio, Θυρεὸς καὶ ὅπλον καὶ τεῖχος τὸ τοῦ διαβόλου σφεγγίς, ἵνα μὴ θίγῃ ἡμῶν ὁ ὀλοθρεύων, τῶν κειμένων ἀνάστασις, τῶν ἐστώτων στήριγμα, αἰωνίου βασιλεία, ποιμαινομένων ῥαβδός, ἐπισκεφόντων χειραγωγία, πεσοῦντων ἐπανόρθωσις, κοπιόντων τελείωσις, ψυχῆς σωτηρία καὶ σώματος, πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἀποτείχισμα, πάντων τῶν ἀγαθῶν θέξεν, ἁμαρτίας ἀναίρεσις, φυτὸν ἀναστάσεως, ξύλον ζωῆς αἰωνίου: Clypeus & armatura, & tropæum contra diabolum, signaculum, ne tangat nos euersor, jacentium erectio, stantium fulcrum, infirmorum scipio, pastorum virga, reuertentium manuductio, proficientium perfectio, anima conseruatio & corporis, omnium malorum auersio, omnium bonorum conciliatio, peccati pernicies, stirps resurrectionis, lignum vitæ æterna. Da hanc nobis ô AETERNE.
units.tr: With Damascene I gladly and rightly bestow these praises upon it: "Shield, armour and wall against the devil, the splendour that keeps the destroyer from touching us; the raising of the fallen, the support of those who stand, the eternal kingdom, the staff of those who are led, the hand-guide of those who turn back, the perfecting of those who advance, the preservation of soul and body, the warding off of all evils, the bestowal of all goods, the destruction of sin, the plant of resurrection, the tree of eternal life" [Θυρεὸς καὶ ὅπλον καὶ τεῖχος τὸ τοῦ διαβόλου σφεγγίς, ἵνα μὴ θίγῃ ἡμῶν ὁ ὀλοθρεύων, τῶν κειμένων ἀνάστασις, τῶν ἐστώτων στήριγμα, αἰωνίου βασιλεία, ποιμαινομένων ῥαβδός, ἐπισκεφόντων χειραγωγία, πεσοῦντων ἐπανόρθωσις, κοπιόντων τελείωσις, ψυχῆς σωτηρία καὶ σώματος, πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἀποτείχισμα, πάντων τῶν ἀγαθῶν θέξεν, ἁμαρτίας ἀναίρεσις, φυτὸν ἀναστάσεως, ξύλον ζωῆς αἰωνίου]. Shield and armour and tropaeum against the devil, the signal that the destroyer may not touch us; the raising of the fallen, the stay of those who stand, the kingdom of eternity, the rod of those who are shepherded, the guiding hand of the wavering, the perfecting of those who labour, preservation of soul and body, the warding off of all evils, the bringing in of all goods, the removal of sin, the plant of resurrection, the tree of eternal life. Grant us this, O ETERNAL ONE.

units.la: ALLOCVTIO.
units.tr: Address

units.la: ADTEXTVM etiam meum, Lector, visum fuit breuiter hæc notare. Cur non in ipso? quia non pro omnium gustu hæc talia, & plerisque satis est capita rerum delibasse. Caussa etiam, quia placuit quædam explicatius aut firmius iterare. Debui sanè, vt hoc æuum est: in quo calumniæ, vt ille inquit,
units.tr: I thought it right, reader, to make some brief notes on my own text as well. Why not within the text itself? Because such things do not suit every taste, and for most readers it is enough to have tasted the main heads of the subject. I also wished to explain certain points more fully or to repeat some of them more firmly. Indeed I ought to do so, since this is the age it is, in which, as a certain writer puts it, slanders:

units.la: Quasi herba irrigua, succrevrunt uberrime.
units.tr: Like watered grass, they have sprung up most abundantly.

units.la: In culpa sumus, siue quid commisimus, siue etiam omisimus: & plerisque pulchrum, non nisi τὰς ἀκανθας τῶν βιβλίων ἐκλέγειν. Ego verò scio neminem esse tam felicem, qui non subiectus sit errori, & hoc non dementis esse proprium, verùm hominis. Itaque ne nunc quidem cum caueo, satis cauero: vtique in isto vario & diffuso scribendi genere,
units.tr: We are at fault, whether we have committed something or left something out, and many people think it fine to pick out only the thorns of books [τὰς ἀκανθας τῶν βιβλίων ἐκλέγειν]. For my part, I know that no one is so fortunate as to be free from error, and that this is not the mark of a madman but of a man. So even now, when I take care, I am not sure I have taken enough care, least of all in this kind of writing, which is varied and diffuse,

units.la: *Spinas librorum eligere. genere, in quo alius alio plura inuenire potest, nemo omnia. Quo magis mirū, quoidam nobis insultare: nec cogitare quàm multa ipsi fortasse non repperissent, si primi quæsissent. Non sum tam Lynceus, inquiunt, quàm mihi videor. Egone? testor te summe Deus, non videor: & siquid olim in calidâ illâ ætate calidius, abijt, & veris me pretijs nunc æstimo & pendo. Quo longius in hac vitæ viâ progredior, magis magisque aspicio circumfusam animo caliginem, corpori imbecillitatem. Heracleitus, opinor, olim dicere solitus, Se cùm iuuenis esset, nihil scire; cùm senex, nihil ignorare: mihi planissimè contrà euenit, & qui olim aliquid scire visus, nunc parum aut nihil. Et ô miseri, quid nos, doctrina, fama sumus? Ipsi puluis, illa opinio, ista ventus.
units.tr: a kind of writing in which one man can find more things than another, but no one can find everything. For this reason it is all the more surprising that some people insult us, without considering how many things they themselves would perhaps not have found, had they been the first to search. "I am not as sharp-sighted as I think I am," they say. Am I? I call you to witness, highest God, that I am not. And if anything in that hot-blooded age of mine was too hot, it has gone, and I now judge and weigh myself by the true measure. The further I advance on the road of this life, the more I see a darkness spreading round my mind and a weakness in my body. Heraclitus, I believe, used to say that when he was young he knew nothing, and when he was old he did not ignore anything; with me it has turned out quite the opposite: I who once seemed to know something now know little or nothing. Ah, wretched creatures that we are, what are learning and reputation? Dust itself, that opinion, and wind, that other thing.

units.la: Atqui etiam tangunt quasi manum iniecerimus scriptis alienis. Vellem parcius: certè non merito meo fit, qui prolixè & libenter honorem ingenijs inuentoribusque habitum iui, nisi sicubi Dialogorum ratio & decorum id impediuit. Tale in Saturnalibus. neque negamus virum magnum multa ante nos tè nos in eo argumento obseruitasse: sed scripta eius exstant, quid detraximus? Illud tamen non arbitror, ibi aut alibi insignior em notam aut correctiunculam malâ fraude in nomen meum transscriptam. Tetigit aliquis hanc aut illam materiam? quid tum? ego fortassis impleui. Et vt serio loquar, lectionis aut collectionis tota ista res est: cur alteri imputemus? Tot iam annos, imo lustra, in ijsdem illis scriptoribus versor, voluo reuoluo in easdem curas: malè mehercules de industria ingenioq; nostro sentit, quisquis aut non lecta ea nobis censet, aut neglecta. Vt è sonte quod haurimus, nostrum est, quisque tamen suo vase: sic quod è communibus illis scriptoribus, sed quisque pro iudicij sui modo. Denique legere aut colligere, parum est: seligere, disponere, eloqui, poscit laudem. Hæc & talia satiare nos scriptionis poterant: melior ratio reuocauit, & suasit publico prodesse quâ possum. Opes atque arma nostra, stilus. Quem tamen in alium nunquam stringam aut proferam: absit: Christianum me comemini, id est, Sacerdotem pacis.Habet gloria, ait Plinius, præ-sertim in studijs, quiddam ἀκοινωνητον: Nolo in me expetat. & quandocumque moriar, feram mecum hanc conscientiam, nullius me famæ inuidisse, quosdam meæ. Quod si æuum hoc parum etiam gratum sit: quid noui? Suum cuique pretium posteritas rependet. Tu Lector vale, & juuantem, aut certè volentem, ama.
units.tr: Yet people also lay hands on the writings of others, as if we had taken them over. I would wish it were less so. Certainly it is not by my own merit that I have been generous, and more than generous, in giving honour to the talents and inventions of others, except where the nature and decorum of the dialogue prevented it. This is the case in the Saturnalia. We do not deny that a great man observed many things on this subject before us, but his writings survive, so what have we taken away from him? Yet I do not think that any more notable mark, or small correction, has been transferred to my name there or elsewhere by wicked fraud. Has someone touched on this or that subject? So what? Perhaps I have filled it out. And, to speak seriously, this whole business belongs to reading and gathering: why should we impute it to another? For so many years, indeed decades, I have lived among those same writers, turning and returning to the same concerns. By heaven, whoever thinks that we have either not read them or neglected them thinks ill of our diligence and of our talent. As what we draw from a spring is our own, though each of us draws it in his own vessel, so what we take from those common writers is ours, each in our own way and according to our own judgement. In short, reading and gathering are of little worth: selecting, arranging and expressing things is what deserves praise. These and similar matters might have satisfied me in writing, but a better consideration recalled me and persuaded me to be of service to the public as far as I can. My resources and my weapons are my pen. I shall never turn it against another or bring it out for that purpose; far from it. I remember that I am a Christian, that is, a priest of peace. Glory, says Pliny, especially in studies, has something unsociable [ἀκοινώνητον] about it: I do not want it sought in me. And whenever I die, I shall carry with me this consciousness, that I have envied no one's fame, while some have envied mine. But if this age is little pleased by that, what is new? Posterity will pay each man his worth. Farewell, reader, and love the one who helps you, or at least the one who wishes to.

units.la: NOTÆ AD LIB. I.
units.tr: NOTES ON BOOK I.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: ABALVM] Exoticam vocem esse per me suspicabar, didici & Hebræam origine à Mart. Antonio Delrio, doctissimo & amicissimo viro. nam illis Gab, excelsum: Gabal, terminus, aut rectus stipes in agris. Quid nisi tale crux, quæ erecta, & in excelso? Reperio & in Persicarum vocum indice (à Franc. Raphelengio nostro habui) Gali notare excelsum. Iam nostras vox quantulum abit, qui Patibulum Galgam appellamus?
units.tr: ABALVM] I had suspected this to be a foreign word, and I have learned from Martín Antonio Delrío, a very learned and dear friend, that it is Hebrew in origin. For in that language Gab means height, and Gabal means a boundary or an upright post in the fields. What is a cross but something erected and set on high? I also find, in the index of Persian words that I had from our Franciscus Raphelengius, that Gali means high. How little does our own word differ, when we call the gibbet a Galgam?

units.la: Cruces Caucasorum.] Potes pro ipsis supplicijs accipere, & cruciariâ morte. Ausonius de hac quoque Promethæâ: Sic inter rupes Scythicas stetit alitibus crux. Vnde Prometheo de corpore sanguineus ros.
units.tr: Crosses of the Caucasians. You may take this as referring to the punishments themselves and to death by crucifixion. Ausonius also speaks of this Promethean cross: "So on the Scythian rocks the cross stood for the birds, and from it the bloody dew fell upon Prometheus' body."

units.la: Iunius Bassus apud Senecam lib. 1. Controu. III. Nihil amplius putabam adjici istius audaciæ posse, quàm quòd in illâ cruce Vestam nominauerat. Nusquam sanè crux, sed virgo deijcienda de saxo erat, Vestam inuocauit, & cecidit illæsa.
units.tr: Junius Bassus, quoted by Seneca in the first book of the Controversies, chapter 3: "I thought no further boldness could be added to that man's audacity than that he had called upon Vesta while on that cross." But there was surely no cross there; the virgin was to be thrown from a rock. She invoked Vesta and fell unharmed.

units.la: AD CAP. III.
units.tr: ON CHAPTER III.

units.la: Confixum esse Christo dicit.] Est illud Pauli ad Rom. cap. VI. Οτι ὁ παλαιὸς ἡμῶν ἄνθρωπος συνεσταυρώθη.
units.tr: He says he was fixed with Christ. This is the saying of Paul in Romans chapter 6: "that our old man was crucified with him" [ὅτι ὁ παλαιὸς ἡμῶν ἄνθρωπος συνεσταυρώθη].

units.la: Cruciarius.] Quo modo & Verberonem, Flagrionem, Mastigiam dicimus, verbere, flagro, mastige dignum. Tertullianus aliter hac voce vtitur. Febris per cruciarios & mortiferos exitus erogat hominem: id est, cruciantes. Quâ mente & Vinum crucium in Lucilio Festus obseruat, insuaue, acerbum.
units.tr: Cruciarius. Just as we say verbero, flagrio and mastigia, for one deserving the lash, the whip or the scourge, so Tertullian uses this word in another sense: "Fever, through its cruciarii and deadly ends, wears down a man," that is, causing torment. In the same sense Festus notes vinum crucium in Lucilius: wine that is harsh and sour.

units.la: AD CAP. IIII.
units.tr: ON CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Σταυρὸς & Σκόλοψ.] Nec tamen nego pluribus etiam verbis in hanc rem vti. Ecce & Ξύλον appellant crucem. Scriptor anonymus apud Suidam: Ξύλῳ Ἰουδαῖοι σωτῆρα ἀνεσταύρωσαν: Ligno recto Iudæi Seruatorem affixerunt. Sunt qui ita hoc verbi explicent & vertant in Thucydidis vitâ, quam scripsit Marcellinus: Ξυλόν ἐπὶ τὸ τάφος νεῖσθαι, τὸ νεκρὸν... ἀρχαῖον νόμιμον ἀπηνὲς... μὴ ἐν Ἀθήναις θάπτεσθαι: Ait quosdam opinari Thucydidem peregrè & in exsilio mortuum. Lignum enim siue Tabulam super sepulchrum eius positum esse. Hoc autem inanis & honorarij tumuli patrium patrium signum & solenne Atticum haberi, in ijs qui tali infortunio obyssent, nec Athenis sepulti essent. Sunt, inquam, qui Crucem aut Furcam vertant, nec mihi probant. Magis est, vt Ixeiov hic lignum nauale sit (peregrinantis, aut absentiæ indiciū, quoniam mari fere ex Attica abitur) de quo Hesychium vide. Ille idem Grammaticus addit: Ixeiov, σανίδωμα, ἢ ξύλον ἐν ᾧ κανεργοὶ ξέονται. Melius δέονται. Id esset, lignum siue axis in quo malefici ligantur. Atque ita Eustathius in Iliad. x. Σανὶς, ἐν ἢ τὰς κακούργες ἐδοῦν: Asser, in quo maleficos ligabant. Item Aristophanes: Βασανίζων πάντα ξύλον, ἐν σανίδι δέσας: Omni modo torquens, in assere ligans. Reperio & in Eusebio Ixeiov pro cruce, & supra adduxi, lib. ii. cap. xii. Σανίδα in hac re dixit Herodotus in extremâ Calliope: Απαγαγόντες δὲ αὐτὸν εἰς τὸ αὐτλὸ, σανίδα προσπασαλίσαντες ἀνεκρέμασαν. Quod vertunt: Adductum hunc in litus depactis humi asseribus suspenderunt. Vide an non σανίδ legas potius, hoc nostro sensu: Abducentes eum ad litus, asseri affigentes suspenderunt. Esset affixio in stipite simplex.
units.tr: Stauros and Skolops. Yet I do not deny that more words are used for this thing. See, they also call the cross xylon [ξύλον]. An anonymous writer in Suidas: "The Jews fixed the Saviour to a straight wood" [Ξύλῳ Ἰουδαῖοι σωτῆρα ἀνεσταύρωσαν]. There are those who explain and translate this word thus in the life of Thucydides, which Marcellinus wrote: "a wood placed upon the tomb, the body... a harsh ancient custom... not to be buried at Athens." He says that some suppose Thucydides died abroad, in exile, for a wood or board was placed over his grave. This empty token of an honorary tomb was regarded as the traditional and customary Attic sign for those who had met such misfortune and were not buried at Athens. There are some, I say, who render it cross or gallows, but I do not approve of this. It is more likely that ixeion here means a ship's timber (a sign of one who is abroad or absent, since people generally leave Attica by sea), on which see Hesychius. The same grammarian adds: ixeion, a plank, or a wood on which malefactors are scraped [ξέονται]. Better is δέονται, that is, bound. The sense would be "a wood or beam on which criminals are bound." Eustathius on the Iliad 10 likewise says: "A plank on which they bound the evildoers." Aristophanes also: "torturing everything, binding him to a plank." I find ixeion used for a cross in Eusebius too, and I have cited it above, book 2, chapter 12. Herodotus, in the last part of Calliope, used sanis in this matter: "Leading him to the shore, they nailed a plank and hanged him." It is translated: "Having dragged him to the shore, they hung him from planks driven into the ground." See whether you should not read sanida, in this sense: "Leading him to the shore, they fixed him to a plank and hanged him." The fixing would then be to a single upright post.

units.la: Κρεμάν. Ita palàm Plutarchus in Cæsare, de piratis: πολλάκις ἠπείλησε κρεμᾶν αὐτὰς: Sæpe minatus crucifigere eos, vt Latini omnes loquuntur & narrant. Est & Antiochi regis edictum, quo philosophos regno pellit, & pœnam etiam assectantibus ponit istam: τῶν δὲ νεανίσκων ὅσοι ἀν ἀλισκόντα πρὸς τούτοις χνόμενοι, δύο κρεμάσονται, ἡ οἱ πατέρες αὐτῶν ἐν αἰτίαις ἔσονται μεγίσταις: Iuuenum vero quicumque reperientur apud istos, ἡ suspendentur, & patres eorum hærebunt in maximâ noxâ. Ita Athenæus recitat lib. xii. sed vtrum de hac nostrâ in cruce suspensione, an de aliâ in trabe accipimus? In trabe, inquam, ad verberandum flagellandumque. quem morem Græcis Latinisque fuisse, comœdiæ atque alia docent.
units.tr: Kremân. Plutarch plainly uses it in the Life of Caesar, of pirates: "he often threatened to crucify them" [πολλάκις ἠπείλησε κρεμᾶν αὐτάς], as all the Latins also say and relate. There is also the edict of King Antiochus, by which he expels philosophers from the kingdom and sets this punishment for those who follow them: "Of the young men, whoever are caught besides these, shall be hanged, or their fathers shall be in the greatest guilt" [τῶν δὲ νεανίσκων ὅσοι ἂν ἁλισκόμενοι πρὸς τούτοις χνόμενοι, δύο κρεμάσονται, ἢ οἱ πατέρες αὐτῶν ἐν αἰτίαις ἔσονται μεγίσταις]. Athenaeus quotes it so in book 12. But do we take it of this suspension on a cross, or of another on a beam, for beating and flogging? On a beam, I say, for beating and scourging; that this custom existed among the Greeks and Latins, comedies and other writings show.

units.la: Aliorum inanes logos. Ita verè, inanes. Nam Alciati quale est? Ait Histiæum Milesium intellegi, quem Sardibus præpositum Artaphernes & Harpagus crucifixerunt, capite desecto & ad regem misso. Ita Herodotus, inquit, libro sexto. Quod verum est: sed quid Histiæo, cum Achæo? Respondet, ideo sic vocari à poeta, quia Histiæus Milesius fuit, Milesij coloni Ionum, Iones Achaiei. Ergo à Patria, Achæus. Quis color in hoc sermone? Sed nec amicum nostrum audio sine auctore scribentem: Achæum intellegi Lydiæ regem, qui ob auaritiam necatus in Pactoli aquis pependit.
units.tr: The empty arguments of others. Truly empty! For what is Alciati's view? He says that Histiaeus of Miletus is meant, "whom Artaphernes and Harpagus crucified at Sardis, after cutting off his head and sending it to the king." So Herodotus says in book 6. That is true, but what has Histiaeus to do with Achaeus? He answers that the poet so calls him because Histiaeus was of Miletus, Miletus was a colony of the Ionians, and the Ionians were Achaeans. So Achaeus comes from his homeland. What plausibility is there in this argument? But I hear that our friend writes without giving an authority: that Achaeus means the king of Lydia who, killed for his greed, hung in the waters of the Pactolus.

units.la: AD CAP. V.
units.tr: On Chapter V.

units.la: Memorem Veneris Proserpina Adonim. Ausonius fabellam aspicit, quæ est ista. Venus iam olim puerum hunc deamauerat, &c vt & vt sola frueretur, clàm depositerat apud Proserpinam. Sed hæc mox in eâdem flammâ: ac repetenti Veneri negat dare. Lis est, itur ad Iouem. Ille rem sic componit, vt Adonis, quod ad vsum, in tres anni partes secaretur. Prima, vt Adonis Adonidis esset: secundâ, Veneris: tertiâ Proserpinæ. Acquieuerunt. sed enim Adonis pronior in Venerem, suum quoque trientem illi tribuit. Hæc Apollodorus lib. iii. Bibliothecæ. Ergo istud est, quod Proserpina nunc cruce vindicat. Theocritus & ipse huc aspexit, Eidyll. xiiii.
units.tr: Proserpina remembers Adonis, whom she loved. Ausonius has in view the fable that goes like this. Venus had once loved this boy, and so that she might enjoy him alone, she had secretly deposited him with Proserpina. But Proserpina soon burned with the same flame, and when Venus asked for him back, she refused to give him up. There is a dispute, and they go to Jupiter. He settles the matter so that Adonis, as far as his use is concerned, is divided into three parts of the year: first, he would belong to Adonis himself; second, to Venus; third, to Proserpina. They agreed. But Adonis, being more inclined to Venus, gave his own third to her as well. Apollodorus tells this in book 3 of the Bibliotheca. This, then, is what Proserpina now claims with the cross. Theocritus also looked to this, in Idyll 14.

units.la: Ἔρπεις ὢ φίλ' Ἄδωνι, καὶ ἐν ϑαάδε χ' εἰς Ἀχέροντος Ἡμιϑέων, ὡς φαντὶ, μονώτατος.
units.tr: Ἔρπεις ὢ φίλ' Ἄδωνι, καὶ ἐν ϑαάδε χ' εἰς Ἀχέροντος Ἡμιϑέων, ὡς φαντὶ, μονώτατος. [You go, dear Adonis, even here, and down to the depths of Acheron, alone of the demigods, as they say.]

units.la: Migras, o bone Adoni, istuc & ad infera regna, Semideûm, vt dicunt, solus.
units.tr: You go, good Adonis, that way too, to the infernal realms, alone, as they say, of the demigods.

units.la: Nam vult non alteri concessum, vt modò ad inferos modò ad superos iret, & alternis copiam sui faceret duabus deabus.
units.tr: For she wills that it be granted to no one else that he should go now to the underworld and now to the upper world, and by turns grant his presence to the two goddesses.

units.la: Arbores recisas leuiter.] Ad has, vel ad nudum alium stipitem, allusit Quinctius in epigrammate quo poëtam Græculum facetè est vltus. Ille Philippum & Macedones insigni victoriâ fregerat, cuius laudem ad Aetolos transferre Alcæus quispiam voluit Græcâ leuitate. Scilicet quia in auxiliis Romanis fuerant Ætoli. Scripserat igitur:
units.tr: Trees lightly cut down. To these, or to some other bare stump, Quinctius alluded in an epigram with which he neatly avenged himself on the little Greek poet. That poet had praised Philip and the Macedonians for a notable victory, and some Alcaeus, with Greek levity, wished to transfer that praise to the Aetolians. Clearly this was because the Aetolians had been among the Roman auxiliaries. So he had written:

units.la: Ἀ̓ηλαυσοί καὶ ἀθανάτοι, ὀδυρόμεθ', τῷ δ' ὅτι τύμβῳ Θεσσαλίας, τρισσαὶ κείμεθα μυριάδες,
units.tr: Ἀ̓ηλαυσοί καὶ ἀθανάτοι, ὀδυρόμεθ', τῷ δ' ὅτι τύμβῳ Θεσσαλίας, τρισσαὶ κείμεθα μυριάδες, [Unwashed and unburied, we lament; for we lie in a tomb of Thessaly, three myriads.]

units.la: Αἰτωλῶν δ' μηθέντες ὑπ' ἄρεος, ἡδ' Λατίνων, Οὓς τίτος ξυρείης ἡμαγ' ἀπ' Ἰταλίας:
units.tr: Αἰτωλῶν δ' μηθέντες ὑπ' ἄρεος, ἡδ' Λατίνων, Οὓς τίτος ξυρείης ἡμαγ' ἀπ' Ἰταλίας: [Subdued in war by the Aetolians and by the Latins, whom Titus had led from Italy.]

units.la: Indesleti, inhumati, his campis ecce iacemus Thessaliæ, cæsi milliater decies, Ætolo domiti sub Marte, & Marte Latino, Quos Titus è latâ duxerat Italiâ.
units.tr: Unburied and unwashed, here on these plains of Thessaly we lie, slain thrice ten thousand, overcome in battle by Aetolian and by Latin Mars, whom Titus had led out of broad Italy.

units.la: En Ætolos Romanis præpositos, & quasi hi accessio illorum. Momordit Titum, & vltus est, sed versus versu. Rescripsit alludens:
units.tr: See, the Aetolians placed over the Romans, and as if these were an addition to them! He stung Titus and took his revenge, but verse for verse. He wrote back, alluding to it:

units.la: Ἀ̓φλοιος καὶ ἀφυλλος, ὀδοιπορε, τῷ δ' ὅτι νώτῳ Αλκαίω σαυρὸς πήγνυται ἠλίβατος:
units.tr: Ἀ̓φλοιος καὶ ἀφυλλος, ὀδοιπορε, τῷ δ' ὅτι νώτῳ Αλκαίω σαυρὸς πήγνυται ἠλίβατος: [Barkless and leafless, traveller, a steep stake is fixed on the back of Alcaeus.]

units.la: Corticibus ṣ & fronde carens, hac monte, viator, Alcæo crux de-figitur aëria.
units.tr: Stripped of bark and leaf, traveller, on this mountain a lofty cross is set up for Alcaeus.

units.la: Quibus versibus significat crucem defixam ibi stare, quæ hominem illum exspectet. Plutarchum in Quinctio lege: & simul nota, altam hic Crucem poni, quasi in scelere insigni, suo loco à nobis dictum.
units.tr: By these verses he signifies that a cross stands fixed there, waiting for that man. Read Plutarch in his life of Quinctius; and at the same time note that a high cross is set up here, as for a notable crime, as I said in its place.

units.la: Isidem vero Cererem.] Ipse Tertullianus hoc affirmat, de Coronâ militis: Prima Isis repertas spicas capite circumtulit. nam quæ hæc Isis quæ spicas repperit, nisi Ceres?
units.tr: But Isis, Ceres. Tertullian himself affirms this, in his book On the Crown of the Soldier: "Isis first carried the ears of corn she had discovered around her head." For who is this Isis who discovered the ears of corn, if not Ceres?

units.la: Ad cap. VI.
units.tr: On Chapter VI.

units.la: Nescio an Macenati descripta.] Ambiguè profero, quia etsi Mæcenatis verba nobis faciunt, vix tamen Senecæ, qui velut interpretans subdit: Suffigas licet, & acutam sessuro (ita legendum, non sensuro) crucem subdas, est tanti vulnus suum premere & patibulo pendere districtum. Atqui pendere,&patibulo quidem, vix est ut conueniat in nostram Acutam. Nisi si tamen patibulum etiam de vno ligno, in quo homo quomodocumque expansus: quod haud nimis velim sperni. Si displicet: alia interpretatio quærenda sit crucis hic acuta. An ideò talis, quia cum dolore acri necat? vt morbi quidam acuti medicis. Lente probem: & mauelim opinari genus aliquod crucium triste, rarum, in quo stipes, cui homo acclinatur, stimulis clauisque acutis sit præfixus, vt cum acquiescere vellet (sessuri vox in Senecâ) pungeretur ac scinderetur in corpore auerso. Nihil super hoc legi, fateor: commentum est merum, nisi si quid iuuat illa Reguli machina, quæ sic armata, & in eam ipse inclusus. Quæ etsi nostra crux non fuit (aumarium potiùs quoddam & arca) tamen & crucem Seneca appellauit epistolâ xcviii. itemque libro de prouidentiâ cap. iii. Certè quidem Acuta vocem in Mæcenatis versibus non sic leuiter & in ventum additam, ipse indicat Seneca, qui eam attollit ac repetit (tu vide) quasi in eâ sententiæ momentum.
units.tr: I do not know whether it was written down by Maecenas. I put this forward ambiguously, because although the words are Maecenas's, they scarcely seem to be Seneca's, who, as if interpreting, adds: "Though you fix it, and put a sharp cross under the one who is about to sit (so read, not sensuro), it is worth so much, to press down one's wound and hang on a gibbet drawn tight." But "hang" and "gibbet" hardly fit with our "sharp" cross. Unless perhaps the patibulum is also made from a single piece of wood, on which a man is stretched out somehow; and I would not like to dismiss this too readily. If that displeases, another interpretation must be sought for the "sharp" cross here. Is it so called because it kills with acute pain, as certain acute diseases are for doctors? I approve this slowly; I would rather suppose some grim and rare kind of cross, in which the post against which the man leans is fixed with sharp spikes and nails, so that when he wished to rest (sessuri, the word in Seneca) he would be pierced and torn in the body turned away. I admit I have read nothing on this; it is pure invention, unless perhaps that machine of Regulus helps, which was so armed, and into which he himself was shut. Although that was not our kind of cross (more a sort of cupboard or chest), Seneca nonetheless called it a cross in letter 98, and likewise in the book On Providence, chapter 3. Certainly Seneca himself shows that the word "sharp" in Maecenas's verses was not added so lightly and idly, since he raises it up and repeats it (note this well), as if the weight of the sentence rested on it.

units.la: Iam olim sic legimus.] Nempe in Curis secundis: idque è libris tantùm? imò ante me Pincianus, vir fidei & iudicij bonus. Muretus tamen aliter: sed qui bene examinat, stabit à nostrâ. cuius sententia, Hanc vitam mihi sustine & proroga, etiam sedenti in acuta cruce.
units.tr: We have read it thus long ago. Indeed, in the Curae secundae: and is this from books alone? No, before me Pincianus, a man of good faith and judgment, read it so. Muretus, however, reads otherwise; but whoever examines it well will side with our reading. His sense is: "Sustain and prolong this life for me, even when I sit on the sharp cross."

units.la: Ad cap. VII.
units.tr: On Chapter VII.

units.la: Ipsi verterunt ξύλον διδύμον.] Quod ipsum pro cruce posuit incertus scriptor apud Suidam: Ευρὼν δ' ἐ ἰλλᾶσον φθορέα, ἐυρέμασεν δὴ διδύμε ξυλα: Inueniens Illustum corruptorem suspendit in gemino ligno. Id est cruce: etsi Suidas interpretatur, τὴν παρὰ ῥωμαίοις φέρναν. Vide ipsum in voce Δίδυμον, & Ἰλλᾶσος.
units.tr: They rendered it ξύλον διδύμον. This very phrase an uncertain writer used for a cross, in Suidas: "Finding Illustus the corrupter, he hanged him on a double wood" [Εὑρὼν δ' Ἴλλυσον φθορέα, ἐκρέμασεν δὴ διδύμου ξύλου]. That is, a cross, although Suidas explains it as the punishment among the Romans called [τὴν παρὰ Ῥωμαίοις φέρναν]. See Suidas himself under the words Δίδυμον and Ἰλλᾶσος.

units.la: Ad cap. VIII.
units.tr: On chapter VIII.

units.la: Penulæ aut manui.] In penulâ aut veste monachorum crux, imò & cruces, si recte capio Nicephorum Gregoram, qui sic de Imp. Andronico monacho nouello: Αναω μὴ ἐρυθρὸν ὣς ἐπ᾽ ἕν... τῆς Θείας σταυρὸς τύπον, κάτω δὲ μέλανα: Superne rubrum prætulit diuinæ crucis signum, inferne nigrum. Duas diuersi coloris cruces appositas videtur dicere: nisi tamen vnam intellegit, sic distinctam. Quod manu autem tulerint, hodieque in Æthiopibus sive Abyssinis ille mos, uti vulgus reliquum cruces e collo pendulas gestet, monachi hoc amplius etiam manu. Auctor Damianus à Goës in illorum rebus. Illud etiam mihi nouitium legi, miseros oppressosq; cruces prætulisse, haud aliter quam olim infulas & velamenta. Ligurinus lib. viii. de Iralis hoc notat, qui ius auxiliumque poscebant ab Imp. Frederico: ex omnibus undique multi Vrbibus ac vicis aderant, querulóque ferebant Innumeras clamore cruces. hoc quippe quercus More solent aperire suas.
units.tr: In the cloak or in the hand.] If I understand Nicephorus Gregoras correctly, there was a cross on the cloak or garment of the monks, indeed crosses, where he says of the emperor Andronicus, a new monk: "He bore on the upper part a red sign of the divine cross, and below it a black one" [Αναω μὴ ἐρυθρὸν ὣς ἐπ᾽ ἕν... τῆς Θείας σταυρὸς τύπον, κάτω δὲ μέλανα]: Superne rubrum prætulit diuinæ crucis signum, inferne nigrum. He seems to speak of two crosses of different colours placed side by side, unless he means one cross distinguished in this way. That they carried one in the hand is still the custom among the Ethiopians, or Abyssinians, where the common people wear crosses hanging from the neck, and the monks carry one in the hand as well. The authority is Damianus à Goës on their affairs. I have also read something new: that wretched, oppressed people carried crosses, much as they once carried standards and veils. Ligurinus, book viii, notes this about the Italians who sought justice and help from the emperor Frederick: from all sides many came from the cities and villages, and with a plaintive cry they bore countless crosses, for thus oaks are wont to open their own.

units.la: Cum anulo vel ansulâ.) Ansulam Becanus facit, & interpretatur (ita ingenium & scopus viri fuit) μυσηικῶς, quasi moneamur apprehendere crucem, & eam tenere. Quid si oculum esse dicam? Iuuet aliquid Macrobius, qui inter notas Ægyptiacas refert, & significare ait Solem. Lib. i. Saturn. cap. xxi. Osirim Ægyptij ut Solem esse asserant, quoties Hieroglyphicis litteris suis exprimere volunt, insculpunt sceptrum, inq; eo speciem Oculi exprimunt, & hoc signo Osirim monstrant: quia Solem, Iouis oculum, appellauit antiquitas. Et sane quia signum hoc Tau Vitam venturam designauit: nónne apposite Sol ascriptus, qui auctor vitæ?
units.tr: With a ring or a little handle.) Becanus takes the little handle to be the ansula and explains it mystically (that was his cast of mind and purpose), as if we were reminded to grasp the cross and hold on to it. What if I say it is an eye? Macrobius may help, who, among the Egyptian signs, reports that the Sun is signified. Book i of the Saturnalia, chapter xxi: When the Egyptians wish to express Osiris in their hieroglyphic letters, as they say he is the Sun, they carve a sceptre, and in it they show the figure of an eye, and with this sign they point out Osiris, because antiquity called the Sun the eye of Jupiter. And indeed, since this sign Tau designated the life to come, is not the Sun fittingly added to it, as the author of life?

units.la: Ad cap. x.
units.tr: On chapter x.

units.la: Vnicornis enim cornua.] Curiosè & pæne dixerim morosè explicat Iustinus. simplicius multo Tertullianus, aduerf. Iud. cap. x. Tauri decor eius, cornua vnicornis cornua eius, in eis nationes ventilabit pariter vsque ad summum terræ. Non vtique Rhinoceros destinabatur vnicornis, nec Minotaurus bicornis: sed Christus in illo significabatur. cuius cornua essent crucis extima. Nam & in antennâ nauis, quâ crucis pars est, hac extremitates huius cornua vocantur. Vnicornis autem medij stipitis palus.
units.tr: For the horns of the unicorn. Justin explains this with a fussy, I might almost say tedious, care. Tertullian is far simpler, in Against the Jews, chapter x: Its beauty is that of a bull, its horns the horns of a unicorn; with them it will scatter the nations together to the ends of the earth. The unicorn was not meant to be the rhinoceros, nor the Minotaur the two-horned beast; rather Christ was signified in it, whose horns are the outermost parts of the cross. For on the yard of a ship, which is part of a cross, its extremities are likewise called horns. The unicorn, however, is the central upright post.

units.la: * Λλων ... ] Mutilus locus. & aptant quidem hæc ad trophæa vulgaria, siue monumenta victoriæ: ego cùm in verba intendo, ambigo: & nescio quid de fasciribus potius suboleret dictum. Per illos (ita verterim δι' ὧν) progressus in publicum fiunt: illi verè signa imperij & potestatis. Atque cum insertâ securi, crucem referunt planissimè. Nónne etiam Tropæa? inquies. Quis nescit? sed præiuit fortasse aliquid de Tropæis illis: hîc magis de fasciibus (mihi quidem (dixisse videtur. Nec moueor quod Τεγνλίων voce vtatur: nónne & suprà Malum in naui nani sic vocauit? & Eusebius etiam Labarum illum militarem. Possunt & verba alia excidisse. Nec pono tamen ista, sed propono.
units.tr: * Λλων ... ] A corrupt passage. These words certainly fit ordinary trophies, or monuments of victory; but when I attend closely to the words I am uncertain, and I do not know what was said that smacks rather of the fasces. Through those (so I would translate δι' ὧν) they come out into public: those are truly the signs of rule and power. And with an axe inserted they very clearly bear a cross. Will you say, "Do not trophies also?" Who does not know it? But perhaps something about those trophies has gone before; here it seems to me to speak rather of the fasces. Nor am I troubled that he uses the word Τεγνλίων [Τεγνλίων]: did he not also call the mast of a ship in the same way, above? And Eusebius also called that military standard the Labarum. Other words may have dropped out. I do not, however, put these forward as settled, but only propose them.

units.la: Αυτοκρατόρων ἀποθνησκόντων τὰς εἰκόνας.) Quae illae sunt? quis me docet? In Nummis, in statuis nihil tale video, nec vsquam in cruce propositos Principes defunctos. Subdubitabam an ad aquilas respiceret, quae volantium habitu, & in caelum tendentium passis alis conspiciuntur in Nummis, & additum Consecratio. Scilicet quasi Iouis illa ales animam defuncti ferret in gremium Iouis. Certè quidem eam formā crucis esse & Patres monent & res ipsa docet. Sed non placet. Hoc nunc magis, intellegere eum imagines defunctorum Principum, quae ordine innexae in militaribus signis. Nec enim viuorum, solum illic effigies, sed magis mortuorum. De isto ipso aeuo Constantini Eusebius, libro II. De vita eius, cap. xv I. Describit Licinij milites in pugnam, more veterum, id est, gentilium exeuntes: οἱ δὲ, inquit, πολυπληθεία θεῶν θαρρῆντες σὺν πολλῇ δυνάμει χειρὸς ἐσεφανωμένης ἐπήεσαν, ἐνεφερον εἰδωλα θανόντων ἐν ἀψύχοις ἀγάλμασι ... μένοι: Hi quidem numero deorum freti cum multa manu militari ingruebant, mortuorum imagines in signis inanimatus praeferentes. Et scripsi de hoc more ad Taciti Annales. Ergo hoc Iustinus exprobrat, Vos, inquit, cruces colitis, cum Imperatorum & quidem Diuorum imagines proponitis in hastis & vexillis, quid nisi in crucibus? Nam ea illis figura. Respexi etiam aliquando ad Tertullianum, in Apologetico: Quod non simulacrum prius argilla deformat, cruci & stipiti superposita? Sed hoc diffusum nimis est, nec tangit Imperatores tantum.
units.tr: The images of emperors who had died [Αυτοκρατόρων ἀποθνησκόντων τὰς εἰκόνας]. What are these? Who will teach me? On coins and statues I see nothing of the kind, nor anywhere do deceased princes appear placed on a cross. I wondered whether he was looking at the eagles, which appear on coins with the look of birds in flight, wings spread as they rise to heaven, with the addition Consecratio: as if that eagle of Jupiter were carrying the soul of the dead man into Jupiter's bosom. Certainly the Fathers warn that the cross had that form, and the thing itself teaches it. But I am not satisfied with this. I now prefer to understand that he means the images of dead princes, which were linked in order on the military standards. For there were displayed there not only the likenesses of the living, but still more those of the dead. Eusebius, in book ii of his Life of Constantine, chapter xvi, describes the soldiers of Licinius going into battle in the manner of the ancients, that is, of the Gentiles. "They," he says, "trusting in the multitude of their gods, advanced with a great army, their hands crowned, carrying on lifeless standards the images of the dead" [οἱ δὲ, πολυπληθεία θεῶν θαρρῆντες σὺν πολλῇ δυνάμει χειρὸς ἐσεφανωμένης ἐπήεσαν, ἐνεφερον εἰδωλα θανόντων ἐν ἀψύχοις ἀγάλμασι ... μένοι]: Hi quidem numero deorum freti cum multa manu militari ingruebant, mortuorum imagines in signis inanimatis praeferentes. I have also written on this custom in my notes on the Annals of Tacitus. So Justin reproaches them thus: "You worship crosses; when you set up the images of emperors, and indeed of deified ones, on spears and banners, what else is it but on crosses? For that is their shape." I once also looked back at Tertullian in the Apologeticus: What image does not first shape the clay, placed upon a cross and stake? But this is too far-fetched, and it touches not only emperors.

units.la: AD CAP. XI.
units.tr: NOTES ON CHAPTER XI.

units.la: Populariter & ad caussam Cicero dixerit.] Quod historica fide, non opinor. Plinius non ei fautor lib. xxxv I. cap. xv. Nouum & inexcogitatum antea posteaq; remedium inuenit ille rex (Tarquinius Superbus) vt omnium ita defunctorum figeret crucibus corpora, spectanda ciuibus, simul & feris volucribusq; laceranda. Nam liquet eum loqui de mortuis & iis qui se interficerent laborum taedio, quos ille crucifixit. At non id in viuis vsurpauit primus, vt ait, vltimusque.
units.tr: Cicero may have spoken this way in a popular manner and to suit his case. I do not think it rests on historical fact. Pliny is no supporter of this view, in Book 35, chapter 15: "That king (Tarquin the Proud) discovered a new remedy, never thought of before: to fix the bodies of all the dead to crosses, to be viewed by the citizens, and at the same time to be torn by wild beasts and birds." For it is clear that he is speaking of the dead, and of those who killed themselves from weariness of their labours, whom he crucified. But he was not, as Pliny says, the first and last to use this on the living.

units.la: Arboribus suspendunt.] Haud iniuria ambigo, ad vtram poenam referam, laquei, an Crucis. Nam nec verba alterutrum euincunt, nec alia exempla. Lego in Martyrologio, die xiiii. Martij. de duobus Monachis, quos Longobardi suspendio necaue-runt in arbore. In ipsis Longobardorum legibus, Tit. c. xiiii. Si seruus regis Morth fecerit, ita decreuimus vt componatur ipsa persona sicut adpreciatus fuerit : & seruus ipse super fossam mortui appendatur, & in eum vindicta detur, & sit causa finita. Plurium (antiquorum quidem) nunc non memini : & haec ipsa incerta, nec diuudicauerint litem.
units.tr: I am rightly uncertain which punishment I should refer it to, the noose or the cross. For neither the words nor other examples settle the matter either way. I read in the Martyrology, on 14 March, about two monks "whom the Lombards put to death by hanging on a tree." In the laws of the Lombards themselves, title 14: "If the slave of King Morth commits (a crime), we have decreed that the person himself be compensated at the value at which he was assessed, and that the slave himself be hanged over the grave of the dead man, and vengeance be given upon him, and the matter be closed." Of other (ancient) instances I do not now recall any; and these very cases are doubtful and do not decide the question.

units.la: IVSTI LIPSI AD LIB. II. NOTÆ.
units.tr: Notes of Justus Lipsius on Book II.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: Chapter II.

units.la: APVT obnubito] Quod plerisque puniendis factum, praesertim si gladio. Hegesippus lib. v. cap. xlvii. Dum percussor moratur, clausis iam fasciola oculis, sese proripuit ad Romanos. In vita Cypriani: Postea vero B. Cyprianus manu sua oculos sibi texit. Sed & cum ducerentur ad carcerem, aut ad mortem, caput tegebatur. Tacitus iiii. Annal. Trahebatur damnatus, quantum obducta veste & astrictis faucibus niti poterat, clamitans. Ammianus lib. xiiii. Carnifex rapinarum sequester, & obductio capitum, & bonorum vbique multatio. Imo & torquendis hoc factum. In Curtio lib. vi. de Philota: Dum obligantur oculi, dum vestis exuitur, deos patrios, gentium iura inuocabat. Proprie autem de crucifigendis, vetus illud carmen quod iam explico: & in libro Esther, cum Aman ad crucem rapitur, Statim operuerunt faciem eius.
units.tr: Covering the head: this was done with many who were to be punished, especially those beheaded with the sword. Hegesippus, book 5, chapter 47: "While the executioner delayed, he tore himself away towards the Romans, his eyes already bound with a cloth." In the Life of Cyprian: "Afterwards, indeed, Blessed Cyprian covered his own eyes with his hand." And when men were led to prison or to death, the head was also covered. Tacitus, Annals book 4: "The condemned man was dragged along, as far as he could struggle with his garment drawn over him and his throat constricted, crying out." Ammianus, book 14: "The executioner of plunder, the covering of heads, and the confiscation of goods everywhere." Indeed this was also done to those being tortured. In Curtius, book 6, concerning Philotas: "While his eyes were being bound, while his clothing was being stripped off, he called upon the gods of his fathers and the laws of nations." But specifically of those to be crucified, the old poem which I am now explaining says so; and in the book of Esther, when Haman is dragged to the cross: "They immediately covered his face."

units.la: AD CAP. III.
units.tr: On Chapter III.

units.la: Ασραγαλωταὶς μάστιγας. ] Addo, si nosse lubet, quasdam etiam dictas σραγγαλωταὶς, istis haud absimiles, contortas scilicet & nodosas. Suidas: σραγγαλιῶδες, διεσραυμένον. Καὶ σεραγγαλωτὴ μάστιξ. Addit deinde verba incerti scriptoris: Ο δὲ ἐκέλευσεν αὐτὸν μαστιγοῦσθαι τῇ σραγγαλωτῇ μάστιγι.
units.tr: Whips with knucklebones [ἀστραγαλωταῖς μάστιγας]. I add, if you care to know, that some are also called "sphragalotai" [σφραγγαλωταί], not unlike those, that is, twisted and knotted. Suidas: "sphragalōdes, knotted and torn" [σφραγγαλιῶδες, διεσφραμένον]. And a "sphragalōtē whip" [σφραγγαλωτὴ μάστιξ]. He then adds the words of an unknown writer: "But he ordered him to be scourged with the sphragalōtē whip" [Ὁ δὲ ἐκέλευσεν αὐτὸν μαστιγοῦσθαι τῇ σφραγγαλωτῇ μάστιγι].

units.la: AD CAP. V.
units.tr: On Chapter V.

units.la: Quid opus erat auxiliatore & subsequâ, qui adleuasset?] Ita vulgata quidem opinio est, dumtaxat adleuasse. At D. Hieronymus in Matthæum censet etiam tulisse, sed seorsim & post Christum. Nam cùm Ioannes apertè scribat Christum tulisse, alij tres Euangelistæ Simonem Cyrenæum : ipse conciliat, & hoc intelligendum est, inquit, quòd egrediens de Prætorio Iesus ipse portauerit Crucem suam : posteà obuium habuerint Simonem, cui portandam crucem imposuerunt.
units.tr: "What need was there of a helper and follower, who might lift him up?" The common opinion is indeed that he merely helped lift it. But Saint Jerome, in his commentary on Matthew, holds that he also carried it, but separately and after Christ. For since John plainly writes that Christ carried it, and the other three Evangelists name Simon of Cyrene, he reconciles them thus: "This must be understood," he says, "that Jesus himself, going out of the Praetorium, carried his own cross; afterwards they met Simon, and laid the cross upon him to carry."

units.la: AD CAP. VII.
units.tr: On Chapter VII.

units.la: Super lignum seipsum extendit.] Quid si de transuersario tantùm ligno capias, in eo figi soliros, & deinde subduci atque appendi? Pugna omnis cesset; & breuiter fortasse rem dixi.
units.tr: "He stretched himself upon the wood." What if you take this only of the crossbeam, on which they were accustomed to fix the body, and then lower it and hang it? All the dispute would cease; and perhaps I have stated the matter briefly.

units.la: AD CAP. VIII.
units.tr: On Chapter VIII.

units.la: Clauis aut funibus] Nescio an Lucanus non vtrosque memoret in his occultioris sententiæ versibus, qui quoniam toti ad crucem, ponamus, & retegamus. Lib. vi. de magâ Thessalâ. Laqueum nodósque nocentes Ore suo rupit, pendentia corpora carpsit, Abrasitq; cruces, percussàque viscera nimbis Vulsit, & incoctas admisso Sale medullas: Incertum manibus chalybem, nigramq; per artus Stillantis tabi saniem, virusq; coactum Sustulit, & neruo morsus retinente pependit.
units.tr: "Nails or cords." I am not sure whether Lucan does not mention both in these verses of more hidden meaning, which, since they all bear on the cross, let us set down and unfold. Book 6, on the Thessalian witch: "She broke with her mouth the noose and the baneful knots, she plucked at the hanging bodies, and scraped the crosses, and tore the pierced flesh with showers, and the marrow baked by the sun, with the salt added; the iron, not known to hands, and the black pus dripping from the limbs, and the gathered poison she took away, and she hung on the sinew that held the bite."

units.la: Quod ait laqucum & nodos nocentes: alij nocentum edunt: atque ita haud incommodè ad vincula aptes, quibus noxij ad cruces astricti. Tamen in aliquot scriptis libris, recentes, & id malim: credamque ad suspendiosos dumtaxat referendum, & qui seipsos illaquearunt. Reliqua iam de Cruce: & percussa viscera nimbis, & incoctas sole medullas, signanter dixit de corporibus quæ (vt lib. II. cap. x v. scripsi) in crucibus relicta, situ marcida & tabida fiebant, quatenus volucres non laniarent. Iam Incertum manibus chalybem, clauos intelligi liquebit, si emendes Insertum. Nam hos quoque appetitos ad Magicas artes. Apuleius ostendit, in describendâ feralis illâ officinâ, lib. III. Hic nares & digiti, illic carnosi clauì pendentium. Sed & amplius de his funibus addo. Videri, quorundam iudicio, necessarios fuisse in omni fixione. Nam volunt manus ligatas, ne se subducerent ad ictum aut commouerent. tum etiam vt firmius & cum adminiculo pendêrent. deinde & alterum funem ad pectus, corpus ambiisse sub ipsas alas, eoque subleuatum hominem & attractum in summam crucem. Id porrò factum admotis vtrimque scalis. Eius sententiæ vir stirpe & moribus antiquis Ioannes Boisotus est, qui amicè hoc suggessit. Et sanè de scalis, apponere eas pænè necessarium videtur, vtique ad Erectam crucem. Quomodo alias subduxeris, aut fixeris? Etiam de funibus sunt quæ suadeant, præter ante dicta. vt Hilarius de Trinitate lib. x. Penduli in cruce corporis pœna, & colligantium funium violenta vincula, & adactorum clauorum vulnera. Iungit simul & funes & clauos, vt Lucanus. Etiam illud Christi vaticinium in Petri mortem, poscit funes. Ioannis cap. xix. Extendes manus tuas, & alius te cinget. Cinctio ista vinculorum in cruce est. Theophylactus: τὴν ἔπι τῶ σωμάτ' ἔκτασιν ἡ τὰ δεσμὰ δηλοῖ: Extensionem in cruce & vincula notat. Tertullianus in Scorpiaco: Tunc Petrus ab altero cingitur, cum cruci adstringitur. Atque ecce in tabula formam duplicem fixionis, pro duplici subductione.
units.tr: As for what he says, "the noose and the baneful knots": others print "of the guilty" [nocentum], and so it fits well with the chains by which the guilty were bound to the crosses. Yet in some written books it reads "recent" [recentes], and I would prefer that, and I believe it refers only to those who were hanged and had noosed themselves. The rest, about the cross: "the flesh pierced by showers, and the marrow baked by the sun," he said pointedly of bodies which (as I wrote in book 2, chapter 15) were left on the crosses, and withered and rotted in the air, so that birds would not tear them. Now "the iron not known to hands" will be clear to be the nails, if you emend it to "inserted" [Insertum]. For these too were sought for magical arts. Apuleius shows this in describing that funereal workshop, book 3: "Here noses and fingers, there the fleshy nails of the hanging men." But I add further about these cords. It seems, in the judgment of some, that they were necessary in every fixing. For they wish the hands to be bound, so that the body would not slip away from the blow or move; then also so that they would hang more firmly and with support. Next, another cord was wrapped about the chest and body, just beneath the armpits, and by this the man was lifted and drawn up to the top of the cross. This was done, moreover, with ladders placed on both sides. Of this opinion is John Boisot, a man of ancient stock and manners, who kindly suggested it. And indeed, about the ladders, it seems almost necessary to set them up, certainly for an upright cross. How otherwise could you have taken him down, or fixed him? There are also things about the cords, besides those said above, which support this: as Hilary in On the Trinity, book 10: "The punishment of a body hanging on the cross, and the violent bonds of the cords that bind, and the wounds of the nails driven in." He joins both cords and nails, as Lucan does. Also that prophecy of Christ concerning Peter's death calls for cords: John 21: "You will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you." That girding is the binding on the cross. Theophylact: "The extension of the body on the cross or the bonds indicates" [τὴν ἐπὶ τῷ σώματι ἔκτασιν ἢ τὰ δεσμὰ δηλοῖ]: that is, he indicates stretching out on the cross and the bonds. Tertullian in the Scorpiace: "Then Peter is girded by another, when he is bound to the cross." And so, in the table, behold the double form of fixing, corresponding to the double lowering.

units.la: Aeschylus μαχανίσης appellat, in Prometheo.
units.tr: Aeschylus calls it "mēchanēsēs" [μαχανίσης], in the Prometheus.

units.la: Tres repperit.] An & duas latronum transtulit, non cultus sed memoriæ caussâ? Videtur ex Suida, si tamen ex meo nunc sensu corrigendus. In voce φόρος inquit: κάτωθεν τὰ φόρς νεχωσμένοι ὑπὸ γῆν δύο σταυροὶ τῶν δύο λῃστῶν, καὶ Σινίου μύρῳ ἠλείψατο ὁ χρι-στὸς, καὶ πολλὰ ἕτερα σημεῖα φοεινὰ, τεθέντα μὲν ὡς δὲ ποσσαντίνε τῷ μεγάλῳ, ἀφανισθέντα δὲ ὑπὸ τῆ μεγάλῳ Θεοδοσίῳ: Nam puto legendum duo σαυροί. Qui vero fuerint σταυροὶ, siue duces duorum latronum? nec id sit idonei vllius sensus. Vertam igitur: Infra forum defossæ erant duæ cruces duorum latronum, & vasculum unguenti quo Christus unctus, & alia multa insignia, posita quidem à Constantino magno, sublata vero sub Theodosio magno. Admonitus postea per litteras sum à Ioanne Liuineio amico nostro, seriò & sine ambitione docto, vitium esse ab imperitia transscriptorum. qui cùm in autographo repperissent σρoῖ, quod compendiariâ illâ scriptura σαυροὶ erat, fecerunt flagitiosè σταυροὶ.
units.tr: "He found three." Did he also move the two crosses of the thieves, not for worship but for the sake of memory? It seems so from Suidas, if however it should be corrected by my present judgment. Under the word "phoros" he says: "Beneath the forum, buried under the earth, were two crosses of the two thieves, and the vessel of ointment with which Christ was anointed, and many other notable signs, placed indeed by Constantine the Great, but removed under Theodosius the Great" [κάτωθεν τὰ φόρς νεχωσμένοι ὑπὸ γῆν δύο σταυροὶ τῶν δύο λῃστῶν, καὶ Σινίου μύρῳ ἠλείψατο ὁ Χριστὸς, καὶ πολλὰ ἕτερα σημεῖα φοεινὰ, τεθέντα μὲν ὑπὸ Κωνσταντίνου τοῦ μεγάλου, ἀφανισθέντα δὲ ὑπὸ Θεοδοσίου τοῦ μεγάλου]. For I think we should read "two" [duo] for "crosses" [σταυροί]. But what the crosses were, whether the "leaders" of two thieves, is not clear, and no sense of any kind fits. I will therefore translate: "Below the forum were buried two crosses of the two thieves, and a little vessel of ointment with which Christ was anointed, and many other notable signs, placed indeed by Constantine the Great, but removed under Theodosius the Great." Afterwards I was reminded by letter by our friend John Livineius, a man learned in earnest and without ambition, that the fault came from the ignorance of copyists: who, finding in the autograph "σρoῖ," which in that abbreviated writing stood for "σαυροὶ," shamefully made it "σταυροὶ."

units.la: AD CAP. IX.
units.tr: On Chapter 9.

units.la: Ἀμεξήτω γὲ] Ita benè & doctè Franc. Nansius, cùm antea esset ὁμοξήτω. Et sanè clauì isti grandes: atque ita ipse Nonnus idemidemtidem σιδήρεα κέντρα appellat, Stimulos ferreos.
units.tr: Amexetō ge [Ἀμεξήτω γὲ]: so well and learnedly Franciscus Nansius, when before it had been homoxētō. Indeed these are large nails, and so Nonnus himself repeatedly calls them iron goads [σιδήρεα κέντρα].

units.la: Contrà tendunt alij, & suggerunt quaternos.] Atque ego, etsi negaui me decidere, pronior sum in hanc partem. In templis Græciæ hodie intellego passim Christum cruci affixum, disparatis pedibus sic pingi. Vidimus id ipsi Venetijs in gentis eius templo, tum & alibi in antiquioribus picturis. Audio & Treuiris clauum qui asseruatur, diserte in memorijs antiquis scribi clauum pedis dextri. Addo autem, Constantinum Imperatorem quosdam ex his clauis (id quoque multitudinem suader) inseruisse capiti statuæ quam suo nomine Constantinopoli posuit. Zonaras: Ὁ δὲ Ἰουστινιανὸς αὐτοκράτωρ εἰς οἰκεῖον ὄνομα τὸ ἀγαλμα (τὸ Ἀπόλλωνος) ἔσησε, τῇ κεφαλῇ τὰς τῶν ἡλίων ἐναρμοσάμενος οἱ τὸ σῶμα τῶν νυείων ... ταύτα τῷ σωτηρίῳ σταυρῷ.
units.tr: "Others, on the contrary, stretch them and suggest four." Although I have said I might decide otherwise, I am more inclined to this side. In the Greek churches today, I understand, Christ fixed to the cross with his feet apart is painted everywhere in this way. I saw this myself at Venice, in the church of that people, and elsewhere in older paintings. I also hear that at Trier the nail which is preserved there is clearly described in the old records as the nail of the right foot. I add, moreover, that the Emperor Constantine inserted some of these nails (which the multitude also suggests) into the head of the statue he set up at Constantinople under his own name. Zonaras: "The emperor Justinian set up the statue (of Apollo) under his own name, fitting to its head the rays of the sun ... with the saving cross" [Ὁ δὲ Ἰουστινιανὸς αὐτοκράτωρ εἰς οἰκεῖον ὄνομα τὸ ἀγαλμα (τὸ Ἀπόλλωνος) ἔσησε, τῇ κεφαλῇ τὰς τῶν ἡλίων ἐναρμοσάμενος ... ταύτα τῷ σωτηρίῳ σταυρῷ].

units.la: AD CAP. X.
units.tr: On Chapter 10.

units.la: Extensus ambas manus.] Proprium hoc Crucis, extendi. Itaque Euangeliorum vetus Gothica translatio (auctor Antonius Morillonus) vertit identidem Crucifigere, Βστracmen, quasi dicas extendere, & quidem proprie de pannis, quos in palis validisq; distendit fullo. Ea extensio ad manus maxime referetur. Artemidorus lib. 1. cap. LXXXVIII. Εἰ δέ τις ὑψηλὸς ὃς ὅτι πνεῖ... Si quis sublimis in locum quopiam saltet, in periculum & metum incidet. maleficus autem exiles, crucifigetur, ob altitudinem & manuum extensionem. Epictetus apud Arrianum, ab hac causâ comparat falsè eos qui in balneis se distendunt & lauandos fricandosq; præbent, cum crucifixis, lib. IIII. Dissertat. cap. XXVI. Ἐν τῷ βαλανείῳ ἐκτεινάμενος ... Vt in balneo exutus & teipsum distendens, ut solent crucifixi, fricēris hinc atque illinc.
units.tr: "Stretched out both hands." This is peculiar to the cross: to be stretched out. Hence the old Gothic translation of the Gospels (by Antonius Morillonus) repeatedly renders "crucify" by a Gothic word, Bstracmen, as if you were to say "stretch out"; and this is properly said of the cloths which the fuller stretches out on stakes and strong poles. That stretching refers chiefly to the hands. Artemidorus, book 1, chapter 88: "If anyone springs up to some high place, he falls into danger and fear; but a wicked man, on account of the height and the stretching of his hands, will be crucified." Epictetus, in Arrian, for this reason falsely compares those who stretch themselves out in the baths and let themselves be rubbed and washed with the crucified, book 4 of the Dissertations, chapter 26: "In the bath, stripped and stretching yourself out as the crucified do, you are rubbed this way and that" [Ἐν τῷ βαλανείῳ ἐκτεινάμενος].

units.la: Vestigium huius tabellæ extare audio.] Imò & video: ac misit ad me Dionysius Villerius vir veteri doctrinæ & mihi valdè amicus ectypon nummi Græcanici veteris, qui aureus asseruatur in monasterio Laetiensi in Hannoniâ, quem ecce habes. Inscriptio in eo est: Κόσμος τὸ λύτρον αἷμα τῆς θείας λόγυ: Mundi redemptio, sanguis diuini verbi. Missus is nummus cum aliis sacris donarijs est ab Henrico Imperatore, tunc Constantinopoli, anno Christi ∞. CC. VIII.
units.tr: "I hear that a trace of this tablet survives." Indeed, I see one too. Dionysius Villerius, a man of old learning and very friendly to me, sent me an impression of an ancient Greek coin, a gold one preserved in the monastery of Lobbes in Hainault, which you have here. It bears the inscription: "The redemption of the world, the blood of the divine Word" [Κόσμος τὸ λύτρον αἷμα τῆς θείας λόγου]. This coin was sent, together with other sacred gifts, by the Emperor Henry, then at Constantinople, in the year of Christ 1208.

units.la: {1} Non ex Cruci suo: sicut est in Coniuratione Hollandiæ.
units.tr: {1} Not "from his own cross", as it stands in the Conspiracy of Holland.

units.la: Ad cap. XI.
units.tr: On Chapter 11.

units.la: Περιαχθεὶς κύκλῳ τῷ ἀμφιθεάτρῳ. ] Id dicunt Circunduci; sicut Traduci, cùm ostentui dumtaxat per ora populi ducebantur, & sæpe alibi puniendi. Suetonius in Tito, cap. viii. Hos (Delatores) nouissimè traductos per amphitheatri arenam, partim subijci in seruos ac venire præcepit, partim in asperrimas insulas relegauit. Nescio an Martialis versus, qui iamdiu cubat in morbo, sic sanandus, lib. i. de hispisis Delatoribus & Titi facto: Turba grauis paci placidæq; inimica quieti, Quæ semper miseras sollicitabat opes: Traducta est titulis, nec cepit arena nocentes, Et delator habet quod dabat exsilium.
units.tr: "Led round the amphitheatre" [Περιαχθεὶς κύκλῳ τῷ ἀμφιθεάτρῳ]. They call this "led round", as also "traduced" (traduci), when men were led through the mouths of the people merely for display, and often punished elsewhere. Suetonius, in Titus, chapter 8: "These informers, lately paraded through the sand of the amphitheatre, he ordered partly to be made slaves and sold, partly to be banished to the most rugged islands." I do not know whether Martial's verses, which have long lain sick, can be cured in this way; in book 1, on the hissing informers and Titus' deed: "A heavy crowd, hostile to peace and to calm quiet, which always troubled wretched wealth: it was traduced with placards, and the arena did not take the guilty; the informer has what he gave, exile."

units.la: Titulis enim vult traductos Delatores. quomodo? nónne omnium vnus est communis? non hîc: quia additum, quos & quàm illustres quisque detulisset. Exempli causâ: Hic est Titius qui Camerinum detulit. Hic, qui Lateranum, & talia. In libris legitur: Traducta est Gætulis, in aliis, Tradita Gætulis: & emendarunt, Traducta est Gyaris, quod ego & ratio facilè refellant.
units.tr: For he means that the informers were paraded with placards. How? Is not the title one and the same for all? Not here, for it is added whom each had informed against and how illustrious they were. For example: "This is Titius, who informed against Camerinus. This is the one who (informed against) Lateranus," and so on. In some books it is read, "traduced to the Gaetulians"; in others, "handed over to the Gaetulians." Editors have emended it to "traduced to Gyarae", which I and reason easily refute.

units.la: Πίνακος αὐτὸν ἀφηρημένος. ] In tabellâ enim hæc talia scribi solent: sicut & Titulus Seruatoris. Cyprianus de montibus Sinâ & Syon: Pontius Pilatus impulsâ mente à Deo accepit Tabulam, & titulum scripsit tribus linguis: & in capite ligni clauis tribus Tabulam cum nomine regis Iudæorum confixit. Ex cuius verbis videtur etiam Tabulam non super lignum (ut multi repræsentant & pingunt) sed in ipso supremo ligno clauis fixam.
units.tr: "Deprived of his tablet" [Πίνακος αὐτὸν ἀφηρημένος]. For such things were usually written on a tablet, as also the title of the Saviour. Cyprian, on Mounts Sinai and Sion: "Pontius Pilate, his mind moved by God, received a tablet and wrote the title in three languages, and with three nails he fixed the tablet bearing the name of the King of the Jews to the head of the wood." From his words it seems that the tablet was fixed not over the wood (as many represent and paint it) but on the very top of the wood itself, with nails.

units.la: De quo more alii.] Inter eos P. Faber libris Semestrium; vbi & sparsim plura de Cruce, & quædam selecta atq. edecumata.
units.tr: "Others have discussed this custom." Among them P. Faber, in his books Semestria, where there is also a good deal scattered about the Cross, and some choice and polished matter.

units.la: Ad cap. XIIII.
units.tr: On Chapter 14.

units.la: Disparata hæc supplicia.] Notauit & publicè ante nos monuit Cæsar Baronius, vir sacra profanaq; doctus, in Martyrologio. Sed cur frangebant ijs, quos statim mortuos vellent, crura? An non causa in Plinio? Ille lib. xi. cap. xlv. notat in ijs vitalitatem esse: atque addit. Namque in ipsâ genus utriusque commissurâ, dextrâ lauâq;, à priore parte, gemina quædam buccarum inanitas inest: quâ perfossâ, ceu iugulo, spiritus fugit. Aliud autem est à fragio crurum, Exsecare crura: quod in Ammiani lib. xxi. leges, in oratione Iuliani: Quisque agmini cohærens incedat, sciens quod, si remanserit vsquam, exsectis cruribus relinquetur. Hoc enim proinde est, quasi dixisset, neruis aut suffraginibus incisis. Vetus sæuitia, & Annibali vsurpata in Romanos. Ennius: His pernas succidit iniqua potentia Pæni. Potentia Pœni, more Græco, est Pœnus. Livius de eaipsâ re, in clade Cannensi: Quosdam iacentes vivos succisis feminibus poplitibúsque inuentos fuisse. nempe ne attollerent se, & vt desolati morerentur. Vsurpatum est Tyrannis in Christianos. Sozomenus lib. i. cap. x. de Paphnutio & Maximo: quos, inquit, Μαξιμῖνος ἐν τοῖς μεταλλοις ἐργάζεσθαι κατεδίκασε, τὰς δεξιὰς αὐτῶν ἐκκόψας ὀφθαλμὰς, ἢ τὰς ἀριστερὰς ἀγκύλας ἀποτεμών: Maximinus ad opus metalli condemnauit, dextros eorum oculos excutiens & sinistri pedis suffragines abscindens. Eusebius ostendit aduri etiam solere, lib. viii. cap. xi. vbi quorundam meminit τὰς λαιὰς πόδας καὶ τῶν ἀγκυλῶν ἑαυτῶν ἀχρειωμένων: qui sinistris pedibus, circa poplites, ferro adusti, inutiles facti essent.
units.tr: "These punishments differ." Caesar Baronius, a man learned in sacred and profane matters, noted this publicly before us and pointed it out in his Martyrology. But why did they break the legs of those whom they wanted to die at once? Is there no reason in Pliny? He, book 11, chapter 45, notes that vitality resides in those parts; and he adds: "For in the very joint of each kind, on the right and on the left, at the front, there is a certain double hollowness of the cheeks, and when this is pierced, as through the throat, the spirit escapes." But it is different from the breaking of the legs, "to cut the legs" (exsecare crura), which you will read in Ammianus, book 21, in the speech of Julian: "Let each man, keeping close to the column, march on, knowing that if he remains behind anywhere, he will be left with his legs cut off." For this is just as if he had said, with the sinews or hamstrings cut. It is an old cruelty, also used by Hannibal against the Romans. Ennius: "Upon these the cruel power of the Carthaginian cut the hams." The "power of the Carthaginian" is, in the Greek manner, the Carthaginian. Livy, on this very thing, at the disaster of Cannae: "Some were found lying alive, with their thighs and hamstrings cut, so that they could not raise themselves and would die forsaken." It was used by tyrants against Christians. Sozomen, book 1, chapter 10, on Paphnutius and Maximus, whom, he says, Maximinus condemned to work in the mines, "gouging out their right eyes and cutting off the sinews of the left foot" [Μαξιμῖνος ἐν τοῖς μεταλλοις ἐργάζεσθαι κατεδίκασε, τὰς δεξιὰς αὐτῶν ἐκκόψας ὀφθαλμὰς, ἢ τὰς ἀριστερὰς ἀγκύλας ἀποτεμών]. Eusebius shows that they were also commonly burned, book 8, chapter 11, where he mentions some whose left feet, about the knees, were burned with iron and rendered useless [τὰς λαιὰς πόδας καὶ τῶν ἀγκυλῶν ἑαυτῶν ἀχρειωμένων].
