units.la: Liberi non immunes. Lego in Eusebij lib. vi. cap. xix. de Apollonio Martyre, cùm is sub Commodo Principe delatus esset vt Christianus, accusatori, ex lege, crura fracta fuisse. Verba huic rei: ὅτι μὴ ζῆν ἔξον ἦν, κατὰ τὸν βασιλικὸν ὅρον, τὰς τῶν Ῥωμαίων μηνυτὰς, αὐτίκα καταγνῶναι τὰ σκέλη: quoniam viuere nefas, iuxta legem Principis, talium delatores, statim crura ei fracta sunt. Sed cuius Principis haec lex tam commoda in Christianos? Non opinor ipsius Commodi. Nunquid M. Aurelij? de quo Tertullianus Apolog. cap. v. Qui sicut palàm ab eiusmodi hominibus (Christianis) poenam dimouit; ita alio modo palàm dispersit, adiectâ etiam accusatoribus damnatione, & quidem tetriore. Et quod ait de damnatione tetriore, possis vel ad Crurifragium istud referre: vel ad Viuicomburium, quo affici accusatores Christianorum iubet eiusce Principis epistola apud Onufrium in Fastis expressa.
units.tr: "Free men not exempt." I read in Eusebius, book 6, chapter 19, about the martyr Apollonius, that when he had been accused as a Christian under the Emperor Commodus, the accuser had his legs broken, according to the law: since, by the royal decree, such informers against the Romans were not allowed to live, they were at once condemned to have their legs broken [ὅτι μὴ ζῆν ἔξον ἦν, κατὰ τὸν βασιλικὸν ὅρον, τὰς τῶν Ῥωμαίων μηνυτὰς, αὐτίκα καταγνῶναι τὰ σκέλη]. But which emperor's law was so convenient against Christians? I do not think it was Commodus' own. Was it not that of Marcus Aurelius? Of him Tertullian says, in the Apology, chapter 5: "He, who as openly kept punishment away from such men (Christians), so in another way openly spread it abroad, adding condemnation also for the accusers, and that a grimmer one." And what he says of a "grimmer condemnation" you might refer either to this breaking of the legs, or to burning alive, to which the accusers of Christians are ordered to be subjected by the emperor's letter preserved in Onuphrius' Fasti.

units.la: AD CAP. XV.
units.tr: On chapter 15.

units.la: A Sole ac pluuiâ corrumpi. Exemplum huic rei etiam in libris sacris, vt Reg. ii. cap. xxi. Dedit eos (septem viros) in manus Gabaonitarum, qui crucifixerunt eos in monte coram Domino. Tollens autem Respha filia Aia cilicium substrauit sibi supra petram ab initio messis, donec stillaret aqua super eos de calo, & non dimisit aues lacerare eos per diem, neque bestias per noctem. Hoc de pluuiâ: de sole, in Artemidoro lib. v. Ἐδόξεί τις λαμπάδας ἀπὸ τῆς ἠλίας μὴ δυνασθῆναι ἀνάψαι, ἢ ἀπὸ τ᾽ ἡλίου ἀνάψαι, ἑαυτὸν ὠθῆσαι. ἢ καὶ τὸν τόπον τῷ ἡλίῳ πυρὶ ἐθάλγετο: Visus aliquis faces è foco non posse accendere, & àcalo eas accendit. crucifixus est. atque hoc modo igne caelesti concalefactus.
units.tr: Corrupted by sun and rain. An example of this also occurs in the sacred books, as at 2 Kings 21: He delivered them (the seven men) into the hands of the Gibeonites, who crucified them on the mountain before the Lord. But Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it for herself upon the rock, from the beginning of harvest until water dropped upon them from heaven, and she did not allow the birds to tear at them by day, nor the beasts by night. That is for rain; for the sun, in Artemidorus, book 5: Someone seemed unable to light torches from the fire, and lit them from the sun. He was crucified, and in this way was warmed by heavenly fire. [Ἐδόξεί τις λαμπάδας ἀπὸ τῆς ἠλίας μὴ δυνασθῆναι ἀνάψαι, ἢ ἀπὸ τ᾽ ἡλίου ἀνάψαι, ἑαυτὸν ὠθῆσαι. ἢ καὶ τὸν τόπον τῷ ἡλίῳ πυρὶ ἐθάλγετο]

units.la: IVSTI LIPSI AD LIB. III. NOTÆ. CAP. II.
units.tr: Notes of Justus Lipsius on Book III, Chapter II.

units.la: VERBERATVM patibulóque constrictum. ] Au ergo huc referas Dionis etiam illud lib. xlix. de Antonij sævitiâ in Iudææ regem Antigonum? τὸν δὲ Αντίγονον, inquit, ἐμαστίγωσε συνρῷ ᾧ προςδῆσας (ὁ μηδ' εἰςἄλλος βασιλεὺς ὑπὸ τῶν ῥωμαίων ἐπεπώνθη) ἡ μετὰ τῦτο καὶ ἀπέσφαξεν: Antigonum flagellavit cruci sine furcæ alligans (quod nemo alius rex à Romanis unquam passus erat) ac postea interfecit. Verba ita præferre videntur: nec abhorreat ab Antonij impotentiâ, ut seruiliter sævierit etiam in regem. Tamen verius puto ut capias vertasque Palum. Ut palo, inquam alligatus fuerit, solenni Romanis more, & tum securi percussus. Quod ipsum huic Antigono factum, etsi Dio non expressit, notavit Strabo, citante Iosepho (nam hodie non exstat) lib. xv i. Antiq. cap. i. Αντώνιος Αντίγονον ἢ Ιουδαῖον ἀχθέντα εἰς Αντιόχειαν πελεκίζει, ἡ ἔδοξε μὲν ἔως ὤρων τῶν ῥωμαίων βασιλέα πελεκίζει: Antonius Antigonum Iudæum Antiochiam perductum securi percutit. & visus est primus Romanorum securi subiecisse regem. Idem Plutarchus, in Antonio.
units.tr: Beaten and bound to the gibbet. Should you also refer here that passage of Dio, book 49, about Antony's cruelty toward Antigonus, king of Judaea? "He flogged Antigonus," he says, "binding him to a cross or to a stake (which no other king had ever suffered at the hands of the Romans), and afterwards put him to death." Antigonum flagellavit cruci sine furcæ alligans (quod nemo alius rex à Romanis unquam passus erat) ac postea interfecit. [τὸν δὲ Ἀντίγονον ἐμαστίγωσε σταυρῷ προσδήσας, ὃ μηδεὶς ἄλλος βασιλεὺς ὑπὸ τῶν Ῥωμαίων ἐπεπόνθει, εἶτα μετὰ τοῦτο καὶ ἀπέσφαξεν.] The words seem to suggest that Antony's savagery was so unrestrained that he behaved in a servile way even toward a king. Yet I think it more accurate to take and render the word as Palum. That is, he was tied to a stake, I say, in the customary Roman manner, and then struck with an axe. Strabo, cited by Josephus (for Strabo is no longer extant today), book 15, chapter 1 of the Antiquities, notes that this very thing was done to this Antigonus, though Dio did not state it. "Antonius beheaded the Jew Antigonus, brought to Antioch, with an axe; and he seemed to be the first of the Romans to have subjected a king to the axe." Antonius Antigonum Iudæum Antiochiam perductum securi percutit. & visus est primus Romanorum securi subiecisse regem. [Ἀντώνιος Ἀντίγονον τὸν Ἰουδαῖον ἀχθέντα εἰς Ἀντιόχειαν πελεκίζει, καὶ ἔδοξε μὲν ἐκ τῶν Ῥωμαίων πρῶτος βασιλέα πελεκίσαι.] Plutarch says the same in his Life of Antony.

units.la: Furcillæ, quibus homines suspendebant. ] Nec negauerim tamen, etiam ita accipi posse, quasi his furcillis sublatum erectumque ipsum patibulum, postquam homo in eo affixus. Non enim dicit in quibus, sed quibus suspendebant. Certum enim est sive funibus subduci in stantem crucem debuisse, sive furcis. nisi quis admotas arbitretur & scalas. Ἀπολογήματα hæc videantur, sed necessaria rei capiendæ.
units.tr: Little forks, with which men used to hang people up. I would not deny, however, that it may also be understood as if the upright beam itself were raised by these little forks once the man had been fixed on it. For he does not say in which but with which they hanged. For it is certain that they had to be hauled up on ropes into the standing cross, or else lifted with forks, unless someone thinks ladders were also brought up. These may look like apologies, but they are needed to grasp the matter.

units.la: Patens hæc tranuersáque pars sic dicta. ] Stricte & proprie inquam. Alias quis nescit totam crucem sæpe venire in hoc nomen? Sallustius vero modo acceperit haud dixerim, in loco viciato. Fragmentum est apud Nonium, e i v. Histor. In quis notissimus quisque aut malo dependens verberabatur, aut immutilato corpore improbi patibulo eminens affigebatur. Lego mutilato corpore: quia mos ille frequens Orientalibus, ut priusquam crucifigerent admutilarent, aut etiam per tormenta necarent. Exempla habes in hoc libro, cap. xii. & alibi. At illud improbi, qui reformandum ignoro. Tentaui olim in proris. An & improbe? quod sic compositum pro simplici, ut inante & talia, apud Tertullianum reperies Exhortat. ad Castitat. cap. x. An etiam improbè? vt sit corpus fuisse improbè mutilatum? Credo enim hæc narrasse de sævitiâ Mithridatis in Cyzicenos, quos terrâ marique obsedit.
units.tr: This spreading and transverse part is so called. I mean this strictly and properly. Otherwise, who does not know that the whole cross is often called by this name? But I would not say that Sallust used it in this way, in a corrupt passage. There is a fragment in Nonius, from book 4 of the Histories: Among whom each most notable man was flogged while hanging, or, with his body unmaimed, was fixed high on the gibbet as a wicked man. I read mutilato corpore, "with his body mutilated," because that custom was common among Orientals, to mutilate before crucifying, or even to kill by torture. You have examples in this book, chapter 12, and elsewhere. But I do not know how to correct improbi, "wicked." I once tried in proris, "on prows." Or perhaps improbe? Such compounds for simple forms, like inante and similar, you will find in Tertullian, On Exhortation to Chastity, chapter 10. Or also improbè, so that the body was wickedly mutilated? For I believe he is describing the savagery of Mithridates against the Cyzicenes, whom he besieged by land and sea.

units.la: Ad cap. v.
units.tr: On chapter V.

units.la: Facie quâ nostrum hodie patibulum.] Quæ sententia fuit Antonij Morilloni, viri summi futuri si diutius vixisset. Argumenta habebat (vidi & legi in epistolâ eius ad Lindanum, quam heredes adseruant) quòd id referret formam Iugi: ferre autem iugum, ignominia & quasi comminatio huiusce mortis. itaque illinc petenda forma. Amplius, Liuius ait lib. 1. Romanos spectasse furcis duodenos à terrâ spectacula alta sustinentibus pedes: eas furcas proclinantia utrimque ligna fuisse cum tertio transuersario supernè immissò, quod genus Capreolos Latini vocant, & nos hodie Schragas: ergo hanc esse faciem Furcæ. Tertiò Hebræos hodieque suum Tau sic pingere: cum eo autem comparari passim: tale igitur esse. Credo etiam addere (non firmiter nunc commemini, sed addi potest) Ausonium cum Φ, litterâ Græcâ Crucem comparare: at ea quoque istuc abit. Sed hæc sententia, etsi arguta, proba mihi non est ob multas causas, atque hanc unicam firmissimam, quòd refellunt spectiones & monumenta omnia antiqua, omnia inquam consensu. Quid Christianis nobis fiet, si ipsa imago crucis aliter ubique non pingenda solùm, sed manibus cottidie deformanda? At enim iugum tale olim. Ita, sed quid ad rem? militaris saltè ignominia illa fuit: & liberorum ea hominum, non seruorum, vt latura furcæ. De Liuio, nihil impedit Furcas nostro vulgarique more intellegi, quibus ligna transuersa iniecta, & super ea afferes, ad spectandum insistendumque. Fit & hodie, & olim primas domos sic erectas ex Posidonij sententiâ puto Senecam alibi tradere, & vti pariter voce furcæ. De Hebræis, verum est, sed hodiernis. Priscas eorum litteras alias & diuersiformes fuisse, periti eius linguæ atque ipse Hieronymus tradiderunt. Iam de Ausonij versu, is talis:
units.tr: In the shape of our present-day gibbet. This was the opinion of Antonius Morillon, a man who would have become outstanding had he lived longer. He had arguments (I saw and read them in his letter to Lindanus, which his heirs assert exists) that it referred to the shape of a yoke, and that to bear a yoke was a mark of disgrace and a kind of threat of this very death. Therefore the shape was to be sought from there. Further, Livy says in book 1 that the Romans watched from the ground twelve forks sustaining high platforms on their feet. These forks were, he says, two leaning pieces of wood on each side, with a third crossbeam placed above, which kind the Latins call capreoli ("little goats"), and we today schragen (trestles). So this was the shape of the fork. Third, the Hebrews to this day draw their Tau in this way, and it is commonly compared with the cross; therefore it is of this kind. I think I could also add (I do not firmly remember it now, but it can be added) that Ausonius compares the cross with the Greek letter Phi. But that too departs from this. But this opinion, though ingenious, does not please me, for many reasons, and this one most firmly: that all the ancient monuments and depictions, all of them without exception, refute it by their agreement. What would happen to us Christians if the very image of the cross were not only painted otherwise everywhere, but also deformed daily by our hands? "But there was such a yoke formerly." Yes, but what does that prove? That was at least a military disgrace, and it was inflicted on free men, not slaves, as the fork would be. As for Livy, nothing prevents us from understanding furcas in our ordinary and common sense, the forks on which transverse beams were laid, with planks above them, for watching and standing on. This is done today, and was done formerly, when the upper floors of houses were raised in this way. I think Seneca elsewhere, following Posidonius's opinion, relates this, and uses the word furcæ in the same way. As for the Hebrews, it is true, but of their present-day letters. That their ancient letters were different and of other forms, experts in that language and Jerome himself have handed down. Now, as to the line of Ausonius, it is this:

units.la: Et crucis effigie Palamedica porrigitur Φ.
units.tr: And by the likeness of a cross the Palamedean letter stretches out Phi [Φ].

units.la: Lectionem non muto, etsi alij libri proferunt gruis: nec id male. Sed esto crucis: verissimum est in nostrâ etiam formâ, quomodo? in cruce inquam vestitâ, & in quâ homo appensus. Vide faciem & pendula à ligno brachia, est hæc ipsa litteræ forma. Sed enim cum multa de Furcâ, & variè dubicque dixerim, hoc etiâ lubet. Quid si ipsa crux nostra vulgaris, vetus furca sit? Plutarchus cum temonis aut * iugi sustentaculo confert: certè in antiquis tiquis curribus tale reperio, qui sunt in Columnâ Traiani aut Antonini. Vide imagines. Dixeris hoc non falsò iugum sustinere aut sufferre, quà collo supero boum impositum est, & iugũ illi adnexum. Sed & ipsum temonẽ: (nam lectio Græca variat, vt dixi) hoc ipso, quòd ita in collo firmum, temonem attollit & prohibet à casu aut delapsu. An & ad Dionysij descriptionem aptari potest? potest dupliciter. Siue vt à pectore stipes longior & ipse temo propendeat: siue potius vt à tergo, quod res magis poscit. In figuris vide & cogita.
units.tr: I do not change the reading, though other books give gruis, "of a crane," and that is not wrong. But grant crucis: it is most true also in our form, how so? In the cross, I mean, clothed and on which a man is hung. See the figure and the arms hanging from the wood; this is precisely the form of the letter. But since I have said many things about the fork, and in varied and doubtful ways, this too I am pleased to add. What if our common cross is itself the old fork? Plutarch compares it with the prop of a pole or yoke; certainly I find such things on ancient chariots, which are on Trajan's or Antoninus's Column. See the pictures. You might say this rightly bears or supports the yoke, where it is placed on the upper neck of oxen with the yoke attached to it. But also the pole itself (for the Greek reading varies, as I said): by this very fact that it is so firm on the neck, it lifts the pole and keeps it from falling or slipping. Can it also be fitted to Dionysius's description? It can, in two ways: either so that a longer stake projects from the chest and the pole itself hangs down, or rather so that it is from behind, which the matter more demands. Look at the figures and consider.

units.la: Subiicio & formam crucifixionis quam imaginabatur & delineabat Morillonus.
units.tr: I add also a figure of the crucifixion as Morillon imagined and drew it.

units.la: Ad Cap. VII.
units.tr: On Chapter VII.

units.la: Impudicas ancillas sic puniri. Et est sane ignaua mors, & Fœminea etiam Panegyristæ dicta. Alteri manibus satellitum Britannorum guladomi fracta, & inuista fœminea mortis infamia, ut scilicet maluisse vir ferri amantissimus videretur laqueo perire quàm gladio. Victor postremam appellauit, vilissimamque in Maximiano : Pœnas mortis genere postremo, fractis laqueo cerucibus, luit.
units.tr: That unchaste maidservants are punished in this way. And it is indeed a sluggish death, and the panegyrist calls it a womanish one as well. The other, with his throat broken by the hands of the British soldiers at home, and with the unconquered infamy of a woman's death, so that the man, most fond of the sword, would have seemed to prefer to perish by the noose rather than the sword. Victor called it the last, and the most base for Maximian: He paid the penalty by a final kind of death, his neck broken by the noose.

units.la: Patibulum vulgò Furca dicitur. Quo ipso sensu inferiores Græci dixerunt φυλλίζειν in furcam agere, asperiore illâ litterâ mutatâ. Cedrenus in Iustiniano Rinotmetâ: Ἐν τῷ τείχει ἀνέζας ἐφέλκισεν. quod vertedum est, In muro omnes de furcâ suspendit. Docet Zonaras qui in ealpla re: Ἐν ξύλοις παρὰ τοῖς τείχεσιν ἀπώρησε : In lignis apud muros suspendit. Credo autem hanc Furcam primò non nisi dimidiatum Patibulum fuisse, id est, facie-adhuc aliquâ Furcæ : paullatim, & quo plures appendi possent, immutasse.
units.tr: The patibulum is commonly called a furca. In this very sense the later Greeks used the verb φυλλίζειν [phyllizein], "to put to the furca," changing the letter to a rougher one. Cedrenus, on Justinian Rhinotmetus, says: "Ἐν τῷ τείχει ἀνέζας ἐφέλκισεν" [En tō teichei anezas ephelkisen], which is to be rendered: On the wall he hanged them all from a furca. Zonaras, who writes about the same matter, says: "Ἐν ξύλοις παρὰ τοῖς τείχεσιν ἀπώρησε" [En xylois para tois teichesin apōrēse]: He hanged them on stakes beside the walls. I believe, however, that this furca was at first only a half patibulum, that is, still with some appearance of a fork, and that it was gradually altered so that more people could be hanged on it. ## Ad Cap. IX.

units.la: Ad Cap. IX.
units.tr: On Chapter IX.

units.la: Iniectis per crura funibus. An magis placet hic sensus, Funes ipsos per crura eorum traiectos & transmissos? Tale in Curtio lego Alexandrum vsurpasse in Batin quendam, lib. IIII. Per talos spirantis lora traiecta sunt, religatumque ad currum traxêre circà urbem equi. Id factum à rege exemplo Achillis, qui Hectorem sic foedauit, ut Curtius inibi notat. Sed tamen Ammianus Iniectos ait, non Traiectos: nec id supplicij credam vulgò visitatum.
units.tr: With ropes thrown around the legs. Or does the following sense please more: the ropes themselves passed and drawn through their legs? I read something like this in Curtius, where Alexander, in book IV, treated a certain Batis in this way: The thongs were drawn through the ankles of the man still breathing, and the horses dragged him, tied to the chariot, around the city. The king did this after the example of Achilles, who disfigured Hector in this way, as Curtius there notes. Yet Ammianus says iniectos, not traiectos; and I do not think this kind of punishment was commonly practised. ## Ad Cap. X.

units.la: Ad Cap. X.
units.tr: On Chapter X.

units.la: Moriturum in ipsis, non per ipsas. Præter exempla quæ dedi hoc rarum videatur in Philippo, de quo Eusebius in Chronico, anno xii Claudii: Philippus Apostolus Christi apud Hierapolim Asiæ ciuitatem, dum Euangelium populo nunciaret, cruci affixus, lapidibus opprimitur. Quasi in ipsa cruce lapidibus obrutus esset. Atque hoc quidem in vulgatis libris, in veteri & probo meo manuscripto vestigium non est horum verborum.
units.tr: About to die in them, not through them. Apart from the examples I have given, this seems rare in the case of Philip, of whom Eusebius writes in his Chronicle, in the twelfth year of Claudius: Philip, Apostle of Christ, at Hierapolis, a city of Asia, while he was announcing the Gospel to the people, was fixed to a cross and overwhelmed with stones. As if he had been buried under stones on the cross itself. Yet in the printed books this is so, while in my old and trustworthy manuscript there is no trace of these words.

units.la: AD CAP. XIII.
units.tr: AD CAP. XIII.

units.la: Viri fide digni asserunt. Inter eos eximius Theologus Alfonsus Ciacco, qui de signis Crucis nunc nuper accuratè scripsit.
units.tr: Men worthy of trust assert this. Among them the outstanding theologian Alfonsus Ciacco, who recently wrote carefully on the signs of the Cross.

units.la: Iam illa Amanis præalta. De quâ accipienda quæ in Codice Iustinianæo leguntur, De Iudæis & cælic. vbi scribuntur Iudai quodam festivitatis suæ solemni, Aman ad pœnæ quondam recordationem incendere, & sanctæ crucis adsimilatam speciem in contemptum Christianæ fidei exurere, atque id facere deinceps vetantur. Totidem pænè verbis in Cod. Theod. lib. xvi. tit. viii. Ex quibus vides Iudæos Amanis inimici sui mortem annuâ memoriâ repræsentasse, & in cruce suspensum cum eâ ipsâ combussisse: specie Amanem, re & mente Seruatorem & nostram crucem. Ideò meritissimò interdicti.
units.tr: Now that very high Haman. Concerning him must be understood what is read in the Justinian Code, On the Jews and the Caelicolae, where it is written that the Jews, at a certain solemn festival of theirs, were accustomed to burn Haman, in memory of his punishment, and to burn in contempt of the Christian faith a figure made to resemble the holy cross, and they are forbidden henceforth to do so. Almost in the same words in the Theodosian Code, book 16, title 8. From these you see that the Jews, by an annual memorial, represented the death of their enemy Haman and burned it together with a cross hung up: in appearance Haman, in reality and in intention the Saviour and our cross. Rightly therefore were they forbidden.

units.la: Nouus etiā orbis. In quo sanè hoc mirum, cruces repertas fuisse plurifariam in templis atque in sepulchris. De India Occiduâ loquor. Quâ origine aut fine? nescimus, nisi si iamtunc prouidus ille Deus exstare voluit omen & signum dominaturæ illic crucis.
units.tr: Also the new world. In which indeed this is remarkable: crosses were found in many places, in temples and in tombs. I speak of the Western Indies. By what origin or for what end? We do not know, unless perhaps that provident God wished even then to set up a sign and token of the cross that would rule there.

units.la: AD CAP. XIIII.
units.tr: TO CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: Edicto prohibitum manet. Atqui in Panegyricâ oratione, sanè diserta, quæ Theodosio dicta, mentio etiam crucis quasi licitæ & manentis. Et post hanc tu vocem, non illum in crucem tolli, non culleo insui, non discerpi in frusta iussisti. Et fieri sanè potest vt apud gentiles, & Christo aduersos, supplicium etiam mansérit, sicut de Slauis in Helmoldi Chronico scriptum lib. 1. In illis diebus Slaui quendam Danum suffixerunt cruci: In ignominiam scilicet diuinæ crucis.
units.tr: It remains forbidden by edict. Yet in the Panegyric, a very eloquent speech delivered to Theodosius, the cross is also mentioned as if it were still lawful and in use: And after this word, you ordered that he not be lifted onto a cross, not be sewn into a sack, not be torn to pieces. And it is quite possible that among the gentiles, and those hostile to Christ, the punishment also remained, as is written about the Slavs in the Chronicle of Helmold, book 1: In those days the Slavs fastened a certain Dane to a cross: namely, in dishonour of the divine cross.

units.la: AD CAP. XV.
units.tr: On Chapter XV.

units.la: In hoc vince. Nummis hoc pluribus expressum cernitur, atque etiam quibusdam vberius, In hoc signo vince. Sanè Christiani libenter appellarunt Signum dei, aut Christi, ipsam crucem, quasi Imperatoris illius tesseram aut vexillum. Iustinianæo Codice veratur, signum saluatoris Christi humi vel in silice insculpi. Quid, quod Græci interpretes sic legem Scævolæ accipiunt. XXXVIII. De aur. arg. mund. ? Fieri volo iubeóque signum dei ex libris centum. Accipiunt inquam,& reddunt Crucem. An verè? minimè. Scimus signum dei statuam esse apud Scævolam siue Solis, siue indigenæ cuiuspiam & familiaris dei. Sed pietas, nō error, Græcos eò traxit. Monuit super hac interpretatiuncula Petrus Oranus, iuris & litterarum consultus, & germanum in modum mihi amicus.
units.tr: In this conquer. This is seen expressed on many coins, and on some more fully: In this sign conquer. Christians have certainly been fond of calling the cross itself the "Sign of God" or "of Christ," as if it were that emperor's watchword or banner. In the Justinianic Code it reads: the sign of the Saviour Christ is to be carved into the ground or into flint. And what of the fact that the Greek translators take the law of Scaevola (38, On Gold, Silver and Pure Things) in this way? I wish and order a sign of God to be made from a hundred pounds. They take it, I say, and render it as "a cross." Truly? Not at all. We know that the "sign of God" in Scaevola is a statue of the Sun, or of some native and familiar god. But piety, not error, led the Greeks that way. Peter Oranus, a learned jurist and man of letters, who is a brother-like friend to me, pointed this out in regard to this little interpretation.

units.la: Ἐκ χρυσᾶ χεδλάσας σαυρόν. ] Quem suo ævo extitisse in Palatio Socrates asseuerat, Eccl. Hist. lib. i. cap. i. Τέτῳ ᾧ εἰδῆς τῷ χρησμῷ, καταστηναι ζει μὲν τὸ σαυρογιδὲς ζόπαιον, ὁ μέχρι νῦν ἐν τοῖς βασιλείοις φυλάττεται: Huic oraculo fidem habens, conficit simile illud cruci tropæum, quod usque nunc in regia seruatur. Idem Cedrenus: τότε σαυρὸν χρυσῆν χεδλάσας, ὃς ἔστι μέχρι τῆς νῦν: Tunc crucem aureaam efformans quæ etiam nunc exstat. Non opinor tamen hanc esse, de quâ Suidas: σαυρὸς δὲ τὸ δόρειον τῆς φόρας μέσης ἱστάσθαι, ὡς εἶδεν αὐτὸν Κωνσταντῖνος, χρυσέμπλασος ἐν τοῖς ἀπροπηλακοῖς σρογγύλοις μήλοις, ἔνθα καὶ αὐτὸς καὶ οἱ ἱερὶ αὐτῆ καθεωρῶντο χρυσέμβαφοι: Crux ad partem Borealem fori stabat, vt vidit eam Constantinus, auro illita in extremis rotundis pomis, vbi & ipse & filij eius conspiciebantur aurati.
units.tr: Out of gold, having shaped a cross [Ἐκ χρυσᾶ χεδλάσας σαυρόν]. Socrates asserts that this stood in the palace in his own age, Ecclesiastical History, book 1, chapter 1: [Τέτῳ ᾧ εἰδῆς τῷ χρησμῷ, καταστηναι ζει μὲν τὸ σαυρογιδὲς ζόπαιον, ὁ μέχρι νῦν ἐν τοῖς βασιλείοις φυλάττεται]. Trusting this oracle, he set up that cross-shaped trophy, which is kept in the palace even now. Cedrenus likewise: [τότε σαυρὸν χρυσῆν χεδλάσας, ὃς ἔστι μέχρι τῆς νῦν]: Then, shaping a golden cross, which still stands today. I do not think, however, that this is the one of which Suidas speaks: [σαυρὸς δὲ τὸ δόρειον τῆς φόρας μέσης ἱστάσθαι, ὡς εἶδεν αὐτὸν Κωνσταντῖνος, χρυσέμπλασος ἐν τοῖς ἀπροπηλακοῖς σρογγύλοις μήλοις, ἔνθα καὶ αὐτὸς καὶ οἱ ἱερὶ αὐτῆ καθεωρῶντο χρυσέμβαφοι]: The cross stood on the northern side of the forum, as Constantine saw it, gilded on its round knobs at the ends, where he himself and his sons were seen, also gilded.

units.la: gemmanti textus in auro Signabat labarum. ] Dixi ipsi velo nomen intextum: & poëta hic aperte. Tamen ex descriptione Eusebij, videbis & supra velum sæpe ex auro statui: & exempla in nummis vtriusque posituræ dedi. illustamen magis crebra. Ipsa Labari vox qualis? vereor vt peregrina, certè nouitia, & sub Traiani aut illud ævum nata. Vetustior Tertulliano, qui hodie extant, non commeminit. Gregorius Nazianzenus, doctus & fortis Orator, ait Καμάτων λυτήεον εἶναι, ἡ κατὰ ῥωμαίας ὀνομάζεσθαι: Laborum leuamen pausámque esse, & a Romanis sic appellari. Igitur à labore deriuauit, eò procliuius, quia ipsi Græci λάβωσεν scribebant. Sed nostri poëtę nónne corripiunt? Quomodo etiam pausam laboris, non aliâ additione, vox ea significet? Nec scio an non mos militiæ repugnet, quia certè sublato signo illo Imperatorio & conspecto, miles ad laborem ipsum & expeditionem, siue prælium etiam, vocabatur. Ita si lubet illinc ducere; magis sit, quòd eo viso miles laborem quoque videbat, & id acclamabat, Labor, labor: atque hinc nomen.
units.tr: Gemmed text in gold / Marked the labarum. I have said that the name was woven into the veil, and the poet here clearly says so. Yet from Eusebius's description you will see that the standard was often set up above the veil, made of gold; and I have given examples of both placements on coins. The first, however, is more common. What of the word labarum itself? I fear it is foreign, and certainly new, born under Trajan or in that age. The writers who survive today, older than Tertullian, do not mention it. Gregory of Nazianzus, a learned and forceful orator, says that it is a relief from toils and a pause, and is so called by the Romans. So he derived it from labor, all the more readily because the Greeks wrote it λάβαρον. But do not our poets shorten it? And how does that word mean a pause from toil without another addition? Nor do I know whether military custom does not contradict this, since surely when that imperial sign was lifted up and seen, the soldier was summoned to the labour itself, to the expedition, or even to battle. So if it is pleasing to derive it from there, it is rather that on seeing it the soldier also saw labor, and shouted it: "Labor, labor!" and hence the name.

units.la: Duæ litteræ Christi nomen exprimentes. ] Ita est, & conspicuæ sunt in Nummis. Ipsum etiam Chi solitarium, signabat Christum. In Antiochenorum dicteriis recensent Iulianus, Misopogone: Τὸ Χῖ, φασὶν, ἐδὲν ἀδίκησε τὴν πόλιν, ἐδ' ἐτὸ Καππα. & addit: ἡμεῖς δὲ ἐδιδάχθημεν ἀρχαῖζόμενάτων εἶναι τὰ χράμματα, δηλῶν δ' ἐθέλεω τὸ
units.tr: Two letters expressing the name of Christ. So it is, and they are conspicuous on the coins. The single Chi by itself also signified Christ. Julian, in his Misopogon, recounts the jokes of the Antiochenes: [Τὸ Χῖ, φασὶν, ἐδὲν ἀδίκησε τὴν πόλιν, ἐδ' ἐτὸ Καππα]: "They say the Chi and the Kappa did the city no wrong." And he adds: [ἡμεῖς δὲ ἐδιδάχθημεν ἀρχαῖζόμενάτων εἶναι τὰ χράμματα, δηλῶν δ' ἐθέλεω τὸ

units.la: Orat. III. in Iulian. λεγν τὸ μὲν Χριστὸν, τὸ δὲ Κωνσάντινον: Chi, inquiunt, & Kappa nihil iniuria intulerunt ciuitati. Nos autem didicimus initia nominum esse has litteras, & significare velle illud quidem Christum, hoc Constantinum. Ita Iulianus, qui has ipsas litteras è Labaro postea conatus remouere. Frustrà, & vicit nomen quod æternum vixit & vincet.
units.tr: Or. III. against Julian. [λεγν τὸ μὲν Χριστὸν, τὸ δὲ Κωνσάντινον]: Chi, they say, and Kappa did the city no wrong. We, however, have learned that these letters are initials, and wish to signify the one Christ, the other Constantine. Thus Julian, who afterwards tried to remove these very letters from the Labarum. In vain: the name which has lived forever has conquered, and will conquer.

units.la: Ω ξύλον μακαρισμὸν.] Verè, quia nos per illud μάκαρες. Atque ita προσκυνητὸν καὶ τίμιον, adorandum & venerabile, Imperator appellat nouella quintâ. Eaque caussâ vetitum in lapidibus sculpi, quæ in solo. Lex exstat in Codice Iustinianæo: & apud Paulum Diaconum sic Tiberius: Crucem domini quâ frontem nostram & pectora munire debemus, eam sub pedibus conculcamus? Tale & Synodus habita in Trullo, can. LXXXIII. Quamquam autem è pauimentis templorum remota, non etiam è tectis. Fulsit iam olim ibi, clarum certumque symbolum Christiani cultus. Nicephorus Gregoras lib. IX. in descriptione tempestatis quæ Constantinopoli: Τυνικαῦτα μέντοι πεσοντῶν ... πολλοὶ τῶν ἔτι τὰς νεὼς ἱδρυμένων ἐπὶ σιδήρᾳ σταυρῶν, ὑπενεγκεῖν ἐ δυνάμενοι τὴν τᾶ πνεύματος ἴαν: Tunc cecidere multa crucium, quæ templis imponi è ferro solent, sufferre non valentes vim venti.
units.tr: [Ὦ ξύλον μακαρισμὸν]: Truly, for through it we are blessed [μάκαρες]. And so the Emperor, in Novel 5, calls it [προσκυνητὸν καὶ τίμιον], "adorable and venerable." For this reason it is forbidden to carve it on stones that lie on the ground. The law stands in the Justinianic Code. Among Paul the Deacon's writings Tiberius says: "Shall we trample underfoot the cross of the Lord, by which we ought to fortify our brow and breast?" The Synod held in Trullo, canon 83, says something similar. Yet although it was removed from the pavements of temples, it was not removed from the roofs. There it long ago shone forth, a clear and certain token of Christian worship. Nicephorus Gregoras, book 9, in describing the storm at Constantinople: Then many of the crosses which are usually set up on churches in iron fell, unable to bear the force of the wind [Τυνικαῦτα μέντοι πεσόντων].

units.tr: I, Henricus Cuyckius, Dean of St Peter's at Louvain, Chancellor of the University, and censor of books appointed by the Pope and the King, testify that these three books on the punishment of the Cross, written by the most distinguished I. Lipsius, Professor of the University of Louvain, together with the notes added to them, contain nothing opposed to or departing from sacred and orthodox faith; moreover, I judge them full of varied learning and most worthy of the press. Louvain, 12th day before the Calends of December, 1592.

units.la: SVpplicij ferale genus, trabs hospita leti, Crux olim, & dirus sontibus horror erat. Tormentum iniisum, durum, execrabile lignum, Quo grauius nullum terra nouerca dabat. At postquam sata patre Deo, sata Virgine proles Diluit in celsa crimina nostra cruce: Victima pro seruis dominus, pro sontibus insons, Pro laesis medicus, pro grege pastor amans; Ilicet ex illo, Crux lux, mors vita, trophaeum Furca, decus probrum, poena medela fuit. Hospite pressa Deo tanti Crux numinis, olim Crux scelerum Nemesis, nunc scelerum vna salus. Hoc olim tam grande decus, tam nobile pignus Terra diu caeco texit auara sinu: Dum veluti postliminio tandem extulit illam, Et luci lucem Caesar habere dedit.
units.tr: The cross was once a deadly form of punishment, a hospitable beam of death and a dreadful horror to wrongdoers. It was a cruel instrument of torture, hard and accursed, and no more painful thing was ever brought forth by a stepmother earth. But after the Son, begotten of the Father God and born of the Virgin, washed away our crimes on the lofty cross, the Lord became a victim for servants, the innocent one for the guilty, a physician for the wounded, a loving shepherd for the flock. From that moment the cross became light, death became life, the gibbet became a trophy, disgrace became honour, and punishment became a remedy. Pressed down by the weight of God the Guest, the cross of so great a Divinity, once the avenger of crimes, is now the one salvation from crimes. This great honour and noble pledge the greedy earth long hid in its blind bosom, until, as if by right of return, it at last brought it forth again and let Caesar's light shine on the light.

units.la: Fallor? an & IVSTVS ceu Caesaris aemulus, atra Nocte laborantem tollit ad astra Crucem? O factum iuste: sic ridení lumina iustis, Inuidia iniustis lumina fracta dolent.
units.tr: Am I mistaken, or is it Justus who, like a rival of Caesar, lifts the cross from the black night and raises it to the stars? O deed done justly! Thus the eyes of the just rejoice in the light, while the broken eyes of envy grieve over the unjust.

units.la: RUDOLPHUS SECUNDUS diuina fauente clementia electus Romanorum Imperator semper Augustus, ac Germaniæ, Hungariæ, Bohemiæ, Dalmatiæ, Croatiæ, Sclauoniæ Rex, Archidux Austriæ, Dux Burgundiæ, Stiriæ, Carinthiæ, Carniolæ & Wirtembergæ, &c. Comes Tirolis &c. Nostro & Sacri Imperij fideli dilecto IVSTO LIPSIO gratiam nostram Cæsaream. Postquam inter alia, quæ DEVS immortalis hominibus liberali manu dedit dona, illustria inprimis illa & quasi diuina sunt, quæ in literis liberalibusque disciplinis consistunt, quibus scilicet homines non tantùm ab animalibus ceteris rationis expertibus, sed à rudi etiam & imperito hominum vulgo ita distinguuntur, vt tanquam Dij quidam splendescere in terris videantur: rem sanè præclaram sequeque dignam illi præstant, qui diligentem iis ipsis in literis ac disciplinis operam ponunt, præclarissimam verò & Reipub. vtilissimam, qui eas ita excolunt, vt aliorum mentí docendo, scribendo lumina præferant, eosque ex ignorantiæ tenebris quasi manu educant. Quos excitare, quos amare atque animare ad dignitatis nostræ munus, ad quod Diuino vocati beneficio, concessiúque sumus, inprimis pertinere existimamus. Cùm itaque ab iis, quorum nobis spectata fides, quíque iudicare de Literis possint, acceperimus, insignes te animi ingeniíque tui dotes tibi à natura insitas à primis temporibus ætatis tuæ ita literarum ac disciplinarum studiis excoluisse atque exornasse, vt olim iuuenilibus adhuc annis præclara florescentis minimeque vulgaris eruditionis specimina præbueris, dum obscura in antiquis scriptoribus loca, quæ quædam tanquam lustra erant, illustrasti, quæque in iis iniuria temporum depravata & corrupta fuerunt, restituisti, dum vetusta Latinæ antiquitatis rudera in nouam subinde structuram singulari artificio eleganter conuertisti: ad exquisitam adeò & raram doctrinam, quæ magnam de te apud doctos quosque viros opinionem excitarit, peruenisse, eamque variis abs te libris acri & graui cum iudicio scriptis atque in lucem editis ostendisse, vt in eo quod tam feliciter tractes scriptionis genere paucos tibi pares hodie reperire sit: iam verò matura te ætate virum, viro magis magisque digna & viris doctis grata ac Reipub. vtilia scribere, quæque à primis illis Romanis olim auctoribus scripta fuerunt, à mendis purgare, & lectissimos quosque ex Musarum hortis, in quibus assiduè versaris, flores colligere, concinnare, quibus Lectores mirificè recrees, & eorum pectus ad prudentiam, probitatemque informes: haud quaquam prætermittere voluimus, quin Reipub. ad quam hæc abs te ornamenta conferuntur, causa, Cæsareo te nostro elogio decorandum, & quamuis per te satis ipse animatus sis, animandum magis patrocinioque nostro defendendum pro benigna nostra in te suscipéremus voluntate. Quoniam verò lucubrationibus atque operibus tuis in lucem edendis, peculiarem te eligere velle Typographum, accepimus; Diplomate hoc nostro priuilegioque te & Typographum tuum aduersus quorumcunque fraudem, qui lucri causa, quod fieri solet, eadem excudere aut typis imitari forte velint, munitos cupimus. Quamobrem pro auctoritate nostra Cæsarea decernimus, statuimus, veramusque, ne quis Typographorum, Bibliopolarum, aut aliorum, qui librariam negotiationem exercent, eos libros, quos tu editurus es, quocunque modo, charactere, aut forma,
units.tr: Rudolph the Second, by the favour of divine clemency elected Emperor of the Romans, ever Augustus, and King of Germany, Hungary, Bohemia, Dalmatia, Croatia, Slavonia, Archduke of Austria, Duke of Burgundy, Styria, Carinthia, Carniola and Württemberg, etc., Count of Tyrol, etc., to our faithful and beloved IUSTUS LIPSIUS of the Empire, our imperial grace. Since among the other gifts which immortal God has bestowed upon men with a generous hand, those are especially splendid and almost divine which consist in letters and the liberal disciplines, by which men are distinguished not only from the other animals that lack reason, but also from the rude and unlearned common crowd, so that they seem to shine upon the earth like certain gods: indeed they render a notable service, and one worthy of that office, who devote diligent effort to these very letters and disciplines; but most distinguished and most useful to the commonwealth are those who cultivate them so that, by teaching and writing, they hold up lights to the minds of others and lead them, as if by the hand, out of the darkness of ignorance. We judge that it especially pertains to our office, to which we have been called and appointed by the divine benefit, to rouse, to love and to encourage such men. Since therefore we have learned from those whose trustworthiness is known to us and who are able to judge of letters, that from the earliest years of your life you have cultivated and adorned the natural gifts of your mind and talent, given you by nature, with the study of letters and disciplines, so that even in your youthful years you offered distinguished examples of a flourishing and by no means common erudition; while you cleared up obscure passages in the ancient writers, which were like thickets, and restored what had been corrupted and spoiled in them by the injury of time; while you elegantly turned the old ruins of Latin antiquity into a new structure with singular skill; that you have attained to an exquisite and rare learning, which has excited a great opinion of you among all learned men, and have shown it in various books written and published by you with keen and weighty judgment, so that today one can scarcely find few equal to you in the kind of writing in which you work so happily; and now that you are in mature age, a man ever more worthy of writing what befits a man, what is pleasing to learned men and useful to the commonwealth, and of purging from errors what the first Roman authors once wrote, and of gathering and arranging the choicest flowers from the gardens of the Muses, in which you constantly dwell, with which you wonderfully refresh your readers and shape their hearts toward wisdom and integrity: we have by no means wished to omit that, since these adornments you bring are for the benefit of the commonwealth, you should be honoured with our imperial commendation, and, although you are already sufficiently inspired by yourself, that you should be inspired further and defended by our patronage, in accordance with our kindly goodwill toward you. Moreover, since we have learned that you wish to choose a particular printer for publishing your labours and works, we wish you and your printer, by this our diploma and privilege, to be protected against the fraud of anyone who, for the sake of gain, as is customary, may wish to reprint these same works or imitate them in type. Therefore by our imperial authority we decree, establish and ordain that no printer, bookseller, or others who carry on the book trade, shall dare, within the boundaries of the Holy Roman Empire and of our hereditary kingdoms and dominions, for thirty years next following, to be counted from the first day of publication, without your consent or that of your heirs, to imitate in type, publish, print or sell those books which you are about to publish, in whatever manner, character or form, whether entire or any part of them: with this law added, that at least three copies of each book, as is the custom, be sent to our Imperial Chancery. If anyone, moreover, is found to transgress, violate or despise this our edict, we wish him to be punished, not only by being deprived of such books, which are to be claimed for you or your heirs wherever they are found, with the aid of the magistrate, but also by a fine of thirty marks of pure gold, half of which is to be paid to our Procurator of the Fisc, the avenger of fraud, and the other half to you or your heirs. We command all and each of our subjects and faithful beloved of the Holy Roman Empire, both ecclesiastical and civil, of whatever rank, degree or order they may be, especially those who are established in magistracy, or who in their own place or in the place or name of their superiors administer law or exercise justice, that they suffer no one to violate, scorn or neglect this our privilege with impunity; but if they find any stubborn persons, let them see to it that those persons are punished by the fine established by us and are restrained in whatever ways, unless they themselves wish to draw upon themselves our most grave indignation. This we confirm by this diploma, signed with our hand and fortified with the impression of our imperial seal. Given in our royal citadel at Prague, on the first day of the month of August, in the year of the Lord one thousand five hundred and ninety-two, in the seventeenth year of our reign as Roman king, the twentieth of our Hungarian, and likewise the seventeenth of our Bohemian.

Mandantes vniuersis & singulis nostris & sacri Romani Imperij subditis & fidelibus dilectis, tam Ecclesiasticis quàm Politicis, cuiuscumque status, gradus aut ordinis extiterint, praesertim vero iis, qui in Magistratu constituti, vel suo vel superiorum suorum loco aut nomine, ius dicunt, iustitiamue exercent, ne quemquam hoc Priuilegium nostrum impunè violare, spernere aut negligere patiantur: Sed, si quos contumaces compererint, constituta à nobis multa, eos puniri & quibuscunque modis coërceri curent, ni & ipsimet grauissimam nostram in se conuertere indignationem velint. Id quod hoc Diplomate, manu nostra subscripto, & Caesarei nostri sigilli impressione munito, confirmamus. Datum in arce nostra Regia Pragae, die prima mensis Augusti. Anno Domini Millesimo, Quingentesimo Nonagesimo secundo. Regnorum nostrorum Romani decimo septimo, Hungarici vigesimo, & Bohemici itidem decimo septimo.

Let no other elsewhere, besides you, by my wish or command, under the law which the great Caesar has laid down.

units.tr: By the royal privilege it is provided that no one may, for eight years, print in any way the three books of Justus Lipsius, De Cruce, together with the Notes, without the consent of Johannes Moretus, printer of Antwerp, nor bring in from elsewhere, sell, or keep for sale copies printed elsewhere, throughout all the territories of the king. Anyone who acts otherwise will be punished by confiscation of the books and a heavy fine, as is set out more fully in the letters issued at Brussels on 23 June 1593.
